articles.text:
SOCIAL CHAR A.CTERISTICS OF
LONDON LIFE,

BY "SCOURGE."

No. lI.—THE LOAN OFFICE SYSTEM.

THE "social evils" abounding in this metro-
polis- are in number legion, but some of. the
most prominent have been lately attacked by
the Christian, social, sanitary, and moral re-
former, with more or less success. Prostitu-
tion—that hideous social evil—has been taken
in hand, and many of its unfortunate victims
rescued by the interposition of Christian and
philanthropic ladies and gentlemen. The
West End night house System has also been
much, checked of late by the aroused activity,
of the, parish and police authorities. The un-
wholesome and wretched state of the dwell-
ings of- the labouring population, a fruitful
source of crime and disease, has engaged the
serious attention of the sanitary reformers.
The ignorance and destitution of thousands of
our juvenile population has been met, by, the
institution of ragged schools and reformato-
ries'; while the vice of. drunkenness has been
held in Check by the extrtions and examples
of the temperance reformers. There is, how-
ever, one social evil in this
.metropolis yet un-
checked and unattended to, and which has
swelled to most gigantic proportions, and is in
its effects most disastrous to working men and
small and struggling tradesmen—an evil which
has been the cause of breaking up many thou-
sand working men's homes, augmenting to an
-immense extent the business of the insolvent
and county courts, and filling the debtors'
prisons with its - unfortunate victims. This
social evil is the Loan Office System.
• An honest and well regulated loan office,
conducted by a company of respectable men of
Capital, with equitable charges, is, no doubt, a
necessity of the times, and a great convenience
to many persons whose pecuniary affairs may
require temporary aid; but, unfortunately,
offices of this description are the exception,
not the rule. It is estimated that there are
about 600 roan offiees in London, excluding
those connected with insurance and building
companies, (which are usually well conducted)
and that of these there are not, at the most,
more than one-third which possess the slight-
est claim to honesty or respectability. Two-
thirds_ of these loan societies are in the hands
of adventurers, destitute alike of capital, cha-
racter, or principle, trading under false names
and with false pretences. • ,
These societies .may be divided into three.
classes, and their modus operandi may be
shortly described .as follows :—ln the first class
a broken-down "betting man," or commission
agent," hirea an office in a leading thoroughfare,
and by the aid of advertisements, handbills,
and window-cards, announces the advent of a
loan company with a high-sounding and phi-
lanthrophic title, guaranteeing an "immediate
advance without delay," on the most "equit-
able terms," but taking care, at the same time,
to impress upon intending borrowers that no
money paid for inquiry can be returned, or
reason given why the loans applied for may
not be granted, thus avoiding becoming amen-
able N the law for obtaining money under false
pretences. Customers are soon attracted by
the specious invitation, and inquiry fees are
paid in; but no inquiries are instituted, or
Only in one or two instances, to keep up ap-
pearances for a time. It is needless to say
that. no bona fide loans are ever made. A few
parties in collusion with the "company" attend
stated nights with their "loan books" to
pay in the instalments on their supposed loans,
so as to make an appearance of business; and
after the neighbourhood has been well drained
of "inquiry fees," the office is suddenly closed,
and the same game is repeated with more or
less success in another locality.
The " societies" in the second class, are
composed generally of men who, possessed of
a little ready cash, and not being particular as
to the manner in which they may add to it,
whether wrung out of the hard earnings of
the workman, or the small profits of the needy,
trudesman, invest it in these societies, appoint-
,
ing as the manager a sharp, unscrupulous man,
supported, in the background, by a low and
disteriutable attorney, ready to undertake any
dirty work. This office is opened in a populous
'working neighbourhood, the " company " is
puffed in all directions, the most liberal terms
are offered, and a large business is soon got
together. But even these offices do not grant
above one-fourth the loans applied for, them-.9.uiry fees for the other three-fourths going
into the pockets of the "company," very fre-
quently consisting only of one man, who fills
the offices of director, manager, inquirer, and
secretary; in short, who embodies in his own
person "the company." The slightest default
in the instalments made on the loans granted
involves , fines: and charges of a multifarious
description, often a,mOunting-to more than the
whole of the instalment, and the lawyer in the
background Is at once brought into operation
to sue for the entire _ amount of the loan un-
paid, the "manager" taking care at the time
the loan is granted to have a promissory note
for the full amount, " payable on demand,"
signed by the borrower and his sureties. Not
only is tfie borrower in default sued, but his
sureties also, whatever their number, and, then
the costs are run up
to double and treble the
.mount of the debt. This is owing to the
arrangements made in almost all these societies
between the, manager and the attorney, where
the attorney is himself, not a partner in the
"company." Should the action fail, the
manager agrees to pay him only costs out of
pocket," but should it succeed, then the costs
are divided between the attorney and the
"company." It is, therefore, manifestly the
interest of both parties to issue as many writs
as possible, and so to enhance the costs. Cases
are of daily Occurrence in, which, on an unpaid
balance of ..t5 Off a £lO- loan, to which there
have been three
.parties—the borrower and two
sureties—three writs are issued at a cost of
£2 Bs. each, or £7 4s• in the whole. These
societies exist, not upon the legitimate profits
O n the loans granted, but upon inquiry fees
and law costs— in other words, On a system
of legalised fraud and extortion, thriving and
fattening upon the poverty and misery of their
sustomers.

. -- •
.however, in the third class that the
largest amount of mischief results. These
fc societies".,,generally. consist of a, Jew bill dis-
counter ana a "black sheep" lawyer, and woe
to those who- get into their clutches. Their
mode of obtaining victims is similar , to, that
pursued by their colleagues in the other two
classes, but the results of_ the connection are
muCh more.fittal. . Having inveigled the victim
to their den, they. speedily find out whether he
IS wOrth ~ potder and shot," . whether any fa-
tare plunder can-be tgo ,from his present neces-
sities; and then measures are taken accordingly.
The inqi4ry kee is' first demanded, and the loan
promised in a certain time, on the faith of
which the unsuspecting and confiding borrower
Makes certain arrangements. Having got the
v,ictina secure, the screw is then put on; ex-
cuSes are made from time to time as to short-

No. 55.

ness of money from previous loans not having
been repaid, until the needy borrower, brought
almost to the verge of ruin, with the prospect
of being compelled to break the engagements
he has made, on which much may depend, and
driven to desperation, agrees to pay an enor-
mous interest, in many cases amounting from
50 to 60 per cent., for the use of the money.
The "society," knowing he will be unable to
meet the payment of both principal and in-
terest, bide their time, and on the first favour-
able opportunity come down with the strong
arm of the law upon the victim, who, glad at
any price to extricate hipiself, consents to more
extortionate terms even than before, thus plac-
cing.himself still further within the power of
the "society." Tihs is repeated, until finding
there is nothing more to be squeezed out of the
dupe, and having already obtained from him, in
the shape of' interest and costs, three or four
times the amount of the loan they originally
granted, they drop him, like a sucked orange,
and consign him to Whitecross Street and the
Bankruptcy Court.
There is competition even in rascality. To
draw custom to these. disreputable loan shops
the practice has lately sprung up of advertising
loans to be granted "upon the personal se-
curity of the borrower only, without any sure-
ties, at a small add.itional rate of interest."
Those who are so foolish as tth suppose that
money lenders will really part with their cash
upon these liberal terms, and apply for loans,
are, of course, cajoled out of a larger inquiry
fee for "additional risk," but the reply, always
sent by written circular,. is invariably as fol-
lows :—" Your application is declined, the in-
quiries not being satisfactory." Not one ap-
plication in a thousand is granted on these
terms, and the advertisement is only a bait to
catch a larger inquiry fee.
Having touched upon the working of this
huge "social evil," and noticed some
,of its
effects, the question naturally arises, cannot
some remedy be found for this great evil? The
, reply to this question will be in the affirmative,
but the mode in which ttiis can be accomplished
must form the subject of another article.

THE' EAST LANCASHIRE' CENTRAL

RELIEF FUND.

An Executive Mooting was hold on Monday evening,
Oct. 23, at the Committee Rooms, Padiham.—Present :
The Rev. E. A. Verity, B.D. (President), Messrs. John
Haworth and James Heap (Vice-Presidents), James
Denbigh, James Caltow (Burnley), George Hargreaves,
H. Whitehead (Habergham), Joseph Peacock (Secre-
tary), William Wilkinson ("Treasurer), &c., &c., &c.
The minutes of the previous week were confirmed.
The Chairman called the attention of the meeting to
the beneficial effects which had resulted from the estab-
lishment of the Operatives' Central, ensuing in the
more generous treatment of the poor throughout the
entire district. The Secretary then read the report,
after which the following resolution was passed, "Chat
the Executive while acknowledging with their best
thanks the services of Mr. Potter, and the proprietors
of the BEEHIVE would esteem it a further favour if
they will kindly send forth with their next issue, if
possible, a collecting bill for the purpose of soliciting
subscriptions from their numerous readers, owing to
the urgency of the distress.' Grants were then made
to Burnley, Habergham, and Padiham, the applications
from which localities were very numerous, and the
Local Committees very pressing. The Chairman
regretted to see that the working classes of Birming-
ham were collecting £2OO weekly and sending it else-
where. Mr. Denbigh proposed that a resolution
should be transmitted to that town calling the attention
of the working men to the fact. The resolution was
then passed. Another resolution was passed thanking
those editors and journalists who had kindly promised
their aid and assistance. Several letters were read by
the Secretary; one from a London clergyman pro-
mising collections, also from provincial trades' secre-
taries. The funds are weekly improving, and much
more called for. -

articles.title: LONDON, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1862.

MR. COBD_EN AT _ROCHDALE.

On Wednesday evening Mr. Cobden addressed a
large meeting of his constituents at Rochdale, at Mr.
Tathem's machine shop, in the neighbourhood of the
railway station. The room, which will hold about
3,000, was densely crowded. The Mayor of Rochdale
presided. There were also present the mayors from
several of the neighbouring towns, a large proportion
of the principal manufacturers, and a mass of opera-
tives. The proceedings having been opened by the
Chairman,

Mr. H. Kelsall moved, and Alderman Liveiey se-
conded, the following resolution :—"rhat this meeting
views with dismay the enormous public expenditure of
the country, which unnecessarily increases the burden
of the people, is subversive of their best interests, and
perilous to constitutional government. This meeting
is also of opinion that comprehensive measures of
parliamentary reform would secure a more faithful re-
presentation of the people, and are absolutely essential;
and, remembering the pledge with regard to financial
and parliamentary reform Fiven by the present
ministry prior to their secession to power, calls upon
them to carry out those pledges or to retire from office.'
Mr. Cobden then rose amidst the most enthusiastic
cheering, to address the meeting. Having taken a
general review of the State of Europe, he proceeded to
treat at some length of the American question. He
said :—We are told very frequently at public meet•
.
ings that we must recognise the South; but that re-
cognition of the South always coupled with another
object, viz., to obtain the cotton you want: because, if
it were not for the distress brought on us by the civil
war in America, I don't think humanity would induce
us to interfere any more than it does in any other war
in other parts of the world. And now let us try to
dispel this floating fallacy, which has been -spread
through the country by interested persons. Your re-
cognition of the South would not give pu cotton;
but the recognition of the South in the minds of par-
ties who use that term is coupled with something more.
There is an idea of going and interfering by force to
put an end to that contest, in order that the cotton
may be set free. If I were President Lincoln,
and found myself rather in a difficulty on account
of the pressure of taxation, or on account of
a discord of parties in the Federal ranks—and
if I wsisted to see the whole population united as
one man ready to make me a despot—l should wish
nothing better than for England or France, or both
together, to attempt to interfere by force in the
quarrel. Their interfcrence in this case would only
do harm; and in the end you would not get your
cotton. Even if you could, what price would you pay
for it? I know something of the way in which money
is voted in the pouse of Commons for warlike arma-
ments, even in a time of peace, and I venture to say
that it would be cheaper to keep all the population
engaged in the cotton manufacture—ay, to keep them
on turtle, champagne and venison—than to send to
America to obtain that cotton by force of arms.
(Laughter and cheers.) It would involve you in a
war; and six months of a war would cost more money
than would be required to maintain this population
comfortably for ten years. (Cheers.) Now, gentle-
men, what we should endeavour to do, as the result
of this war, is to put an end to that system of warfare)
which brings this calamity home to our door, by mak-
ing such alterations in the maritime law of nations
which affects the rights of belligerents and neutrals as
will render it impossible in future for innocent non-
combatants—neutral here—to be made to suffer almost
as much as those carrying on the war there. (Cheers.)
The Hon. member concluded a speech which lasted
an hour and fifty minutes by contending that we had
not an honest state of parties in Parliament. We have
(said Mr. Cobden) a Premier who professes to lead the
Liberals, and he is about the staunchest Tory in the
House. As a consequence, he receives the support of
the antiquated and incorrigible Tories, because he
spends more money, and obstructs •reform more
effectually, than if they themselves were in office. He
(Mr. Cobden) believed we were now spending five
millions more annually than we should if we had a
Tory Ministry at the head of aflairs. If his voice was
not lost during the present winter he would certainly
protest against the present position of political parties
early next session. He believed, however, that the true
solution of this unsatisfactory state of things was only
to be found in a reform of the representation.
The hon. gentleman resumed his seat amid enthu-
siastic cheers, and the resolution was put and carried
unanimously.
A second resolution, expressingapproval of Mr. Cob-
den's parliamentary conduct, having been adopted, the
proceedings, which throughout were marked by great
enthusiasm, closed. •

Ma. BOUVERIE, M.P., AND HIS CONSTITUENTS.—Mr.
Bouverie, M.P., addressed his constituents, at Kil-
marnock, on Monday. The right hon. gentleman, in
a comprehensive speech, reviewed recent legislation,
and expressed his approval of the French treaty and
the financial policy of the Government. He entered
into lengthy explanations in reference to the expendi-
ture. As to Italy he expressed his opinion that the
time was not far distant when the Emperor of the
French would see his way to the emancipation. of
Rome. He then referred to America, and reviewed its
wonderful progress up to the time of' the war. Ad-
mitting that it was strange to find people in England
sympathising with the Southerners who were the
upholders of slavery, he pointed out that the essential
principle of the American constitution was the right of
a people to cheose its own form of Government. lie
expressed a hope that the war would not be of much
longer duration. A vote of thanks was given to him
at the close of his speech.
THE FRIGHTFUL DEATH OF THE ALLEGED SO3l-
- Tuesday afternoon Mr. J. Humphreys
held an inquiry at the London Hospital, respecting the
death of Robert May, aged 36, who lost his life under
the following shocking circumstances: Mr. A.
Kennedy, 25, Camomile-street, City, shipping agent,
said that deceased was his cousin, and was a farmer in
the neighbourhood of Belfast. On last Tuesday night
deceased and Mr. Jones arrived in London en route for
New Zealand. They paid for their passage on board a
vessel that had since sailed. Mr. R. Spill, boarding-
house keeper, of 40, High-street, Shadwell, said that
deceased and Mr. Jones had lodgings at llis house, and
they returned home at eleven o'clock on Wednesday
night in a state of intoxication. Deceased boasted that
they had drunk 100 glasses that day. Deceased had to
be assisted to bed, and he was so drunk that he took a
lighted cigar from witness's mouth and placed the
lighted end in his own. The following morning he was
discovered lying in the yard, in an insensible condition,
having evidently fallen headlong from a window forty-
five feet high. He was forthwith removed to- the
hospital. Witness did not know that deceased was
a somnambulist. A police sergeant, 21 IC, said he found
that deceased had contrived to force hitnself through the
window, which was only eighteen inches in width, hav-
ing previously carefully removed the looking-glabs to a
place of safety. Mr. Jackson, house surgeon, satd that
deceased had his skull fractured and his arm and leg
broken. He died from the injuries received. The jury
returned a verdict, 'That deceased died from certain
injuries, but there was no evidence to show how they
, were indicted.'

THE HACKNEY CARRIAGE ACT.

CABDRIVERS' DISTRICT MEETINGS.

The general Of -delegates appointed by the
cabdrivers in the metropolitan districts to prepare a
revision of the present Hackney Carriage Act, having
so far completed their labours, meetings have been
called in the various districts during the present week
to receive and confirm, if approved, the minutes of the
delegates. To these meetings the proprietors in the
districts have been specially invited, and many pro-
prietors have attended and generally expressed their
approval of the proceedings of the men.
SOUTH LONDON DDITUICT.—This district held its
meeting on Monday evening last, at eleven o'clock, at
the Cabmen's Club Rooms, Francis-street, Newington,
Mr. Cocke in the chair. Messrs. Pickering, Emmett,
Farmer, and other proprietors were present, and there
was a good attendance of drivers. Mr. Cooke having
explained the proceedings of the delegates, and the
objects of the meeting, in a few appropriate remarks,
Mr. Towel' proceeded to read the minutes Of the alte-
rations and additions proposed by the delegates to be
made in the present Hackney Carriage Act, comment-
ing upon and explaining the bearing of each, seriatim.
At the conclusion of Mr. Towell's remarks, considerable
discussion ensued, and various questions asked rela-
tive to the minutes, which were severally replied to by
Messrs. Smith, Towell, Wellman, and the Chairman,
the delegates for the district. In the course of the dis-
cussion it was mentioned by Mr. Smith, the Secretary
of the South London Cabmen's Club, that the Surrey
Hackney Carriage Proprietors had resolved to apply to
the club when they wanted drivers, Instead of engaging
them in the yard. This he considered would be bene-
ficial to all parties—to the proprietors, the club, and
the men; and the latter would see the necessity of
joining the club, which they could do, and obtain all
the advantages of a comfortable room to sit in while
waiting for employment, the use of the newspapers
and a library, and many other advantages, fur the
sum of 6d. per quarter, as any man could join the
club without becoming a member of the benefit society
connected with it. This announcement appeared to
be well received by the meeting. The following re-
solution was then unanimously adopted :—"That this
meeting is of opinion that the minutes of the delegates,
now read and explained, are what is required for the
improvement of the Hackney Carriage Act, and do
pledge itself to use every exertion to obtain the same,
and hope to receive the assistance of the proprietors in
so doing.' Mr. Smith then made a statement of the
receipts and expenditure connected with the move-
ment in that district, after which a collection was made
in aid of the same. The meeting broke up at two
o'clock.

EAsTERN COUNTIES RAILWA.Y.—A crowded meeting
of the drivers connected with the Eastern Counties
Railway was held on Thursday morning, at one o'clock,
at the Crown and Sceptre, James-street, Globe-road,
Mile. end. Mr. T. Mites occupied the chair, and Mr.
Smith acted as vice-chairman. The Chairman opened
the business by reading a letter from Mr. Clark, the
extensive cab proprietor and contractor with the
Eastern Counties Railway, employing, about ninety
drivers, regretting his inability to accept the invitation
he had received to attend the meeting, but fully sym-
pathising with its object. The Chairman then went on
to give an account of the delegate meetings that had
been held, and read the minutes at length, which .
ap-
peared to give general satisfaction. A discussion ensued
upon one or two of the minutes, more particularly re-
lating to that which took away the power of the pro-
prietors to summon the drivers before a magistrate and
have him committed to prison for not paying the agreed
earnings upon the cab, and referring the proprietors to
the County Court for redress. Some little confusion
took place by Mr. Lewis and one or two of the drivers
insisting upon introducing the question of signing,'
which they strongly denounced, and which they
thought ought to have been condemned by the dele-
gates. The Chairman, however, restored order by an-
nouncing that he would mention the subject at
the next meetinc, of the delegates. A resolution
was then agreed to unanimously, as follows :
That this meeting approve generally of the minutes
adopted by the delegates, and hereby pledges itself to
support them in all legal measures they may take to
procure a revision of the Hackney Carriage Act.'
Another resolution thanking the delegates for their
services was adopted, b.nd a liberal collection having
been made in aid of the funds for carrying on the
agitation, the meeting broke up at 4 o'clock in the
morning.
WESTMINSTER DISTRICT.—A meeting of this district
was held on Thursday night at the Cabmen's Club
Rooms, Wilton-road, Pimlico, Mr. Wise in the chair,
when the minutes having been read, were confirmed
and a vote of thanks given to the delegates for their
exertions. _

The Paddington and East London districts met
last evening, and the .11ghbury district on
Monday evening.
Next week we shall publish the delegates' minutes
at full length, with any alterations that may be made
at the district meetings.

DEATH THROUGH THE FALLING OF A TELEGRAPH
WIRE DURING THE LATE GALES.—An inquest was
opened late on Monday night by Mr. Carter, at the
William the Fourth Tavern,
_Camberwell New-road,
relative to the death of Mr. M. Jacobs, aged 23, who,
it was alleged, lost his life through the fall of part of
the telegraph wires crossing the Blackfriar's-road near
the bridge. During the height of the gale on Thurs-
day one of the wires suddenly gave way and fell
partly across the road. The wind again carried it
upwards, and it was twisted with considerable violence
round the throat and body of the deceased, who was
seated on the top of an omnibus which was passing at
the time. Mr. Jacobs was hurled into the road, and
on being picked up was found to be insensible. He
was conveyed home, but never recovered conscious-
ness' and expired from an injury to the skull which
affected his brain. As no one, however, attended who
distinctly saw the wire touch the deceased, under the
direction of the coroner the inquiry was adjourned to
a future day.
IRISH MOTS AT KNU'FSFORD.--MUCh apprehension
has been caused lately in Knutsford by the formidablel
appearance of the Irish. On Sunday evening, the
19th inst., several Englishmen were talking together, '
when they were attacked by a large gang of Irishmen
and women, and one of them was severely hurt with
bricks, &c., which the Irish used very freely. On
Thursday night last the Irish again turned out in
strong force, and armed with shillelaghs, marched in
couples down King-street, where they formed two
companies, one taking King-street and the other Prin-
cess-street, and several persons were assaulted by
them. At one o'clock on Sunday morning a riot
occurred, in which sticks and stones flew in all direc-
tions. Several rioters were, apprehended, and police-
constable Broome was hurt, though not seriously.
Five rioters were brought before Sir H. Mainwaring
on Monday, and were remanded until eleven o'clock
On Thursday; three were allowed bail. Sir H.
Mainwarint,n., addressing Sergeant Morgan, said: I
have heard several times in the last half hour that
there are several young men in the town who are in
the habit of shouting 'Garibaldi for ever.' Sergeant
Morgan: I have never heard anything of the sort—,
Sir H. Mainwaring : If you hear any more, apprehend
them, and I will close their mouths. Sergeant
Morgan: I'll attend ta it, sir.—Xanchwer 4xcfnlitwr,

articles.title: PRICE Two PENCE.
articles.text:
PRICE Two PENCE.

DREADFUL ACCIDENT AND LOSS

OF LIFE.

On Wednesday evening the inhabitants of Tooley-
street were thrown into a state of the greatest excite-
ment, in consequence of a loud rumbling noise pro-
ceeding from the premises in course of reconstruction,
and which were destroyed by the great fire on the 22nd
of June, 1861. In the course of a few minutes many
of the inhabitants, with a body of the M division of
police, under Mr. Inspector Beckerson, hastened to the
spot, and upon entering what is termed Cotton's Depot
(Scovell's Wharf) they found that three of the arches
just completed, or nearly ISO, had one after thd other
given way, and three men who were at work at the
time were buried in the ruins. Mr. Oliver, who was
superintending the erection of the works, at once
summoned all hands to his assistance, and one
man was taken out alive, bit.; so much injured that
he was removed to Guy's Hospital. His name as
James Small, and he resided at 16, Princes-street,
Deptford. Owing, however, to the prompt surgical
assistance he received in that admirable institution he
was able to be removed to his residence during the
morning. Two other men, named respectively Robert
Hawten, of 36, Snow's-fields, Bermondsey, and Thomas
Howard, of the Curtain-road, Shoreditch, were found
to be completely embedded in the ruins, and a consider.
able time elapsed before they could be got out, and then
both were found to be dead. The appearance of the
bodies indicated that death must have been instan-
taneous. The arches abutted upon Chamberlain's
Wharf, which was destroyed by fire at the same time,
and has only just been rebuilt. The cause of the acci-
dent is not precisely known; but from the examination
made by the district surveyor, he ascertained that men
had been engaged driving piles into the river during
the day, and the inference was that the vibration caused
upon the shore of the river hat.l so shaken the founda-
tions of the arches as to cause them to give way, and in
consequence he issued orders that no more piles were
to be driven in at present.

articles.title: TEE LATE EXTRAORDINAI?,Y CASE OF CHILD DESERTION.
articles.text:
TEE LATE EXTRAORDINAI?,Y CASE
OF CHILD DESERTION.

It will be remembered that a few weeks ago we
published some particulars of a case of alleged child
desertion, from which it appeared that a young lady
(married), residing in Bristol, had been the unwilling
recipient of the child ot a woman whose name was
unknown. The story, as told by the young woman,
was, that she met, in one of the carriages of the Great
Western Railway, a female with a baby in her arms,
and that this female asked her to 'take the baby' for
a few minutes, which she did. The artful mother
shortly afterwards disappeared, and the child, being
left with the young lady, was brought by her to
Bristol, and taken home with her. Subsequently the
child was removed to St. Peter's Hospital, where it
has since remained. On Friday the very strange
affair assumed a new and still stranger aspect. At
a meeting of the guardians, a woman, residing
in Chatterton-street, Bristol, came forward and
stated positively that the young lady was her-
self the mother of the child. She said she
knew this because the young woman had been
confined at her house about eleven months ago.
The witness, if we may call her such, said she had not
seen the child since it was three months old, but after
she examined it she said she could swear to it among
ten thousand as the same child of which the young
woman was confined. The young lady and her father
were in attendance, and the former denied all know-
ledge of the woman who thus accused her of being the
mother of the child, and the father declared it was a
conspiracy got up by a woman who was 'jealous' of
his daughter. In the course of the proceedings the
young lady fainted, and had to be taken out of the
room. The husband of the woman living in Chatter-
ton-street, at whose house the young woman is said
to have been confined, was sent for, and he recognised
her, and told the same story as his wife. Some of the
guardians wished the girl's father to take the child
with him; but he, being convinced that there is a
conspiracy in the matter, resolutely refused, alleging
that he was prepared to prove by independent wit-
nesses that his daughter was at home when she was
said to have been at the house of the woman in Chat-
terton-street. Here for the present the affair rests,
but we are informed that the subject will be brought
before the magistrates.

EXTRAORDINARY OCCURRENCE IN HYBE-PARIL—On
Saturday an inquest was held by Mr. Langham, at
St. George's workhouse, on the 'body of a female child
which had been given birth to in Hyde-park, by a
young woman, named Sarah Smith, in the service of
Captain Cox, of No. 5, Kensington Park-terrace. She
had obtained leave of absence for a couple of days,
avowedly to give rest to a bad hand, and on Thursday
Park Constable No. 4 had observed her strolling about
in an unfrequented part from eleven till about three
o'clock, when finding her sitting under the dry arch
leading into Kensington Gardens, he spoke to her,
advising her to move on, In five minutes after this he
saw her again with a bundle, and •on asking what she
had there she told him she had just given birth to a
child, and that it was dead. He requested her to
accompany him to the Mount-stteet Workhouse, and
she did so, carrying the bundle, which was tightly
tied up, under her arm. On reaching the workhouse
the bundle was opened, and found to contain a female
child alive. A nurse put the child into a warm bath,
which appeared to revive it very much, and under the
care of the surgeon it lived twelve hours. The medical
man was of opinion that death had resulted from con-
gestion of the heart and lungs, but he could not under-
take to say if it was produced from severe labour or
from natural causes. The coroner, in summing up,
made a strong point against the accused, on the ground
that she had made no provision whatever for the child;
but the jury returned a verdict in' accordance with the
medical testimony.
EXTRAORDINARY COURT-MARTIAL.—A court-martial
was held on board the Victory, flag-ship, on Saturday,
to try Mr. James R. Marsden, sub-lieutenant of her
Majesty's ship Resistance, Captain Chamberlain, first,
for behaving in a .disrespectful manner, by having his
hand in his pocket when addressing Commander
flume; and secondly, for disrespect to Captain Cham-
berlain, when the latter spoke to him upon the impro-
priety of addressing Commander Hume with his hand
in his pocket. It appears that the prisoner was not on
deck at the time 'all hands' were turned up to weigh
anchor on the evening of the 18th of October, and he
was therefore sent for by Commander Hume, before
whom he stood with his left hand in his pocket when
spoken to. The commander did not speak to him
concerning the alleged impropriety, but Captain
Clamberlain noticed the circumstance and expostulated
with him. The prisoner, it seems, 'did not take his
hand out of his pocket when first spoken to, but on
the second occasion, when addressed by the captain
before some of the crew, he replied, Very well, sir.'
Captain Chamberlain said in evidence that he con-
sidered the prisoner's tone direspectful, although the
prisoner did not speak louder than usual. In his
defence prisoner denied any intention, to, be disre-
spectful, and said that, when remonstrated with before
the crew, he was very confused, and might have
omitted to salute his superior officer, The court found
both charges partly proved, and sentenced the prisoner
to be severely reprimanded, and ackackiliecied, to be
more carttfal ii the future.

articles.title: TRADES' GARIBALDIAN DEMONSTRATION.
articles.text:
THE TRADES' GARIBALDIAN
DEMONSTRATION.

TO THE TRADE AND FRIENDLY SOCIETIES
OF LONDON.
Brother Unionists and Fellow-Workmen,—The
Provisional Committee, formed for the purpose of
promoting a public welcome by the working men of
London to the illustrious Italian hero and patriot,
General Garibaldi, on his visit to this country, which
will take place as soon as his health is sufficiently
restored, have much pleasure in laying before you
the following resolutions, unanimously adopted at a
preliminary meeting of officers and members of
Trade Societies, and attended by a deputation from
the London Trades' Council, held at the office of the
BEE-HIVE Newspaper, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-
street, on Wednesday evening, Oct. 22.

"That this meeting, Composed of officers and members of
various Metropolitan Trade Societies, having been made ac-
quainted with the intention of General Garibaldi, as soon as
the state of his health will permit, of visiting England for
the purpose of thanking, in person, the English people for the
sympathy they have bestowed upon him, and the cause in
which he is engaged—the unity of Italy—and having heard
that it is intended to give the illustrious Italian patriot a
public welcome to London, hereby recommend the Trades
Societies and Friendly Societies of the metropolis to take part
in such public demonstration, in such manner as may hereafter
be determined.

" Thnt every Trnde,Society, or Friendly Society, willing to
co-operate in such a demonstration of welcome to General
Garibaldi, be requested to appoint a delegate, or delegates, to
assist in carrying out the object on behalf of their respectiva
societies ; and Let in the meantime the persons present forms
themselves into a Provisional Committee, with power to add
to their numbers, to act until the delegates are appointed."

_
The Committee feel confident, from the universal
feeling of sympathy pervading all classes of Eng—
lishmen with General Garibaldi in his present suffer—
ings, and the admiration i generally entertained
for his nobleness of character, his social virtues, his
freedom from political trickery, and his pure and
disinterested patriotism., the above resolntions will
be cordially and heartily responded to.

The form the demonstration shall assume has not
been decided, that will remain to be settled by the
delegates when they meet; the committee who now-
address you have merely taken the initiative for
bringing the proposition before you, and to set in
motion a movement that they feel certain will find a
ready response in the hearts of their fellow workmen
of all sects and parties. It is not proposed to make
the demonstration one of a party character—it is
desired that it should be one in which working men
of all opinions should take part—one simply expres-
sive of sympathy and admiration of the personal
character of the man, and of the purity and patriotism
of his motives and actions. If certain parties choose
to place any political significance on the demonstra-
tion, they will be at liberty to do so; inasmuch as
It will naturally be concluded that the great majority
of those who assemble to do homage to the hero of
Italy, not only sympathise with him, but desire the
success of that cause to which he has devoted his
best energies, and risked his valuable life, viz, the
complete unity of Italy.
Fellow workmen, General Garibaldi is not only a
patriotic citizen, and a gallant soldier, but a social
reformer. The elevation of the toiling masses is one
of the principles he has ever maintained, his voice
and influence has always been exercised in favour of
the lifting up of labour from its present down-trodden
position; he is the friend of, and beloved by, our
Italian fellow workmen, and therefore must be the
friend of, and beloved by, the brotherhood of labour
in all countries.

Garibaldi's fame has spread, far and wide through-
out the world, that the Committee deem it unnecessary
to further enlarge on the subject, and have refrained
from making any stirring appeal to your passions or
feelings; they desire your action should be as much.
as possible of a spontaneous character, and would
only observe that by honouring one of the noblest
men of the present age, that honour will be reflected
back upon yourselves.
The Committee .in conclusion, hope that every
Trade or Friendly Society intending to take part in
the proposed demonstration, will appoint their dele—
gates without delay, and when a sufficient number
have been chosen, they will resign the further con—
duct of the business into their hands. Speedy
action is requisite, as from the favourable accounts
just received from Spezzia, the time is not far distant
when General Garibaldi will be in England. A com-
mittee, composed of many well known and influential
citizens, has been formed in the City of London,
with whom it is suggested the Trades' Committee
should co-operate.
Until the meeting of delegates all communications
are to be sent to the Honorary Secretary, Mr. IL
H rtwell, at the BEE-HIVE Office, 2, Bouverie
Street, Fleet Street, by whom every information.
will be afforded.

We remain, Brother Unionists and Fellow Work-
men, the Members of the Provisional Committee.
Signed on their behalf by the following sub-committee
W. CREMER, (Joiner).
R. W. GREY, (Mason).
W. TREMLETT, (Joiier).
a ODGERS, (Shoemaker).
G. POTTER, (Treasurer).
R. HARTWELL, (Hon. Sec.)
Committee Rooms, 2, Bouverie Street, Fmet Street, Oct.
30, 1862.

The following letter has been sent to General Gari-
baldi on behalf of the committee

'Dear and Honoured General—The committee of
the Trades' Garibaldian Demonstration, a body of
working men, being officers and members of London
trades' societies, numbering about 100,000 skilled.
artisans, desire to convey to you the expression of their
deep sympathy with your present bodily and mental
suffering; a suffering that must be rendered. more
acute by the knowledge that the bullet which has laid
you wounded on a bed of pain and sickness was
a fratricidal one directed against you by the
orders of a so-called Italian ministry, but
who, in reality, were the instruments of a foreign
ruler, to remove whose unrighteous grasp from that
fair city which ought to be, and ultimately will be, the
capital of a free Italy, you were devotingyour energies,
and risking your valuable life, that you might add
another jewel to the crown of that king to whom you
had already presented two kingdoms won by yourself
and your brave comrades from a corrupt and. odious
Government, whose existence was a blot upon civilisa-
tion. The working men of London know you to be
the friend of, and beloved by, their Italian brethren,
the producers of their country's wealth; and they
long for the time when, Providence permitting,
you will be able to come amongst them, that
they may prove to you personally how much they
admire your nobleness of character, your social virtues,
and your pure and disinterested patriotism. When
that day shall arrive, you will receive the un-
bought homage of hundreds of thousands of Eng-
land's workmen, who, in common with all classes of
their fellow-countrymen, will deem that moment to be
a proud one in their lives when they will thus be
enabled, publicly and before the world, to express theie
admiration of Italy's noblest son, hero, and. patriot.
That this hour may speedily arrive, and that your
valuable life may yet be spared to see your fondest
hopes realised—Venice liberated from Austrian rule,
and Rome, freed from French bayonets, become the
capital of a free, united, and constitutional ;Italy—
is the sincere and earnest prayer of the working. men
of London.'
On behalf of the committee, I 'remain, dear General,
yours faithfully,
ROBERT Hiaawma., Honorary Secretary.
[The above letter was forwarded to Spezzia on Mon-
day last, and endorsed by Mr. Richardson, of the
Common Council, to General Garibaldi, of whom he is
a personal friend.j
The Provisional Committee will moot at 8 o'clock
en Tuesday evening next, at the Beehive Office, when
officers of Trade Societies, or of the Foresters, Odd-
Fellows, Old Friends, and other similar friendly
societies, are invited to attend. No persons uncon-
nected with any of the above will be admitted to this
meeting.

_SYMPATHY WITH THE NORTII.—A public meeting
will be held on Monday evening next, at 8 o'clock,
at the Metropolitan Institution, Clevelaad - street,
Fitzroy-square, to protest against the recent expres-
sions of opinion in favour of the South; and to suppor t

articles.title: FASHIONS ,FOl NOTXIrBER!
articles.text:
FASHIONS ,FOl NOTXIrBER!

(From the 'Paris BkgatlO
Tt seems to be understood among the leaders of fashion
that rotondes are to be very much in use this winter,
either to matek with the dresses, or to consist of some
warm stuff, such as cloth or velvet. The•e rotondes are
longer than the collars, but Shorter than the Talmas.;
they are very convenient; because you can 'readily put
. them over the; shoulders, or take them off if they dis-
commode you But the question is, are they warm
They let the air through everywhere, and that ought to
be considered. However, these rotondes are not
inelegant; they bear large plaits, for they are very full,
• and have a graceful turn: saw at Baden, during my
. meat visit, a white cloth cloak, trimmed all round
with a wide grecque of chestnut ribbon, quilted with
white silk; it was veiy rich, nothing could be more
beautiful for evening dress. I should'.'ncit recommend
• a lady to wear such a toilet in walking out: but at the
theatre, at the opera, nothing could be desired more corn
pletely elegant and distinguished.
Astra= and Chinchilla will, they say, be less in
fashion this winter. :We always come back, to sables.
They are very serviceable and, durable, and. so, various
that every taste may. be satisfied by. them. The real
sable is too Costly for common wear, and a lady must be
really elegant to venture.to adopt it. ,
I have seen a morning -wrapper made of white cash-
mere as fine as Indian. At the skirt there was a wide
eolferino band, edged on both sides with black suipure,
laid on the cashmere. The front was adorned with two
montants-to match, divided lay' a row Of "large Solferino
buttons, surrounded with black guipure.
The &nave is'. made of Solfermo cashmere, lined with
white taffeta,. adorned above' and below with black
' guipure to 'match with that at the skirt of the wrapper.
Here and there are dotted large buttons to match those
in front. The chenlisette is a white foulard, adorned
with similar insertions in front, at the neck and sleeves.
smaller buttons of the samekind are pit on to fasten it
_in front and at the wrists.

Petticoats with embroidered sashes, others a tablier,
and some loaded with ribbons. Neck-Landkerchiefs
,
too, Marie Antoinette fashion, of extreme elegance,
covered with guipure and embroidery.
The latest novelties of fashion in bonnets are a hat
,of white crape, with velvet ornaments; a 'grey crape
cloak, awl green velvet head-dress, with black lace or-
nanients ; a lovely coiffure, Mary Stuart form, with
lappets and red -velvet trimming; children's capotes,
made of white taffeta, with blue velvet ornaments, and
neat little blondes. ~

Velvet will be very much worn this coming season,
and mixed colours too. There are some evening coiffures
ehiffonnees of unrivalled taste. The Teal art is to suit
them to the particular look, of each face.

There is 'a
talk of reviving for ball dresses the
trimmings with flowers. These in my opinion are
Preferable to any. What adornment can be more
delicate, chaster, or more incoming to a young lady?
The fashion of' wearing plumes in the hat and bonnet
likewise continues. From the bird of paradise and the
majestic ostrich down to the little fly-catcher,, all furnish
us with feathers. Moreover, they assert that those
pretty gems from India, the butterflies, the god-wiiiged
flies and the like, are mingled with our present evening
toilets. ,

Another word or ..two about furs; for winter is
coming, and furs will soon be required. The muffs, the
cloaks, the tippets are getting ready, and this is a luxury
.7whith affords a stamp for the most distinguished lady to
be known by. Astracau; though no longer the rage,
may yet be assumed a& a fincy ;, but marten skins and
sables are the principal favourites. Some few ladies of
fashion strove to bring the blue foxskins into use, but
they are not likely to spread, being so very dear andraze
to boot.

articles.title: BARON THIERRY AND LORD PALIM'RSTON.
articles.text:
BARON THIERRY AND LORD
PALIM'RSTON.

On Monday his Excellency Baron 'Merry paid a visit
to Southampton, to inspect the dock is and commercial
facilities of the port, in reference to a' steath-packet cora-
raunieatiou. between Southamptom and. Trieste. After
the inspection, the baron was invited. to a banquet by
Mr. J. R. Stebbing, the president of the Chamber of
Commerce, in the reading-room of that establishment.
The banquet took place at 2p m. About thirty gentle-
men were invited to meet the baron.

His Excellency stated that he had not peen South-
ampton for thirty years, and was surprised at its progress
as a commercial port. He expressed himself pleased at
its facilities for trade, and said be should do all in his
power to establish a more intimate commercial union
between Austria and. England.
At about 5 p.m., just as the party was about to break
up, Lord Palmerston and the Hon. W. Cowper rode up
to the Chamber of Commerce. His lordship heard that
Baron Thierry was in Southampton, and rode over from
Broadlands to see him, and on inquiring at the baron's
hotel, he found that the latter was then as; the Chamber
of Commerce. The president, the mayor, and other
gentlemen went to receive " his lordship. On entering
the reading-room Lord Palmerston and Baron Thierry
greeted each other most cordially. His lordship's health
was drunk, and in returning thanks he spoke of the
adirande which free trade' had contributed to the com-
mercial and agricultural interests of this country. The
opposition to it h3d, he said, been most powerful, but it
had yielded to the force of public opinion in this country,
and to the will of the reigning head of Frazee. With
regard to Austria, its riches in mineral and agricultural
produce were immense, but unsufficiently developed.
Nothing more fortunate could happen for the statesmen of
Austria than that they..should be led to seethe benefits of
freedom of commerce. He was not one of those who
believed that the extension of commerce annihilated war,
but it tended to draw closer the bonds of friendship be-
tween nations, and thus prevented war. His object in
coming to Southampton was to invite Baron Thierry to
Broadlands. His lordship remained ,about an hour,
when he took leave.

THE 111TrUDElt OF TTIE CAPTAIN OF THE SUMTER.—The
report of the murder of the captain of the Sumter is
confirmed by the arrival of the Peninsular and Oriental
Company's steamer Ellora:—' On the evening of the
15th instant a dreadful tragedy occurred on board the
Confederate steamer Sumter, lying at Gibraltar. The
crew of this vessel, it will be remembered, were paid off
several months ago, and she has since been in charge of
two officers and a sufficient number of hands to take
care of the ship. Between seven and eight o'clock on
the evening of the I§th, Mr. Joseph Hester, the second
officer, deliberately shot Mr. William Andrews, the
officer in command, as he was lying in his berth: The
latter expired almost immediately, three shots frOm a
revolver having been fired into his body. The criminal
was arrested, and a coroner's inquest held on the body
of the deceased officer, which resulted in a verdict of
Wilful Murder' against Hester. No particulars are
published as to the causes shich led to the commission
of the crime.'

LORD DALHOUSIE'S PROPERTY. - The Montrose
Standard publishes the following statement, which evi-
dently. refers lo the Earl of Dalhousie and Provost
Guthrie, of Brechin A nobleman, a distinguished
statesman, and an extensive proprietor, who, on his ac-
cession to his patrimonial estate, ten years ago, honour-
ably placed himself under trust, and on a comparatively
limited allowance, in order to provide for heavy debt
necessarily undertaken previous to his coming into
possession, will, within a few months, have cleared off
these obligations. It is understood that the estates will
then be placed under the management of a commissioner,
and a gentleman, well known for his business habits,
has been mentioned as likely to receive this appoint-
ment.'

THE Fnrais BLownrs.—On Friday last the heroine
of the Crystal Palace in 1858, and of the transit of the
Thames on a tight rope 2,000 feet in length in August,
1861, was removed on crutches from St. Bartholomew's
Hospital, a cripple for the rest of her life, from the ac-
cidental fracturing of the neck of the thigh-bone, more
than two months ago, at Highbury Barn, while obeying
the morbid and romantic desire of the present age for
perilous adventures. The finetured limb is three inches
shorter than the other, andperfectlyaseless. The heroine,
with a courage truly characteristic' wished the surgeons
to amputate the limb, if it could not be rendered service-
able, rather, as she observed, than have it dangling
uselessly by the side of the other, and requiring support
which she might find very difficultto obtain for the main-
tenance of the sound one. What renders the case of
this unfortunate artist the more distressing is, she was
the only support of an aged and infirm father and an
invalid sister.—Express.

THE EASTERN FxSURRIES.—During the late gales
considerable damage was inflicted on nets, &c. off the
eastern coast, but only one Great Yarmouth lugger is
known to have been lost. This was the Ann, which was
run down by a French vessel. The fish landed at Yar-
mouth during the last few days have been small in
quantity, but their quality has been good. Prices have
ranged at from £lO 10s. to £23 per last (13,200 fish).
From Lowestoft it is stated that operations have been
much interrupted by the late stormy weather, and rather
gloomy apprehensions appear to be entertained as to the
prospects of the season.
MEMORIAL TO THE LATE BISHOP VILLIERS.:LA mom"-
ment has just been erected in the parish church of St.
George's 13loorosbury, to the memory of the late Dr.
Henry Montague Villiers, Bishop of Durham. It is a
plain unornamented tablet, and bears the following in-
scription :--‘ To the ,nemory of the Hon. and Right
Rev. Henry Montague Villiers, late Lord Bishop of
Durham, for fifteen years rector of this parish, who died
August 9, 1861, ,aged 48 years. This tablet is erected in
grateful recognition of the services of a faithful minis*,
=din affectionate remembrance of a valued friend.' '

L.4IV CASHIR.A DISTRES,S..I
'
,
(From the Times, Oct. i 3.)
The time is at hand, if it has not already come, when
we - must prepare ourselves for a mere vigorous and
united effort to relieve the distress in Lancashire. The
two letters which we published on Saturday and yester-
day,. from our own Correspondent, confirmed as they are
by the , eekly returns from the Statistical Department
of the Poor-law Board, and by private testimony too
overwhelming to be doubted, - prove that things have
gone on from bad to worse, and have not yet reached
their climax. Every week mills are stopped. because
cotton cannot be had except at a price which must
.entail ruinous loss on the manufacturer unless the
scarcity should continue
,till he has sold hiS goods..
Strange as it may wand, it wouktbe weirfor.the opera-
tives during the ensuing , inter if the continuance of the
war could be guaranteed for a twelvemonth or, more, for
then all the cotton that could be procured would be turned
to account. As it is, employment is steadily diminishing.
The week before last showed an increase of paupe,rism
to the amount of more than 7,000 persons over that
which preceded it; last week shows a further addition
of 1.3,201 recipients of parish relief. 'No Union has
less.paupers ' th ,n before; 'twenty Unions have more,'
i and n one of these, Ashton-under-Lyne, more than
2,000 names appeared on the list for the first time. In
these twenty Unions the total number of paupers seems
already to have exceeded 200,000—some four times as
much as the average for this time of year. Moreover,
we learn that 'the physical condition of the people is
rapidly deteriorating,' that low diet and cold weather
are beginning ta tell on broken spirits, and that ' Preston
has already been attacked by 'a virulent form or' typhus
fever.' .‘ A settled glom hangs-over ' this town, the only
place which has' yet availed itself of Mr. Villier's Act.
Of its 87 mills, 34 are shut up, and very few are work-
ing full time; while out of its 83,000 inhabitants,
32,000 are on the books of the Guardians or of the Relief

cause, about 150,000 factory workers are entirely out of

mittee have fixed their expenditure for the present at

general fund of any considerable, amount, and if we
reckon the produce of the poor-rates at £ll,OOO a-week,

subscriptions) at £5,000, and the Manchester subsidy

allows no margin for the prospective incresse of the
claims for assistance by the, spread of pauperism, if, not
by the accession of disease. ,
Now, the question is; what is our duty as the country-
men of those upon whom this great calamity has fallen?
Can any one of us, who have comforts enough and to
spare hear these authentic reports and yet refuse to
come forward? We say that the claim upon us, as
Englishmen, is independent of the claim upon manu-
facturers and landowners. It may be that those who
have hitherto hung back will now come to the rescue;
but, whether they do or not, our' ourse , should 'be the
same. We cannot afford. to wait any longer for them.
In the presence of such widespread misery we cease to,
ask who ought to take the initiative, and whether we
who did olot* share in the prosperity of 'Lancashire
should be called upon for aid in her adversity. We
think only of the magnitude of the evil, and of our
own power to alleviate it. It would be discreditable to
the nation if a resort to the Consolidated Fund should
become necessary on their behalf.. It is not 'Ministers,'
but the landed and commercial aristocracy of Lancashire
in the. first instance, and the richer classes of this
country in the next, who should 'look this evil, in the
face.' What the Poor Law fails to do should be done
by private benevolence. Let no one be taxed for a
charitable purpose against his will. There are enough
who will find pleasure in carrying out so good a work
at their own expense without marring it by the creation
of an evil precedent..

CROPS OF COTTON I:7 THE
SOUTHERN STATES IN 1860-2.

• The following correspondence has been addressed to
the Manchester Cotton Supply Association :)y order of
Earl Russell:—

Foreign-office, October 25

Sir,—l am directed by Earl Russell to transmit to you
herewith, to be laid before the Cotton Supply Associa-
tion, a copy of a dispatch from her Majesty's Consul at
Charleston, containing observations on the cotton crops
in the Southern States of America during the years
1860, 1861, and 1862, together with information as to
the stock of cotton now on hand.

articles.title: I am, Sir, your most obedient humble servant,
articles.text:
I am, Sir, your most obedient humble servant,

E. HAMMOND.
G. R. Haywood, Esq., Cotton Supply Association.
British Consulate, Charleston, Aug. 13.
My Lord—The near approach; of 'the close of the
cotton year,' which is compiled from September 1,
seems to render appropriate a few remarks upon the
condition and amount of the crop which has been
planted during the last spring and summer, as well as
some general information on the subject of the cotton
supply from the Southern States of America I begin
by expressing ray regret that the disturbed state of the
country and the irregularity of communication render it
more difficult than usual to procure trustworthy details.
But I have taken some pains to collect the information,
and venture to think that it may be depended upon.
There can be little doubt that the crop of 1862
would, under• ordina:ry circirastances, have reached
4,500,000 ' bales ; but, in consequence of the •aivil
war, not more than 1,500,000 have been planted.
It is thought by some that the present crop will
riot exceed 1,000,000 bales, but I have rel son
to believe that the supply from Texas has been
underestimated. That State has been as yet very little
disturbed by military operations, so that agriculture has
been less interfered with than elsewhere. On the
banks of the Mississippi very little cotton has been
planted, as the danger is too great. It is only in the
interior of the various States, at a distance from the
great rivers, that the crop of this year is to be found.
The crop of 1860 was disposed of, and, in a considerable
measure, exported before the blockade of the Southern
ports was established, but it is calculated that 750,000
bales still remain on hand. The crop of 1861 amounted
to about 2,750,000 bales. Of these about 1,000,000
bales have been destroyed at various places to prevent
their falling into the hands of the Federals ; the rest is
stored in the interior of the different States. Much of

it has been bought by foreignell, who hope to preserve
it as neutral property through all ;he dangers of the war.
About 50,000 bales have run the blockade successfully,
chiefly to Nassau. One cargo has gone to Barcelona,
and one to France; I do .not take into account the pro-
duct of the sea islands of South Carolina and Georgia.
They are in the possession of the Federals, and I have no
means of ascertaining whether any cotton at all has
been grown there during the present season. The
amount, therefore, of cotton remaining in the Southern
States at this date, which might be available to foreign
commerce as soon as the blockade is removed, may be
said to stand thus:—

Bales.
•
Remainder of crop of 1860 .. 750,000
Undestroyed crop of 1861 .. .. 1,750,000
Crop of 1862 (not yet pioked) 1,600,000

4,000,000
Shipped through the blockade .. 50,000

Remaining in the South .. 3,950,000
It must, of course be remembered that a portion, or
the whole, of this accumulation may be destroyed at
any moment by the Southern people.

A CHAPTER ON WHlSKEMS.—Whiskers are a growth
of nature, and, like other natural productions, may be
almost indefinitely improved by cultivation. If the
soil be good and the plants strong, everything is to be
hoped for. Let the aim, the ideal to be cultivated up
to, be to have the whisker black, bright and bushy;
brushed at an angle slightly dipping forward from the
horizontal lint—shaved into a graceful curve from the
hinge of the jaw; not p'unging beneath the cravat into
the neck—that is wasteful, as well as injurious to the
important part which is visible; for permission of the
growth of a superabundant hair will tend to Sap the
Vigour of all the rest; curled a little outwards at the
extremities—such is the great exemplar at which we
are all to shave. Of all things avoid a vulgar whisker.
This is of various kinds. A short, scrubby, indomitable
red whisker is a vulgar whisker; a weak, fuzzy, white,
moth-eaten, mouldy whisker is a vulgar whisker; a
big, black, bluff, brutal-looking whisker is a vulgar
whisker; a twisting, twining, serpentine, sentimental,
cork.-screw of a whisker is a vulgar whisker; a mathe-
matical, methodistical, maiter-of-artsical diagram of a
whisker is a vulgar whisker. Whatever is not any of
theie—will do.

Wuo ,is OLD ?-7-.A wise man will never rust out. As
long as he can move and breathe, he will do somethinc,
fur himself, his n( ighbour, or for posterity. Almost to the
last hour of his life Washington was at work. So were
Franklin, and Young, and Howard, and New ton. The
vigour of their lives never decayed. No rust marred
their spirits. It is a foolish idea to suppose that we must
lie down and die because we are old. Who is old? Not
the man of energy; not the day-labourer in science,
art, or benevolence; but he only who suffers his energies
to waste away and the springs of life to become motion-
less; on whose hands the hours drag heavily, to whom
all things wear the garb of gloom.
CRINOLINE AGAIN.--On the 25th an inquest was held
at Leamington, touching the death, on the previous
evening, of Mrs. M. Vane, of Fulham Villa, who by
marriage is related to the Duke of Cleveland. It
appeared from the evidence adduced that deceased had
been left by the servants in the dining-room of her
residence, reading the Illustrated London Hews, and that
one of the town policemen, who happened to pass the
villa, noticed an unsual illumination in the hall. • On
breaking into the house the balustrades of the staircase
and the dining-room door were found to be on fire, and
the charred corpse of the lady lying on the inside of the
latter door. She was wearing steel hoops, and as a
cambric handkerchief was found within the fire-place,
near which she had been sitting, it is supposed that to
the great distention of' crinoline' must be ascribed her
death. The flesh Was burnt down to the bones, one
arm was off, and the body presented a frightful appear-
ance. Deceased was sixty years o: age, but of active
habits. The jury returned a verdict of 'Accidental
death.'

lately on several occasions in a gentleman's establish-
ment near Leominister. It adds to the impudence of
the performance that her mistress was at home in happy

articles.title: FEES LY 7111, _HOUSE OF VOMIONS
articles.text:
FEES LY 7111, _HOUSE OF VOMIONS

An alteration is about to be made in respect to the
payment of fees in the House of Commons on what may
be termed Private Bill Legislation.' A recently issued
report of the House on standing orders revealed a State:
of things; hitherto a mystery to the public, with regard
to the enormous fees paid on private and local bills,
It seems that an unopposed bill will cost £3OO, of
which about £2OO is expended in fees, and when a bill
is opposed, which is generally the case in railway
matters, the fees are very large. Such an impression
did the evidence make on the -select eommittee., that
they strongly recommended a reduction in the fees,
and that it should take effect as early as possible. It
is probable that at the commencement of the next session
the recommendation will be acted upon. Before the
committee Mr. Jones, the clerk Of the fees, gave evidence
4nd disclosed how a certain Chancellor Of the Eichequer
very adroitly 'put his hands upon' some .£170,000 to.
'make up a good budget. In the last to years there had
been an overplus in the fees compared with the expenses,
.but for six years there had been a deficiency of 'some-
where about £lO,OOO a-year. Last year the expenses of.
the House of Commons amounted to £51,000, and the
fees to £70,000 giving a surplus of £25,900, whilst in
the year before the expenses were about the same, arid
the nes £57,000 ; so in.the words of Mr. Jones as there Wit:S
no great surplus, 'we paid our way.' The officers of
the House were transferred to the Consolidated Fund in
1845, and in the opinion of Mr. Jones the fees for the
last six years, with the exception of the last two years,
had not paid the expenses of the establishment.
Another question was raised .before the. committee a 3
to the printing of all the documents connected with the
Private Bill Department: Hitherto such matters have
been written for the committees, such as short-hand
writers', notes ; biit the evidence given was in favour of
printing, and the matter will no doubt be brought before
the House of Commons and decided by the Speaker. It
would appear that printing will shortly supersede in a
great measure writing. Already it has been introduced
into the Court of Chancery, and next term will witnes.s
printed affidavits and depositions of evidence in the bands
of the Judges, counsel, and solicitors, instead of written
copies, and now it is proposed that the evidence given
before the committees and other matters connected with
private bills should be printed and ready for delivery by
nine eclgek the following morning. ,

FEARFUL GALES Off THE SOUTH:
:EA S Th..P.llr COAST.

Dorm, Sunday, 5.30 p.m.—Throughout the whole of
the day and this morning a succession of strong gales,
rains, and heavy seas have been raging; indeed since
the wreck of the ill-fated Violet (Imperial mail packet)
on the Goodwin Sands, in 1857, such rough weather
cannot well be remembered. During the whole of the
night the piers and harbour approaches have been kept
in a continuous state of excitement by fears for the
safety of that magnificent new iron steamer the Maid
of Kent, Captain Bennett, belonging to the London,
Chatham, and Dover Railway Company, which had
been telegraphed as leaving Calais Harbour at four
o'clock in the afternoon.

Shortly before midnight the steam-tug Resolute (No.
1, Liverpool), having the electric coil on board, got her
steam up, and proceeded in search of the. Maid of Kent,
it being supposed that her peculiarly constructed
engines had been found inadequate to the 'green seas'
which prevail during the equinoctial gales;' but at
11.10 this morning the Resolute returned to the har-
bour without tidings.
Telegraphic communications from point to point of
the coast had in the meantime been resorted to, and at
11.20 a telegram from Deal announced a large steamer
with yellow funnels had been scen in the vicinity of
the Downs, and near to the Goodwin Sands.

At 11.30 the Vivid (Imperial mail packet) steamed
out of harbour. At this moment a large steamer,
with her foremast and bowsprit gone, was observed
struggling in a tremendous sea; with some difficulty
she was boarded by a Trinity pilot (Moon) and brought
safely into harbour; she proved to be the Jovellanos,
bound from London to Lisbon. The schooner Petrel,
which sailed from Dover last week, also put back, and
the Mary Stuart (Liverpool steam-tug), with jury-
masts, got in with her funnel red hot, after beating off
and on for 30 minutes.

At four o'clock the Vivid returned to Dover with
thirty-five passengers and luggage from the decks of
the Maid of Kent. She had fallen in with her on the
outside' of the Downs, and near to the Gull stream;
both anchors were down, and the chains entangled, 80
that it is impossible to get her off until the morning
tide; her windlass is also gone. A number of carpenters
and sailors having been procured, the. Vivid 'again
started for the spot where the Mold of Kent has been
anchored from two a.m._

The shipping casuWfties on the Dover coast have
been but few during the week, although a serious en,
croachment of the sea has swept away half a mile of
shingle, destroyed the Marine-parade, and laid bare
the faggot-groins that have been buried in beach and
sand lateen years.

ORIGIN OF THE PRISTER'S DEVIL.—An anecdote of
the origin of the 'printer's devil' runs as follows :
When Manutius, the elder, set up in business in Venice,
he came into possession of a little negro boy who had
been left by some merchant vessel at that city to be
properly cared for. This boy was known over the city
as the little black devil' who helped the mysterious
bibliofactor along ; and although no one had ever seen
him, yet perhaps there was a great dread raised among
the children concerning the hobgoblin. Some ignorant
persons believed him to be none other than the embodi-
ment of the evils of Satan, who helped Aldus in the
prosecution of his profession, for many persons who were
personally unacquainted with him thought he had 'deal-
ings with the old boy.' One day Aldus determined to
dispel this strange hallucination by publicly displaying
the young imp to the poorer classes. Upon the occasioD
he made a very characteristic speech—' Let it be known
in Venice that I, Aldus Manutius, printer to the Holy
Church and Doge, have this day made a public exposure
of the printer's devil! All those who think he is not flesh
and blood may now come forward and pinch him!' He
was the first negro roller-boy, and he must have been
much more intelligent than thoss we have met with in
some printing-offices, or else Manutius' fame would not
have been so bright, perhaps, for he was one of the first
to discover that the pressman's first rule was to have the
ink well distributed/ with balls or any other contrivance.

articles.title: P_RUSSLIN .DUMOLLARD.
articles.text:
A P_RUSSLIN .DUMOLLARD.

A Pomeranian workman, naMed Maascb, has lately
been detected, by accident, in the course of a murderous
cafeer closely resembling that of the notinious French-
man Ihimellard. He has, 'together with his accom-
plices, of whom his mother is one, counnitted thirteen '
muiders. On one occasion he murdemed at. Cursdorf a
miller and his family,. comiSisting in all, of six Persons.
R 6 baffled All the researches of the ,police, and was de-
tected at last by mere chance: A nerlin correspondent,
describing the facts revealed on' the trial says
'Two farm farm labourers of the village of Warsin, near
.Staigardt, were one morning walking together on their
way to their work in: the fields, when it came on
• to rain. • For the sake of greater shelter 'against
the wet, one of them proposed that they should
probed& to their destination for -the rest of the way
by a path leading'lthrough • the woods. This being
•agreed" On, the peasants had.not long been in the forest
when one of them espied at some distance through
the, trees the tipper half of the body of a men sticking
up- out of thU ground. Their hearts leaped to' then-
mouths. One started off with all the speed:l4'o Could put
forth, while the ather,-..mora-mself-pos,sessad, retreated
more slowly, keeping his eye fixed on the object in
question, whieh gradually sank into the earth. The
peasants instantly made known to the owner of the
estate the strange thing they had witnessed. The
police were sent ior, and a number of persons, with all
dispatch, proceeded, to the mysterious spot which was
pointed out by the labourers. At first it seemed as
though the men must havedeceived themselves, or were
tatrying on a practical joke,: for at the spot indicated
there appeared to beano thing like a hole in the earth, as
-the grass covered the ground all mound About. .On .
closer investigation, however, a slit was found in, the
grass in the form of a square: It was but the work Of
an instant to discover that this Was the top of a trap-
door, Covered with turf: On forcing this open and
descending, a large cavity was discovered, from which,
however, the late occupiers had already fled: This cave
was found to be the.house of the wretch Adaasch, who
has been condemned to death, together with four others.

articles.text:
-VALUABLE LIFEBOAT SERVICE.

LYTEAM, Monday night.
The lifeboat on this station, belonging to theicational
Lifeboat Institution, has again, rendered most im-
portant service in saving a vessel and five men from
destruction. Yesterday, -at about three p.m.,
.the
schooner Ceres, of •Arbroath, attempted to come Into
poroja a fresh breeze fro= t/aa westward and a heavy
sea.; but, being a stranger and unable to make out the
buoys, she ran upon the Salthoue Sandbank. The
vessel struck heavily, 'sad sustained a great deal of
damage. The Lytham lifeboat 31, U 8 immediately
launched to her assistance. She soon reached the,
eclirooner, when the captain and crew were induced to
remain by their vessel, and attempt to bring her oil
next tide. With the assistance of the lifeboat they
Were fortunately successful, and succeeded in beaching
the schooner in a place of safety. Tirthe absence of the
lifeboat the vessels' crew would assuredly have aban-
donedler. The pumps had to be .kept going all the
Way. It is only justiee' to add, that under the excellent
management of Mr. John Edmondson, and an active
!ilia-committee, the Lytham lifeboat is always found
1,,,r1 first-rate order, and ready for instantaneous service.
During the past few years she has been instrumental,
ulader God, in rescuing the
~,following shipwrecked
crews :—Ship Annie, E. Hooker, of Baltimore, U.S.,
14,; brigantine Nancy, of Teignmouth, 9; saved the
lacuc'ner Turner, of Preston, and crew of four min;
brigantine Han h Jane, of London, 7; schooner E.D.,
of Salcorabi,
0 brigantine, Robert and Henry, of
Dundalk, 67 The lifeboat has also saved the following
vessels :Schooner Philanthropist, of Aberystwyth,
ernack nacteuitoyal, of Preston; schooner Chance,
of Preston, alld the schooner Ceres; of Arbroath.

articles.title: BANK NOTES AND THE DIMINUTION OF GOLD IN THE BANK.
articles.text:
THE BANK NOTES AND THE DIMI-
NUTION OF GOLD IN THE BANK.

(From the Money Marketleview.)
In the Money _Market Review of August the 16th we
made some.remarks on the means .of preserving bank
notes from forgery, and, •by a singular coincidence on
the afternoon of that day the Bank of England issued a
notice to the effect that it had recently come to their
knowledge that some of the paper manufactured. for
their notes had been feloniously taken from the mills,'
and they cautioned all bankers, money changers, and
other persOhs, in taking payment by Bank, of England
mites, not to depend -upon the apparent genuineness of
the paper alone, but ,to examine with increased care the
printing also; .and in all eases, for their own protection,
to obtain and preserve the names of the persons from
whom the bank notes were received.' Of course this
Was a 'very proper notice on the part of the Bank of
England; but when-iiro consider the sensation ,which it
caused we are inclined to think that the contin,' ed weekly
diminution of gold in the coffers of the Bank may,
apart from other circumstances, not be entirely uncon-
nected with the anxiety Of persons both at home and
abroad to prefer gold to bank notes let" they should
get into their possession notes printed on the stolen
13ank of England paper. To show that there are grounds
for this surmise we may refer to the distrust which has
been occasiOned on the Continent, where travellers have
occasionally had great difficulty in changing their notes;
and the same ,kind of difficulty has been experienced at
home in country parts, though naturallyto a less extent.
The Bank returns seem 'to' throw some further light on
the Mater. We will take it return issued b' the Bank
of England previous to the, public announcement of this
theft,-and,. comparing it with the latest returns, see how
far it bears out the surmise that the active circulation
has diminished by an unusual exchange of notes
_for
gold. By the return dated the 6th of August, the
active .eirculation in the hands of the pnblic was
22,536,520 ; on the .22nd; October. it was £21,463,330;
showing a diminution of £1,123190.
The diminution is the more wOrthY of notice from its
occurring in face of the large dividend and other
quarterly payments fniade on Government account, the
effect of whigh isnsually to cause a larger Circulation of
Bank of England notes.
This view is further confirmed by a comparison of the
stoek of 'coin and bullion in the Bank of England at the
two periodS:—On the 6th of Auguat 'the total 'was
£17,506,938, on the 22nd of Oct. it was £15,912,699
,
decrease, L 1,594,239.
This decrease, which will probably cause the Bank of
England rate of diScOnnt AO be speedily raised to 21, if
not 3 per cent., iw bnly partly-to be accounted for by the
known exports of geld. , We are inclined, therefore, to,
think that the diminution of geld for the last few weeks
has occurred rn some degree throrigh the fear on the
part of -file public--espeCially of the foreign public—
lest they should take bad bank notes.
It would be well if the Bank of England, in order to
restore public confidence, would take an early opportu-
nity of informing the. public, not only that they have
recovered all their stolen piper •and renewed.the out-
standing note circulation, ba also thatthey have deter-
mined teadopt a new form of note which it is
.impossi-
ble to forge. This plan would be w complete antidote
to the public distrust on a proverbially delicate point.
