SiQURL TO A STRANGE STORY.—Some short time since
an account was publish 4. of a yonng woman, who was
coming from Paddington to Bristothy an excursion train
'having been accosted by a stranger, who requested her
to take charge of her' baby, about ten months old, while
,she looked after her other children. The stranger never
reappeared, and the young woman had to bring.on the
infant to Bristol, where, after some difficulty„ it was ad-
mitted as .an 'inmate of the Bristol ITnion. From
inquiries -which have been instituted by the Bristol
guardians there is reason to.suppose that the tale about
the desertion of the child by its supposed mother is a
pure fiction, and that the little one is the offspring of
the- Young woman by whom it was broughtlto Bristol,
and who, having been separated from her husband for
some time, is suppOsed.to have resorted to the ingenious
dlvice of getting rid of her liability and covering' her
disgrace by representing it as a heartless case of child
desertion. '
A Calcutta letter of the 22nd ult. says:—' At present
it isinriliing to .ebserve the way in which cotton is
pouring into Calcutta., The jetties on the Ai.o_ghly and
the tricks On the line are covered with great bags, un-
screwed; and in some'eases almost unsown. No care
has'.been shown in packing it, and little is given by the
railway officials in the transit. The road and the river
are often covered with it; natives as they pass, and. the
birds of the air, help themselves to it; and all because
there are no screws in the interior. Yet so largely have
prices risen in the interierlhat it can afford to pay the
high rates demanded.necessarily by the railway for cot-
ton so packed. Little over, 30 cwt. of unscrewed cotton
can be ,stowed away in one -waggon and each waggon
costs from 30`t0 35 rupees, and at that sum hardlypays.
This rupee a cwt. to transport cotton from Agra arid
Allahabad to Calcutta 'is due solely Au the want of
screws. The river presents a. similar scene. Great
boats,. which are as safe is they , are unwieldy
and Unshapely, are borne down by the current
-onto Calcutta. ThiA is the' result of prices having at
last risen above the' level of 1859, when they reached
their highest point during the past 20 years. For-
tunately, too, the rise took place about • sowing time,
and the fact 'that native capitalists are eager for cotton
gives the people' so often deluded .by the fickleness of
Manchester, confidence in the permanence of the rates.'

AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.

This week opened as last, with a heavy fall of rain,
commencing at 2 p.m., and continuing nearly all night.
For a few hours it rained in torrents' a violent gale of
wind blowing from the southward. The land was too
wet on the Monday for any sowing of wheat to be pro-
ceeded with, and little work was accomplished on that
day.
Tuesday Was a drier day, but very cold; the
thermometer down to 60 demi with a S:W. winds
Autumnal tillage was proceeded with °la all the lighter
soils, but on heavy stiff clays no progress could be
made and many farmers, who have gOt so little seed
into ;he ground, are showing anxiety, as it is becoming
later than they like. Those who succeeded in planting
a portion during the first week of the mouth,, have the
satisfaction of seeing it vegetate, and promising to be
strong to stand against cold sharp weather. •
The sorts alluded to in our last week's 'impression
are still in request. Thebreadth of land- to be planted
this season must be much less than the last, if it was
really to the extent generally represented. ,
On Wednesday morning Aome 'heavy rain fell, with
a gale blowing from the south-4est. - /n Scotland
harvest work was checked by stormy weather,. and
with much rain in all the later districts, a considerab,le
quantity in such situations is still abroad. In seine
parts of England, too; there are both wheats and beans
to secure, and we shall hear of harvest work being
carried on in the month of Novembera long pro-
crastinated time—while the condition of all grain now
being secured must be worse than that got in earlier.
At present' two sample's out of every three are ungi, for
the millers' use, and this circumstance tends to prevent.
any material improvement in its vilue, although a
slight amendment is springing up, and with more
favourable weather probably a better trade may be
experienced for at least a few weeks, until supplies
after seed-time increase. The old' 'wheats brought for-
ward this week have commanded prices nearly as high
as those obtair,ied before the harvest. commenced.
Thursday was a boisterous cold day, with the wind
north-west, and Some work Weald be accompliihed,
heavy-land farmers remaining very anxious. One
article at least is now, taking 'favour, fox the cold
weather of this week has set many maltsters at work,
and there has been a great run after barley. The de-
liveries have increased, and prices in all the agricul-
tural districts have advanced is. to 2s per qr for the
better qualities, whild 'intermediate descriptions'arc
now looked after, and every,sort is tending upwards.
The farmers will, therefore, thrash this grain instead
of wheat, and until the large maltsters have got into
stock, prices may yet improve, at least for choice quali-
ties. This is the best part of Agricultural Prospects'
of the. week, and may cheer up the Norfolk farmers
more than any Other, from their having secured a
good deal in prime condition' and With a quality on
the whole superior to either Suffolk or Essex. In Kent
there are' the finest qualities of white of any county;
but these are not numerous, and high prices are paid
for them at home, thus, preventing the usual supplies
of that county coming to Mark-lane where they are
much wanted for nbitholrn buyers. Most sorts of Eng-
lish are now germinating well, which has rather tended
to cause the present lively, demand. The Scotch
barleys in this respect are also well spoken of, whilst
some of the foreign do not please as mu& as last
season. The brewers of Burton-on-Trent will have
the Seale qualities for their fine ales, and large quan-
tities have been sold to them. , The French barleys
grow well, but want substance, being occasionally thin,
but they all are kindly.
Vriday was a cold, bracing day: wind N.W., ther-
mometer 50 des., barometer 29. 20 inches.
Saturday was a tolerably dry day, and some further
field work would be accomplished in tolerably good
order, but the week closed dull and threatening, blow-
ing strong and squally. On the whole the progress
has been to a very moderate extent, from the drench-
ing rain at intervals.

articles.title: DARING, OUTRAGE ON A JUDGE,
articles.text:
DARING, OUTRAGE ON A JUDGE,

•
In the course of the criminal business at rinperary
. , ,
Quarter Sessions, on Friday, a young man naraedi
Richard Carey, aged 23, who also went by the names
of APDonnel and Reardon, was indicted for the robbery
of two shirts, and being found guilty, was sentenced by
Sergeant Howley to three months' imprisonment and
hard labour. No sooner was this sentence uttered than,
with a rapidity almost inconceivable, and while unper-
ceived by perhaps not more than three persons in court,
Carey drew back in the dock, arid, drawing his arm
round, flung a stone of nearly one pound weight, with
his full strength, direct at the learned Serjeant. - It
passed as if out of a sling, se rapidly did it go from the ,
hand of the prisoner to the place where his worship was
sitting in the centre of a full bench df magistrates. The
Serjeant had not taken his eye off the prisoner after sen-
tencing him, and to this might he attributed, under Provi-
dence, his escape; for he perceived ,the sudden move-
ment, and, seated on a light chair with castors, he moved
back and threw himself off the chair. So rapidly did the
whole thing take place that the stone passed across the
spot that the chairman had left, and struck the panell-
ing behind his chair. The violence of the blow smashed
the stone, and a small portion of it remained imbedded,
firmly in the wood-work. Th,a learned. Serjeaiat was
speedily assisted to his seat by the magistritte sitting be-
side him, and the 'stone was picked up; and in a short. con-
sultation by the Bench, it 'WM agreed to return an, infor-
'nation against the prisoner for next Assizes, the grand
jury having just been discharged. The occurrence df
this dreadful outrage created a deep sensation, happen-
ing as it did in the presence of twelve magistrates, over
thirty of the constabulary and a densely crowded court.
The prisoner alone appeared indifferent at the terrible
natire of the offence he had committed. The commo-
tion in court did not subside• for several minutes, and it
is_worthy of remark that amongst those who seemed
most astonished and confounded at so extraordinary a
circurristance were many of the 'three and four year
olds,' who were at the time awaiting their trials for dif-
ferent assaults, and whose skulls, which were patched
• with sticking-plaster, bore testimony of the nature of
the feuds,in -which they had been exgaged. • •

An action of considerable importance was tried at the
Guildhall, Nottingham, on 'Monday. Messrs. "Barber
and Walker, colliery proprietors, claimed of the Great
Northern Railway Company (the owners of the Notting-

have been sustained by the plaintiffs during the sinking
of the shafts of the High Park Colliery; by. reason Of an
.obitruction caused by the water frein the canal com-
pany's reservoir flowing into the works. The isstio'was
left to the decision of a jury of twelve persons residing
in the town and neighbourhood of Nottingham, and five
cothmissioners.

Mr. Field appeared for the clainiants; Mr. Phipson
defended the action on behalf of the Great Northern.

The main facts of the case were stated by Mr. Robert
Harrison, the manager of Messrs. Barber:and Walker's
collieries. A. lease devising to Messrs. Barber, 'Walker,
and Company, the bed of coal and certain' land
situate in the parishes of •Greasley and Selston, the pro-
perty of Lady Palmerston, was produced. The sinking-
of the shafts was commenced in August, 1854. They
were situate about three hundred and eighty yards from
the reservoir at the nearest point. They commenced to
.digiwenty yar& at a time in.each pit. At forty yards
depth they came to a porous rock, from which a great
deal of water flowed, and the .consequence was that
purapd had to be pat down. When they reached a depth
of sixty-one yards the water burst frOrn a fock below,
,
ancl completely drowned them out. On the Gth Decem-
ber 1855 they stopped the water. in 1856. Mr. Wood-
house Was called in, and, under his direction, certain
experiments Were Made. In 1858 the work of sinking
the shaft was resumed. MeSsrs. Barber and Walker had
been concerned in collieries half a century. There was
a good deal of water in the strata of the district, and
some obstruction had been caused by the water flowing
into other pith, but witness did net remember that the
orks had been stopped for any length 'of time. The
Willey-lane .Collieries are about a mile from the reser-
voir, and. in 1855 some obstruetion was there caused by
the water. In 1859 some water came from 'The Hol-
lows ' into the Underwood pits, but he fresh shaft-had
to be sunk. The reservoir covered an area of fifty
acres..

A number of witnesses were aft!rwards examined,
and Mr. liawksley, thei,pmingat civil, engineer, was
called in on behalf of the respondents.
M. Field having replied at some length, the learned
assessor, Mr. Boden Q.C., summed up, and the jury
found for the plaintiffs—Damages £4,902, 9s. 10d.

SHOCKING AFFAIR AT GOOLE,—At Goole, on Saturday,
-George smith, aiarge farmer, residing at Goole Grange,
was committed for trial on a charge of killing his servant,
an old man, named Thomas Duckles. It seems that
Smith had been labouring under an attack of delirium
tremeni. Ile kept a revolver in his room, but his house-.
keeper managed to conceal the weapon from him. On
Monday week his manner appeared. very strange, and he
shut himself up in a room where he kept a gun and some
powder and shot. The housekeeper and Duckles entreated
him to open the door, but he refused to do so unless they,
restored his revolver. Duekles at length agreed to his
terms, the door was opened, and deceased was shot by
his master. The prisoner at once left the house, and,
when questioned by a friend whom he mat, he said he
Was going to give himself up to the pollee, as. 'he had
shot a man.' Deceased died the same day.

Pt Pt-Obre

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1862.

TITE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

TO OUR READERS.

WE invite the attention of our readers to a
Subscription Sheet, on behalf of the Distressed
Operatives, which will be found ..enclosed in
the folds of the present number of the BEE-
Him We hope that a LARGE AMOUNT may
be collected on behalf of the distressed ope-
ratives of the manufacturing districts, from
working men who may be desirous to help in
this work, but whose means may not enable
them to send.indepen dent subscriptions. We
have enclosed a subscription sheet in each
paper, in order to ensure its reaching every
subscriber; but should any reader fail to
receive a sheet, we shall be happy to forward
one upon the receipt of his address.

SUMMARY.
FOREIGN.

Greece has ejected its King and Queen, and
the King has replied by resigning Greece. The
revolution was accomplished on Friday last with
little excitement or resistance. The causes of
-this movement are not yet fully known. Per-
haps the intrigues of France and Russia, and the
natural restlessness of the Greeks, have origi-
nated the deposition of Otho. This King was
a Bavarian Prince, and his family are unfortu-
nate; for the ex-Queen of Naples was a Ba-
varian Princess. The King of 'Greece has seen
three Sultans on the throne of Turkey, and his
reign has extended to more than thirty years.
He never was a man of brilliant parts, and
never, probably, had any sympathy with Gre-
cian history, hopes or traditions. The Greeks
have not expelled a great tyrant, but the King
was childless, perhaps he was stupid, otherwise
he may have been as good as any other Prince
for the place, but his death must have raised
the difficulty that has arisen during his life.
Some Greeks propose Prince Alfred for
their second king, but his friends will remem-
ber that he is heir apparent of the Cobourg
dukedom, and the probabilities of another
ejection, before they advise them to accept the
honour of rebuilding the Byzantine empire.
The arrangement would be disliked by France
and Russia.

The Prussian king goes on spending -taxes,
and the Prussian people feast the deputies
who refused the money; but this is a harm-
less and interesting mode of protecting the
constitution, which may be followed for a few
years.

- The French court is said to be b.ostile to our
government on Grecian and Italian affairs, and
the State business. Napoleon desires, according
to rumour, the recognition of the Southern
States, and our government consider that the
time is not yet arrived for a ceremony that
could have no particular result on the war.
The Grecian dispute cannot have gone far
et and the Italian shadow has darkened our
entente cordiale for a long time. It may have
recently become rather gloomier, but the na-
ture of the case is quite unchangeable. Britain
seeks for political reasons the establishment of
Italian unity. For the same class of reaso

France dislikes this possible consequence of its
Austrian war.

The annual elections in the Northern States
now divide attention with money and war, and
as the polling is favourable to the Democrats,
who are unfavourable to the Republicans, the
voting may affect the war.
According to the Confederate accounts their
attack on Corinth was repulsed after two days
of fighting, or they retreated to avoid being
surrounded. On their retreat they defeated at
Davis-bridge the Federal force employed to
intercept them. This latter event was omitted
in the bulletins of the North. In all the en-
gagements the Confederates return their loss
at 5,000 men, alleging, however, that between
Corinth and Davis-bridge, their opponents had
a greater number of killed and wounded.

-The Confederates also claim to have taken
9,000 prisoners at Perrysville—a place where
the bulletins of the North marked down a
victory. The regiments in Kentucky and
Tennessee are probably new, and badly organ-
ised; and thus the great number of prisoners
is explained.
General Steuart's raid into Pennsylvania,
noticed in our last number, was intended to
supply his friends with boots, clothes, and
horBes, and was quite successful. He entered
the Federal territory on the right of the army
of the Potomac, and getting over nearly one
hundred miles in twenty-four hours, he rode
out on their left flank, with many loads of
spoil one New York correspondent says
sixty-thousand uniforms, but that is a probable
exaggeration.

articles.title: DOMESTIC.
articles.text:
DOMESTIC.

The Queen returned from Germany last
week, arriving at the Nore on Saturday even-
ing._ _ _ _

-The storms of the last and the previous week
have caused the loss of more than three hundred
lives around our coast by shipwreck. In one
instance more than twenty lives were lost, and
the vessel was badly foun d and undermanned. As
the shipping acts were disregarded in reference
to the manning of the ship, the agents or the
owners should be made personally liable.
The Scotch authorities have apprehended
several of the servants of the Edinburgh and
Glasgow Railway, and among others the
manager of the line, who will all be tried for
"culpable homicide," or manslaughter, on ac-
count of the recent loss of life on the line. The
criminal punishment will not militate against
the claims on the company for damages.
Cotton arrives in gratifying quantities at
Liverpool and London, but passes not to the
factories, but to the warehouses. As the price
of the material is relatively higher than that of
its productions, onlyrich manufacturers desirous
to keep on their operatives can yet afford to
spin or weave..

- The cotton is chiefly Indian, and a steady
supply may be expected from that country to
the month of February next, or perhaps
March.

articles.title: PERILS OF NEWSPAPERS.
articles.text:
PERILS OF NEWSPAPERS.

As the annual meeting of the shareholders
of the BEE-HIVE was held on the evening of
Tuesday last, some reference to the business
history ofmour journal may not be improper in
this number. The publication of the paper was
commenced with the design of establishing an
organ that, belonging to a numerous propri-
etary, might represent the opinions of the
Trades on their own affairs, and this object
has been kept steadily in view by the few
individuals who have really maintained the
BEE-HIVE, and brought it to a paying position,
at a great outlay and a large risk to them.
The reduction of the weekly papers to one
penny, immediately after the publication of our
prospectus, was a serious hindrance to fair
trading. That war of the weeklies, which still
continues, exhausted in one case an old and
highly respectable house in the printing trade;
who, after expending it has been said, £35,000
in attempting to establish a penny weekly
paper, were at last obliged to abandon the
enterprise. The paper still exists, we under-
stand, but the money sunk in its commencement
is lost, and lost for ever, to its originators.
Some days ago, among some old papers, we
found a solicitation by circular for subscriptions
to discharge the debt incurred by the association
organised for the abolition of the paper duty.
The debt amounted to £5OO, and the first name
appended to this application for relief is that of a
publisher who then held three orfourpublications
weekly, on which, according to his subsequent
statements, the actual gain by the repeal of the
duty was equivalent to £6,000 in a single year,
A trader, so much helped by the repeal of the
duty, might have paid the debt of the associa-
tion without asking from the public, or even
minor persons in the business, the money in
half sovereigns. With this addition to large
profits, £6,000 in a single year, given to one
individual, and likely with common tact in
trading, to be an annuity of that amount for
life, he was pressed down in the competition
among the weeklies. Literary property, that
apparently resembled an estate for its security,
was sold at half the price which had been
offered, and, we believe, paid for it before the
repeal of the ...duty, and the exertions of a
highly successful life were by a foolish com-
petition lost, squandered, or hopelessly sunk.i
Other publications felt the shock of an un-
wise haste to be rich. We disclose no secret
by stating that among the multitude of new
magazines, commenced within two or three
years, scarcely one has yet reached the position
of paying interest on the capital sunk at its
commencement. Fabulous sums, equal to the
price of a good estate, have within three years
been paid for advertising, placarding, and push-
ing single magazines or single newspapers.
Capital has been ruthlessly employed; and
now, as formerly, it has taken wings and fled
away. One large manufactory of publications,
from one halfpenny to twenty-four of them,
has stopped its business, with responsibilities
that appear moderate and modest amid so
much excitement and waste. A sum of
£30,000 to £40,000 is small in cases of this
nature. We have heard of £20,000 going for
the advertising of a single magazine, and one
penny paper consumed £30,000 as already
stated, in efforts to be known without being
established.

The nominal list of commenced but aban-
doned journals since the repeal of the paper
duty- would occupy a half column, and the
capital lost in them would make a railway or
build a national ship, not unlike the Warrior.
Even literary publications have fallen in the
general tremor. Some cf the literary papers,
backed by publishers of long standing, have
only been a loss and a vexation. The origin-
ator of one well-conducted paper of this
character, after paying £7,000 for the honour,
was compelled to part with the publication.
The oldest weekly paper in the ,field has been
sunk. Another of mature age, and once most
respectable in its 'character, after many changes,
has made the last. A journal influential from
the position of its publishers, despicable from
its management, the Literary Budget, expired
with a denunciation of the public for not appre-
ciating its talent; forgetting that lb literary
Satirist is not necessary.

In our immediate clepartment, several at-
tempts havebeen 'nab to establish "industrial"
journals, even in "our time." One magazine,
under respectable management and associated
with a great union of the working classes,
stopped. We offered to revive the publication,
but the originators preferred its conversion
into a weekly paper, and that also stopped.
Two similar efforts have been alike unsuccess-
ful. In these, and in nearly every case referred
to, the publications deserved permanence and,
prosperity, but they did not minister to morbid,
tastes, they did not present engravings from
representations of events, neither drawn nor
photographed—they were not in the sporting
way, and they were not supported by a capital
almost inexhaustible. The world would have
room for many journals connected with the
industrial classes, if they comprehended their
interests and earnestly sought to promote
them.

The BEE HIVE has always secured a fair cir-
culation, much larger than any journal of its
natuie or objects ever reached. In the troublous
period through which we have passed, the cir-
culation has been better supported than that of
any other weekly journal. It never has on the
other side of the a‘.lcount commanded a reason-
able share of adirertising. New journals do not
easily fall into that part of the trade, especially
in a period of general depression, when adver-
tisers limit their orders.

I We believe that this disadvantage of the
past will be gradually surmounted in the future,
and that with the proportion of advertising
which might, advantageously for the parties
concerned, appear in our columns, we will be
enabled to increase our expenditure, and to
combine all the objects originally contemplated
in our prospectus.
While the circulation of the BEE-HrvE has
perhaps been equal to all that could have been
anticipated from the necessarily contracted
expenditure on its publication, the capital of
the company has not been subscribed for to
the anticipated amount. It was fixed at a
modest sum—certainly not more than had
been paid for a month's advertising and
placarding on some journals—and with the
most economical and prudent management,
the amount should have been expended in the
operations of the past year, As the company
did not find the money, the enterprise must
have stopped, except for the perseverance of
its originators. All the capital paid up, and
all the responsibilities incurred, are much
within the nominal capital of the company, and
no journal has achieved a similar standing by
an outlay so limited.

The re-sult Las been partly accomplished by
labour cheerfully contributed to the publica-
tion; and now that the two sides of the account
are brought together, we entertain no doubt
that the object will be achieved of securing for
the trades' 'a journal that may represent their
special interests, and afford to its shareholders
a full return for the small capital employed in
its establishment.

THE WORKING CLASSES AND THE
DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.
THE manly fortitude and patient spirit with
which the cotton operatives bear their unexam-
pled calamity, has elicited from all nations a tri-
bute ofadmiration and sympathy. Even the Pasha
of Egypt, seated on the banks of the ancient
Nile, has sent a token of benevolence to a noble
race, who know how to bear affliction as well
as suffer injustice. Europe and her aristocratic
courts are penetrated with surprise, and regard
with unaffected astonishment the attitude of
Lancashire workmen, who display under cir-
cumstances of unusual severity the moral virtues
supposed to belong Solely to the "upper ten
thousand." Nor have our colonies in any way
come behind the example'of others who contri-
bute during our national affliction. Bombay,
Melbourne, Montreal, the Cape, in short where-
ever the trumpet of fame has heralded our
wants, and sounded the token of alarm, these
British hearts and English bosoms have gener-
ously responded, and thousands of pounds have
winged their golden flight to the cotton districts.
At home, no less than abroad, a fountain of
ready sympathy has been opened, and all
classes, from the Queen to the London shoe-
black, have evinced their hearty desire to sup-
plement with their means the efforts of Lanca-
shire lovingkindness. The press pours forth
on every side a weekly, and,we might say of some,
a daily account of the progress of the devouring
monster, hunger, and deseribes minutely the
manly and courageous endeavours put forth to
arrest his march. Journals and magazines
teem with suggestions and hints for its allevia-
tion, and itinerating members of Parliament, as
they occasionally address their "independent
constituencies,"congratulate them upon the fate
which has not consigned them to live upon cot-
ton, while at the same time they feelingly offer
their sympathies of admiration. It is amusing,
in some instances, to notice the charitable spirit
of eccentric natures, and the singular offerings
, laid upon the altar or sacrifice. An old lady
in Rutland proffers fourteen loads of hay; not
that she mistakes the species of the recipients,
and believes them to be horses or other beasts of
burden, but simply because it is, perhaps, more
convenient to contribute in kind than in money.
A farmer in Cumberland subscribes ten pigs,;
' a labourer in Dorsetshire six loads of potatoes;
I and a Bedfordshire barber, we have heard,
has actually offered to shave, gratuitously, any
son of theloom or spindle,whose supply of copper
under the crisis should fall short of the usual
requirement. All this is very refreshing to
hear of.
We cannot help turning our attention, never-
theless, to a great and important class of
mcli-
viduals whose interests we are anxious to re-
present, and whose sympathies, as yet, have
only been spasmodically evoked. We allude,
of course, to the working classes and trade so-
cieties of the united kingdom whom this extra-
ordinary calamity does not directlyaffect; whose
homes are not invaded by famine, and whose
incomes are unscathed. What are our friends
the working classes doing, to assist their un-
fortunate brethren in distress, and to render
that assistance worthy of the class who offer to
extend it? Our thousands of societies,
organised for benevolent and trade purposes,
are mighty in their action and very wealthy in
their power to do good. Will these stand by
in silent apathy and indifference, while queens
and pashas, earls and merchants, are exerting
themselves to save.a host of working brethren
in distress? Shall it be said that the rich feel
for the poor, and the poor feel not for their
Own? The lords and merchants have already
Central Relief Fund in Manchester, will the
, workmen of the metropolitan and provincial
trades not exert themselves to help the Work-
ing Man's Central Relief Fund, established in
Padiham, East Lancashire? We earnestly
hope they will; and are ready on our part, as
journalists, in the interest of our fellow work-
men, to do our utmost to aid their benevolent
service. The weekly pennies of the workman
can build up as substantial a 'fund as the nu-
merous pounds of the nobility. Let working
men then do something for their own class and
earn an enduring reputation. Their aid is
needed. The distress is rapidly spreading like

a poisonous ,illcer. Let us work with a will.
Let us bend eptu• broad backs and tretch our
strong arms under the accumalating burden.
Our columns should t3II weekly 6f the strength
and ranks •of a sovereign people. Let them
send their subscriptions; we will forward them
weekly to the distressed operatives. The time
may .arrive, when applying for the extension of
the franchise to the working classes, our
opponents will be effectually silenced when we
recall the attitude of the Lancashire cotton
operatives, and:the generosity of their brethren
who nobly came to their rescue.

GARIBA_LDI AND THE TRADES.
GA.RIBALDI'S health, according to the reports
received within a few days past, improves, and
we hope that the amputation of the limb will
be unnecessary, and that the bullet is not in
the wound. His removal from the place of his
confinement as a prisoner to a better residence
may promote his recovery, and he may pro—
bably be enabled to carry out his purpose of
visiting this country within a short time.

The- committee Of the Trades Garibaldian
Demonstration have adopted measures neces-
sary in their opinion to elicit the feeling of the
tradesmen of the metropolis for a man who
has passed through the ordeal of great political
temptations unstained. They transmitted a
letter to him, which appears in our columns,
and may be regarded as the expression of the
reasons for their attachment to a foreign
soldier.

The attempts to create riots in some parts of
the country as in London on this subject have
been extremely mistaken assaults on freedom
of discussion. Garibaldi's services in the cause
of Italian unity are not ecclesiastical, but po-
litical. The Irish of the Roman Catholic faith
who oppose expressions of sympathy with the
man, and his objects, cannot dissever the loca-
lity of their Pontiff from his influence, purpose,
or utility. His duties could be discharged in
Corfu or Malta, or in Pernambuco, quite as
effectually as in Rome. With them, doubtless,
the existence of a temporal dominion as the
heritage of their spiritual ruler may be a
matter of feeling, gratification, and prestige.
That temporal sovereignty must always, how-
ever, be a dependency op Austria, France, or
Italy, and thus any benefit to be derived from
its existence is entirely neutralised, and the
whole matter is in dispute between the mem-
bers of the same communion: Irish and others
against the Italians and others.
_

-We honour GA.RIBALDI as a self-sacrificing
man, whose life has been a continued effort for
the benefit of his nation and the world. He
may have mistaken the road or the time on
more than one occasion; but his eye was ever
on the right, and no living man more clearly
represents to us the old Roman dictator who
came from the plough to save the state—saved
it from great peril, and returned again to
plough and reap his ancestral soil. GARIBA.LDI
reproduces in life the noblest character in old
Italian tradition. He has even improved on
the classic model.

Old Roman heroes gave all for their land—
its glory, honour, and power—when these
objects were not always pursued in consistence
with the liberties of other peoples. GARIBALDI
has given much to mankind; and loving Italy
well, he loves right more; combining with a
stern patriotism a feeling that might be called
patriotism for the world. The self-denying
virtues of many great old Romans were
grounded on selfishness for the aggrandisement
of their country; but the same feelings are
modified in GARIBALDI'S history by the influ-
ences of a Christian loving kindness; and thus
the best of Roman heroes is re-produced in life,
under the elevating and softening influence of
Christian principles. The tradesmen of Lon-
don may do him honour as a daring soldier,
whose sword has only been drawn for freedom,
but they sympathise with him more as a repre-
sentative man, whose life exhibits that political
uprightness which the world needs more even
than political wisdom.

articles.title: IRON SHIP BUILDERS.
articles.text:
IRON SHIP BUILDERS.

WE extremely regret that the dispute be-
tween the iron ship-builders and the ship car-
penters is not yet brought to an amicable
settlement.. We published in our last number

the particulars connected with the discharge of
two iron-platers from the Keyham Yard.
The officials of the yard say that the men
were not discharged, but left the place, resign-
ing their situation. This description of the
case is not justified by the statements. Orders
had been given to the iron-platers to prepare
the plates for the shipwrights. This portion of
the work requires harder labour and greater
skill than the rivetting, and the men declined
to do a part of the job, unless they were per-
mitted to finish the work. This request was
unsuccessful and they only then left the yard.
We consider that the iron-platers were jus-
tified in the policy pursued by them. The
Admiralty endeavour to reduce the wages of
iron ship-builders, and not to increase those of
ship-wrights. They pursue a process of com-
munism or equalisation, by depressing one class
instead of elevating all classes. It is an ex-
pensive process: it is a dangerous process.
The navy needs iron-plated ships, but if the
work be badly done it would be better undone.
It cannot be so well performed by persons unac-
quainted with the trade as by others who have
made it the business of their lives. At any price,
therefore, the iron plating of the naval yards
might be dear, but then the price is exorbi-
tant. Nothing is dearer than a crotchet, on
which the owner spends like a drunkard or a
fanatic. On this part of the subject the nation
should hear the iron platers. Experimental-
ising in the Admiralty yards has cost us an
immense treasure, and they might have been
paved with gold by the money wasted in them.

- Work wo-rth seen shillings and sixpence, if
done by regular iron-platers, is
.said to have
cost six pounds on the economical practice.
According to this scale, any vessels built and
iron-plated by the Government, will be the
dearest ships on the ocean; although they may
not be the most efficient, the strongest, or the
"swiftest."

Doubts are expressed regarding the efficiency
of the Armstrong guns, on which successive
Governments have expended money at a fear-
ful rate for several past years.
If we are left without good guns or strong
vessels, we might as well save money. We do
not envy the character of alarmists, but we are
slightly alarmed at circumstances which fre-
quently occur; for the money voted for the
navy and the ordnance departments, produce
no great results. Millions are expended; and
we are always experimentalising. This last
experiment of doing work by men not trained
to the trade is likely to be more unproductive
than some of our other experiments, and
while the public do not grudge men or money
for any- rational. system of defence, while
volunteering is active and popular, the nation
must not allow
.the iron shipbuilders to be
driven from its service. They make
no appeal for assistance because it is
not apparently required. They can have
engagements abroad or at home. So far

therefore, this is no common trades' question
involving some quarrel respecting time or
wages; but one Concerning the strength and
vitality of the navy; and if ever again the
nation should be suddenly drawn into hostili-
ties it might fare ill with us if the Admiralty
are able to banish skilful iron ship-builders to
foreign states; by their policy of doing im-
portant work in a wrong a way— and experi-
.
mentahsing on the capabilities of one trade
to accomplish
,the labour of another trade, and
the good nature of the latter to help the
former over the more difficult and laborious
portions of the job, in order to reduce their
own wages!

articles.title: CAPITAL PUNISHMENTS.
articles.text:
CAPITAL PUNISHMENTS.

A woman was executed on Monday- -week, in
London, for the crime of poisoning another
woman six years ago, and since that day strong
doubts of her guilt have been entertained.
rhe doubts involve the first element in such a
case—namely, was murder done, and the
medical testimony is extremely doubtful; in-
clining to the contrary opinion.
Upon the second element was the murder, if
murder there was—done by the prisoner, now
hung for the supposed crime, no farther evi-
dence exists than that during part of her
neighbour's illness she administered the
medicine prescribed •by the physician, and
might have mixed it with poison. Other per-
sons had a similar opportunity, and might have
also committed the offence.
The jury, we suppose, found this woman
I guilty because Dr. Taylor swore that poison-
ing was really common; and the judge in
his summing up gave the prisoner a bad cha-
racter, which had nothing to do with the ques-
tion that the jury were empowered to try.
Another woman might have been hung some
time ago in Glasgow, except for the interest
evinced in her case by the public. She desired,
six weeks before her trial, that a statement
made by her to the gentlemen who kindly con-
ducted her defence should be its basis and her
answer to the charge. They, following the advice
of counsel, refused to admit anything. After
the jury returned their verdict, the woman's
own statement was read. The judge on the bench
characterised it as "a tissue of falsehood." The
people thought differently, and insisted on
an investigation. The sentence was respited
until to-day, an investigation was ordered by the
Home Secretary, and conducted by an advo-
cate—that is to say, a "barrister," according
to our phraseology—from Edinburgh, and the
execution is delayed "during Her Majesty's
pleasure "—a mode of expression that is em-
ployed in those cases where execution will not
follow.

We stated the circumstances minutely some
time ago, and notice the results now, partly to
say that juries must not confide altogether in
medical testimony, although that is not in-
volved in the Glasgow case; and chiefly that
judges should not be allowed to travel out of
the record before them, or express opinions
from the bench, on points not put in evi-
dence.

CAB LAW. -NECESSITY FOR A CHEAP

APPEAL.

A CASE was heard by Mr. Maude, at the South-
wark Police Court, last week, which shows the ne-
cessity for a cheap appeal for cab drivers from
magisterial decisions. A driver was summoned for

leaving his cab unattended in the station yard of the
South Eastern Railway. The case was defended by
a solicitor, and also by Mr. Smith, the indefatigable
secretary of the South London Cabmen's Club.
It was contended, for the defendant, that a railway
station was not a place of "public resott," within
the meaning of the Hackney Carriage Act, the de-
fendant paying a weekly sum to the railway company
for the privilege of standing with his cab upon
their premises. The case was ably argued, but the
magistrate decided against the defendant. The
solicitor asked the magistrate to allow an appeal,
who at once said that as there were some nice points
about the subject he should have no objection. It
was, however, found that the expenss of this appeal,
which must be made to the Queen's Bench, would
be at least £2O, with the chance of success; and as
this amount was beyond the means of the defendant
or his friends, he was obliged to forego the right
which even the magistrate admitted was necessary.
it is quite time a cheap and speedy mode of ap-
peal was granted. This will be provided for in the
amended act now !under the consideration of the
cabmen's delegates, a body of men of whose valu-
able labours we have before had occasion to speak.
When the result of their labours are before the
public, it will be seen that while they have taken all
nt.cessary measures for the protection of themselves
from magisterial dictation, or police rascality, they
have also considered the interests both of the pro-
prietors and the public. Considering the "beasts "
the cabmen are said to be by the Editor of a liberal
newspaper, it is surprising the rationality of their
proposed alterations in the Hackney Carriage Act.

articles.title: BOATSWAIN SMITH.
articles.text:
BOATSWAIN SMITH.

AN appeal for this veteran Sailor's Missionary,
and Temperance advocate, has appeared two or three
times in our advertising columns. We now call
special attention to it in the hope that some of our
readers may be induced to render pecuniary help to
a man, who, in various ways, has done much to ad-
vance the best interests, especially of sailors, and
working men in London, and elsewhere. Boatswain
Smith, as he is familiary called, must be known to not
a few readers of the BEE HIVE, but they will be
pleased to have a few of the facts connected with his
remarkable history recorded. He was born in 1782,
bound an apprentice to an American captain in 1796,
and the same year pressed into the British navy. He
served as seaman, midshipmen, and master's mate,

till he reached the battle of Copenhagen, where he
received a medal in 1803. He became a student
under the Rev. Isaiah Birt, Baptist minister, of
Devonport, and pastor of the Baptist Chapel, Pen-.
zance, Cornwall, in 1807, and in 1809 he gave him-
self thoroughly to the promotion of the spiritual
welfare of seamen. He was the means of introduc-
ing the Lancasterian school system into France, and
he devoted six months of the year 1813 on a mission
to the Duke of Wellington's army in Spain. In
1816 he commenced open-air preaching, which led
to the formation of the Home Missionary Society.
He soon found his way to London, and began to ope-
rate on the Thames amongst the sailors of all nations.
Here he pursued quite a missionary course, preaching
anywhere and everywhere, as occasion offered. In
1825 he opened the first Mariners' Church in Well.
East Smithfield, where he laboured
with great popularity and success for a time. His
open-air labours brought him into frequent collision
with the police, to whom he gave battle single-
handed, till he was allowed to prosecute his labours
without interruption. After establishing the Do-
mestic City Mission and the Asylum for Starving.
Sailors, he formed the first Temperance Society in
England. To them followed the Maritime Penitent
Female Refuge, since carried on at Bethnal-green.
The next great event in his life was the falling of
Brunswick Theatre,
where he directed the opera-
tions for the rescue of the dead and wounded
Several institutions were subsequently formed, and
thus he went on, through evil report and good re-
port, till last year, by special invitation from New
York, he paid a visit to the United States. - -

Such, then, are a few facts of the history of 0.
C. Smith, now lu the eighty-first year of his age.

THE HEALTH OF GARIBALDI. '

TILE CONSULTATION TESTBRDAY.

SPEZZIA, Oct. 29, 3.30 p.m.
A grand consultation of all the surgeons in attend-
ance upon Garibaldi, including Dr. Nelaton, of Paris,
and Dr. Partridge, of London, has just been held. An
exploration of the wound was made with the finger,
but the ball was not reached. The articulation of the
ankle joint was pronounced sound; and it was judged
that no operation to extract the ball is necessary.
The general state of Garibaldi's health is good, and
his convalescence is certain; but the cure will take a
long time.

TURIN, Oct., 30 (Evening).
Dr. Nelaton, in passing through Turin this after-
noon, is said to have stated that the extraction of the
ball from Garibaldi's wound would not be difficult,
and that a cure was certain. There will only remain
a slight stiffness of the ankle joint. Upwards of
twenty physicians were present at the consultation.

articles.title: GREEK INSURRECTION.
articles.text:
THE GREEK INSURRECTION.

ATHENS, October 28.
The Greek revolution is complete. The King an
Queen have taken their departure, and gone to Venice.
The National Assembly will meet within eight days
hence, and will, it is said, offer the crown of Greece to
Prince Alfred of England.

ATHENS, Oct. 30.
The members of the Provisional Government have
given assurances to the representatives of England,.
France, and Russia that the revolution will be con-
fined to Greece. The elections will take place in
Greece on the 10th November.

articles.title: REV. F. D. MAURICE.
articles.text:
THE REV. F. D. MAURICE.

A weekly religious journal yesterday announced
that the Rev. Frederick Denison Maurice President of
the Working Men's College, and one 'of the writers of
the 'Essays and Reviews,' had resigned his preferment
in the Church of England. Although the actual.
resignation has yet to be made, and may be delayed
for a fortnight or three weeks, we understand that the
announcement of our contemporary correctly expresses
Mr. bli.urice's firm resolve. The fact has been known
for several days to Mr. Maarice's more immediate
friends, causing the profoundest grief, in which many
of our readers will share. It is probable that before
long the world will learn from Mr. Maurice himself
the reasons which have led him to take a course for
him so full of sacrifice.

articles.title: IMPORTANT CAB QUESTION.
articles.text:
IMPORTANT CAB QUESTION.

APPEAL TO THE QUEEN'S BENCH.

_
An adjourned summons respecting cabs at railway
stations came before Mr. Maude at the South wark
Police Police Court for his decision, wherein William
Besley, cab-driver, badge No. 1,079, was charged as
follows: 'For that on the 3rd day of October instant,
at half-past nine in the evening, he did, in a certain
place of public resort, to wit, the South-Eastern Rail-
way station, in the parish of St. Olave's, Southwark,
unlawfully leave his hackney carriage unattended,
contrary to the statute.' The court was rather incon—
veniently crowded by cab proprietors and others
anxious to hear the decision.

Mr. Barnard, from the office of Mr. Smith, solicitor,
of Stepney, appeared for the defendant; and Mr. Smith,.
the secretary of the South London Cabmen's Club,
attended to. watch the proc,eedivs.
The complainant, Mr. Abercrombie Thompson stated
that he came by train to the London Bridge Railway
Station, and seeing a cab in front he jumped in and
called out for the driver. He had a lady with him,.
ani had to remain a quarter of an hour before the
driver came, consequently he was compelled to take
another cab to get home. Witness, considering that
an abuse of the Act of Parliament had been committed,
the number of defendant's cab, and on public grounds,
obtained the present summons.
Mr. triith contended that the man was not bound to.
be in attendance with his cab. He was privileged by
the railway company to enter their premises and take-
up passengers, according to the regulations of the rail-
way company, which he was bound to abide by.
Mr. Thompson urged that a railway station, in his
opinion, was a public place, and where there were cabs
plying for hire they came under the meaning of the:-
Act of Parliament.

Mr. Barnard did not dispute the facts as stated by
the complainant, but he contended that his client was
not liable under the sections of the act. He was a.
privileged cabman, and paid 38. 6d. weekly to the rail-
way company for being allowed to stand inside their
Station.

Mr. Maude considered that the railway station was.
a place of public resort within the meaning of the Act,.
and that the defendant had committed a breach of the
law. He should therefore fine him 20s.

Mr. Barnard observed that he had no wish to say:
anything disrespectful to his worship as to the deci-
sion, but he disagreed with him, and with his consent.
he would carry the matter to the Qtteen's Bench, pro-
vided his worship would grant him a case.
Mr. Maude expressed himself, as the point was Of.
some importance, willing to do so.

THE DISTRESS IN LAxca.sutnE.—The working classes
of Notting Hill held a preliminary meeting at the,
Mall Coffee House, on Thursday evening, when a pro-
visional committee was appointed to organise a public
meeting for the purpose of laying the present distressed
condition of the Lancashire operatives before the dis-
trict, and adopting measures, by subscription or other-
wise, to aid in their relief. The meeting was unani-
mous in the necessity of doing all that was possible for
the relief of their starving brethren.

Dr. Lankester held an inquest at the Bank of Eng..
land, Cambridge-place, Paddington, yesterday, as to,
the death of Mary Anne Holland, aged 40, of 14, Stan-
ley-street. It appeared that, as the deeeFied, who was
the wife of a coachman, was employed in washing at
the Marylebone Baths, Marylebone-road, her arm was
caught in the washing apparatus machinery. The.
limb being fractured, the woman was removed to St.
Mary's Hospital, where she died from the effects of
the injuries. Verdict, Death from peritonitis, occa-
sioned from compound fracture of the arm.'

o'clock yesterday morning, as Mr. Joseph Neven, pro=

MISERABLE DEATH OF A CLAIMANT TO A FORTUNE:
OF £3,500,000.—The inquest into the cause of death
of a widow lady, Mrs. Elizabeth Mobbs, was resumed.
That the woman died from disease caused by destitu-

tion and want of the common necessaries of life was
proved. What rendered this case of interest was,
that deceased was the claimant of the above large
fortune, left by her husband some years ago, but
which had become the subject of litigation. Some
documents were produced in court to prove the right-
fulness of the claim of the deceased. A verdict to the
effect above stated was returned.
THE FATAL BUILDING ACCIDENT IN TOOLEY-STRZET;
The inquest on the bodies of Henry Barton and
Thomas Howard, was opened yesterday by Mr. Payne,
at St. John's Vestry Hall, Horselydown. Great in-
terest was excited, and the hall was crowded. The
evidence of several witnesses ha,ving been taken, the
inquiry was adjourned.

TRADE UNIONISTS AND POLITICS.—A numerously
attended meeting of members cif trade societies was
held on Tuesday last, at the Brown Boar, Broad-
street, Bloomsbury, Mr. Facey, painter, in the chair,
for the purpose of forming a political associationi
amongst the members of trades unions. Mr. Howell,
bricklayer, proposed, and Mr. Cassidy, boiler maker,
seconded, a resolution, pledging the meeting to estab-
lish a political union on the basis of Manhood
Suffrage, which was carried unanimously. On the
motion of Mr. Applegarth, joiner, seconded by Mr.
Marston, paper hanger, a aub_computtee, consisting of
Messrs. Applegarth, Howell, Odgers, Cromer, Pether-
bridge, Facey, and Richards, were appointed to draw
up an address and programme to be submitted to a
public meeting to he held at the same hotise on
Thursday evening next, Nov. G. Mr. Creme r was
elected to act as honorary secretary. Not receiving
the report of this pleating until our first edition was
ready for press, we have been reluctantly compelled to
condense it. Reports to insure insertion in full should
be sent to the office not later than seven o'clock on
Thursday evening.

articles.title: TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

THE TRADES' NEWSPAPER COMPANY.

(LIMITED.)

The first annual meeting of the shareholders of this
company was held on Tuesday last, at the Whittington
Club, Arundel-street, Strand, to receive the report and
financial statement of the directors, to elect a new
board of directors, and other officers, and to consider
measures for raising additional capital.
Mr. Burgess having been called to the chair, con-
gratulated the shareholders that the directors met then
with a more cheering prospect than on the last occa-
sion.

Mr. George Potter (manager) then read a lengthy
report, which detailed the origin of the BEEHIVE IleVrB •
papey,its progress during the past twelve months, its
position at the expiration of its first year, and its future
prospects. The difficulties inseparable from a new
paper were explained. The BEEHIVE had not only to i
contend against those, like all other papers, but t had
also to contend against the apathy of many, and the
Opposition of a few, amongst that class whose interest
it had been established to protect and support. The
energy of the directors, and the zealous support of the
shareholders, had, however, carried the paper over
i
many of its difficulties, and t was now in a fair way of
success. Let the paper go on as it had been doing for
the last few weeks, and the second annual report
would be one of a most satisfactory nature, financial
and otherwise. The report concluded with a strong
appeal to those trade societies who had not hitherto
taken up shares to do so at once, and to the share-
holders and subscribers generally, to promote the
BEEHIVE Share Clubs, which had been found a most
efficient method of disposing of a large number of
shares.

The Chairman, in some excellent observations point-
ing out the duty of the working classes towards the paper,
and expressing the great obligations it was under to the
Editor, Bub- editor, the 3lanager, and Mr. Dell, moved
the adoption of the report.
Mr. Graham thought the report, on the whole, was
a very gratifying one, which he would cordially sup-
PoDt. He begged leave to second its adoption.
The motion was agreed to unanimously.
Mr. Garland (auditor) then read the financial state-
ment which showed a considerable increase in the adver-
tisement accountl in the last quarter, and a close ap-
proximation to receipt and expenditure. The financial
statement appeared, like the report, to give general
satisfaction.

On the motion of Mr. Graham, seconded by Mr.
Hibberd, the report of the auditors was received and
adopted.
The following were those elected as the Board of
Directors for the current year :—Messrs. Petherbridge
(joiner), Murray (boot-closer), Dell (upholsterer),
Burgess (joiner), Sibley (painter), Odgers (oord-
wainer), Coulson (bricklayer), Graham (joiner), Shave
(plumber), Butler (tin-plate-worker), Vize (painter),
Hamlyn (joiner), Miles (cabman), Vickery (painter),
Jones (tin-plate-worker), Burridge (ropemaker), and
Wright (painter). Messrs. R. Shaw and Buckley were
elected as auditors. The re-election of Mr. George
Potter as manager was carried by acclamation.
On the motion of Mr. Hartwell, seconded by Mr.
Odgers, a resolution was adopted empowering' the
directors to raise additional capital by way of loan, in
such manner as they might deem fit, all monies ad-
vanced to bear interest at 6 per cent., with the option
of the parties advancing taking the amount of their
subscriptions in shares.

A vole of thanks to the editor, sub-editor, manager,
the outgoing directors, and the chairman, concluded a
very satisfactory meeting.

articles.title: LONDON TRADES' COUNCIL.
articles.text:
LONDON TRADES' COUNCIL.

A special meeting of the Trades' Council was held
on Monday last, for the purpose of considering how
the trades could best render sure and permanent relief
to the distressed operatives in the north. After some
discussion it was proposed by Mr. Murray, seconded by
Mr. Devine, that a meeting of delegates of the whole
of the metropolitan societies be called as soon as pos-
sible, m.order to bring their united power to bear upon
the rbject in the best possible manner. Carried
unanimously.
The Trades' Council having been called upon to
take part in a demonstration to the great patriot
Garibaldi, it was proposed by Mr. Trentlett, and
seconded by Mr. Wilson, that the question be sub-
mitted to the delegate meeting, for their opinion as
to the steps to be taken by the council in the matter.
Notice of the time and place of meeting will appear
in the BEEHIVE next week.

articles.title: SHOEMAKERS' SOCIETIES AND
articles.text:
THE SHOEMAKERS' SOCIETIES AND

THE BEE-HIVE.

At a meeting of delegates of the whole of the London
trade of boot and shoemakers, held on Wednesday kst,
October 29, at the Three Crowns, Richmond-street,
Soho, the following resolutions were unanimously
carried

Moved by Mr. Charles Murray, President of the
West End Boot Closers; and seconded by Mr. William
Clark, of the West End makers,
That this meeting, being composed of delegates of
the Metropolitan Operative Boot and Shoemakers'
Societies, feel the necessity of having a newspaper to
represent the interest of trade societies generally, and
believing that the BEEHIVE newspaper is calculated to
promote the welfare of the productive classes, politically
and socially, we earnestly recommend to our shop-
mates in the United Kingdom to support the BEE-
HIVE, by taking up shares, or by such means as may
lay in their power.'

That the- above resolution be printed, and that Mr.
Dodshon, Registrar, be empowered to print the same
in his quarterly report to the Amalgamated Society of
Cordwainers.'

Shares may be had on application to Mr. George
Potter, BEEHIVE Office, 2, Bouvere-street, Fleet-
street, E.C. ; or Mr. Charles Murray will undertake
to forward to any trade or shopmate,.and see the shares
are properly made out, on a deposit of 2s. ad. per share
being sent to him at No. 26, Gerrard-street, Soho.

TILE MANCHESTER STONEMASONS.—This dispute is
still pending. Several of the black brigade' have
gone into work, and several of them have come out
again. Placards are posted up throughout the towns
in the north offering employment by the lock-out
masters in Manchester to 500 stonemasons, and
counter-placards have been issued by the men warning
their fellow workmen against accepting employment
in Manchester during the existence of the present dis-
pute. The men who have gone to work in defiance of
the trade are as yet but few in number.

INTIMIDATING WOREMEN.—A provincial paper has
the following paragraph :—A week or two since we re-
ported a case of intimidation on the part of some of the
tailors employed by Messrs. Smith (now on turn-out.)
,s
Another case was investigated by the magistrate a few
days since, and the offender (Geo. Smith) was com-
mitted to prison for a fortnight, with hard labour, a
sentence which much surprised him. [George Smith
must be very 'green' to feel any surprise at the sen-
tence inflicted upon him. We do not know the facts
of the ease, or whether George Smith had been guilty
of intimidation or not, but he was a trades' unionist,
and, in the eyes of most magistrates, especially the
country justices, that of itself is an offence sufficiently
heinous to warrant them in inflicting the above punish-
zaent.—S.]

DIRECT TAxArtorf.—At the meeting of the West-
331„.iaster Reform Association, on Wednesday, at 209,
riceadilly, Mr. James Beal, who was in the chair, in,
trodueed the subject of direct taxation. After an able
review of our present system of taxation, he quoted
Adam Smith's dictum, that even", man ought to be
taxed .2.c-cording to his means. What, he asked, if that
were the true principle, could be thought of a system
which taxed a distressed Lancashire operative in the
hour of his deepest poverty in an infinitely higher scale
than Lord Derby? He showed that the effect of the
zeduction of custom
and excise duties was invariably the consum
to increase ption of all the articles upon
which those dutif s were
levied. He proposed that all
indirect taxes
should be repealed and in their place a
simple system of direct taxation adopted. He suggested,
in order to raise the present amount of money required
for our aminal expenditure, that trading incomes
should pay a direct tax of 2s. .od. in the pound, in-
comes from wages, is. 6d. in +l,-
---... pound, and in-
comes from real property 4s. in the Pound. By figures
be showed how much cheaper this would be to all
parties than the present system of taxation. At the
close of the address, which was a most able one, a dis-
cussion took place. Finally, however, it was decided
to resume the subject at the next meeting, with special
reference to the actual amount now paid by working
men in indirect taxation. Working men are to be in-
vited to join in th(> discussion, which iS to take place in
some central locality.

articles.title: CO-OPERATIVE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
GENCE.

ST. JAMES'S (LoNnoN.)—The members of this society
held a public meeting on Tuesday evening, in the
schoolroom, Portland-street, for the purpose of receiving
from the committee their eighth, quarter's balance-
sheet, and to hear explained to them the causes which
had led to such disastrous results in the business trans-
actions of their society. There was a large attendance;
Mr. Vizard occupied the chair. The Secretary (Mr.
Edgar) read the balance. sheet. Considerable discussion
now ensued, several members expressing themselves in
strong terms upon the conduct of the late manager, to
whom the evils which have befallen the society were
attributable. The society has now selected one from
their own body as chief shopman, with an efficient
assistant. The change is already felt, the society's
weekly receipts having risen to nearly £BO. Amount
of business done during the quarter, £798 is. 11d. Paid
for goods, £750 102. 2d. Paid-up shares, £306. Divi-
dend on members' purchases (consequent on bad
management), 6d. in the pound. The meeting broke up
at a late hour.

THE SHEFFIELD EQUITABLE CO-OPERATIVE AND IN-
DUSTRIAL SOCIETY.—The sixth quarterly meeting of
the Sheffield Equitable Co-operative and Industrial
Society was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday,
Oct. 21 st ; Mr. Jas. Dodworth in the chair. The
balance-sheet was read by the Secretary, and taking
into consideration the great depression in trade, gave
general satisfaction. After paying bonuses to non-
members to the amount of £26 6s.7 and £7 10s. to tile
reserve fund, a dividend of 6d. in the pound was
declared on members' purchases, and 5 per cent. on
capital. The committee propose having a soiree on
Tuesday, Nov. 25th, in the Hall of Science, Rocking-
ham-street; tea on the table at 5 o'clock, when they
will be happy to see their ;:o-operative friends from
the adjacent towns. In addition to the grocery and
provisions, they have now entered into the boot and
shoe trade, every attention being paid to quality and
cheapness.
SUNDERLAND CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.—This society
still pursues its career of prosperity, and the quarterly
balance-sheet, from June 18 to Sept. 23, just pub-
lished, gives evidence that the business transacted at
the society's store is decidedly increasing. For the
past quarter the cash for sales received at the store
amounted to £2,653, from which we may infer that the
society's yearly takings will now reach an aggregate of
£10,500 a year—a position of prosperity which must
be gratifying to all the parties concerned. The cash
received for grocery goods during the quarter amounted
to £2,438 13s. p.d., and for butcher meat £214 14s. 8(1.
For the same period £2,312 Is. 31d. was paid for pur-
chases of grocery goods, and £193 4s. 9-1. for pur-
chases of butchers' stock. The balance profit amounts
to 1.31 2s. 9d., of which £lO 4s. 2d. will be paid as
interest on members' capital, £lOB 10s. as dividends on
members' purchases, £6 applied to the reduction of
fixed stock, and £6 Bs. 7d. as balance reserved. The
members purchases amounted to £1,736, and they will
receive a dividend of is. 3d. in the pound. This is anl
improvement on some previous quarters, but it is pro-
bable that the dividends will never equal those of
country societies, existing in places where rents and
rates are low, and where no expenses have to be '
incurred for the delivery of goods to customers. The
society is, however, aiming at a reduction of its
expenses by removing from the High-street to a bye.
street, where suitable premises.at a low rent are obtain-
able.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEE HIVE.

Sin, —I see by the Bath newspapers that one of the
two Co-operative Stores in that city has been burnt
down, and as I believe that all true co-operators must
read your valuable paper, will you allow me to suggest
to the Bath co-operators, that if they wish to have
legitimate and large dividends for their shareholders
and friends, then they should reduce their working ex-
penses to the minimum that will give all fairly engaged
a proper remuneration for their toil. And as the Stores
in that city are within a short distance of each other,
I beg to kindly suggest to the Bathonians that they
may materially increase their usefulness to the com-
munity generally, and their shareholders and customers
particularly, if they blended their two societies together,
thereby saving at least 70 per annum in their working
expenses, which may be divided as dividend, or added
to stock, whichever they thought best would serve
them; and as I consider that the person who makes
the first advance for so laudable a cause worthy of a
special recognition, then I hope that no time will be
lost in taking advantage of this opportune circum-
stance to further promote the cause of
London, October 29, 1862.

CO-OPERATION.

articles.title: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

ODD FELLOWS (LONDON UNITY).
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sin,—l have much pleasure in informing you that
at a meeting of the St. Pancras Lodge, held at the
Exmouth Arms, Exmouth-street, Euston-square, the
subject of your valuable paper was brought forward,
and expressions of gratification and approval, that it
was a great boon to benefit societies and working men
generally to have such an organ, whereby they may
be fairly represented, &c., and ought to be supported
by the entire working class, both as shareholders and
subscribers; and finally resolved, That this Lodge,
having experienced the utility, and convinced of the
good resulting from the support of the BEEHTTE news-
paper, do hereby empower G. P. Myerson to take up
four shares on its behalf, hoping this will induce other
societies to follow this example on a much larger
scale.'—G. P. M.

RUMOURED EMBEZZLEMENT EY THE TREASURER OF A
DUNDEE BENEFIT SOCIETY.—A report is in circulation
that the treasurer of a benefit society in Dundee has
been accused of embezzling the funds in his charge to
a large extent—the sum mentioned varying from £7O
to £l2o.—Dundes Advertiser.

NEW TEMPERANCE BENEFIT SOCEETY. —A meeting
was held at Albion Hall, London-wall, on Friday
evening, for the purpose of establishing a Teetotal
Benefit Society upon a safe and equitable basis. W.
Taylor, Esq., occupied the chair, and urged the
formation of a new benefit society which should avoid
the errors and objections of some of the old ones. Mr.
Bunn gave a. brief outline
.of the objects contemplated,
which comprise relief in sickness, a sum of money at
death, endowments for youth, annuities for old age,
and provisions for the widows and orphans of deceased
brothers; and also by giving extracts from the tables.
Messrs. Jones and Vincent spoke in support of the
proposal, and at the conclusion of the meeting a large
number entered their names as members. Meetings
will be held every Frie.ay till the end of November, to
receive the names of all who intend supporting this new
enterprise.

articles.title: CORRESPONDENCE.
articles.text:
CORRESPONDENCE.

EMPLOYERS AND EMPLOYED.-THE HOUR

SYSTEM.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

' Sta,—Now that the working classes have an organ
established to promote the interests of labour, I feel
surprised that they do not take more advantage of it,
and make known to the community the many acts of
injustice practised towards them by the employing
classes. You may think the following case worth in-
sertion. Seeing with what eulogy the hour system
was ushered into existence, one would have thought,
so far as the employers were concerned, that it was to
be a final settlement of the time question. One, at
least, of the large employers has, for his country jobs,
given it up. The firm of I'Anson having a job in
Sussex, sent some men from the metropolis down to it
without mentioning anything about the terms of
working. They, therefore, supposed that they were
going to work on the same terms as they had been
working in London. They were told to work till four
on Saturday, and supposed that they were to be paid
for the extra two hours. When they went, however,
to receive their wages, they were told that the hour
system did not extend to the country, and that if they
did not like it they had their remedy, to leave, and pay
their expenses home again out of their own pockets.
One of the men left with the intention of sueing the
firm for his expenses, but having spoken to his mates
about it they thought that, as he left the employment,
he could not make a claim for it, and would be likely
to lose the suit.—l am, &c. FAIR PLAY.

SHAM LIBERALITY.
TO THE EDITOR OF TILE BEEHIVE.

- Sth,—My attention has been drawn by a friend of
mine to a notice in Lloyd's Weekly Newspaper, the
proprietor of which states he will give a certain
amount of his profit away for a period, for the benefit
of the distressed operatives in Lancashire. The affair
is too transparent to escape the notice and attentien
of all thinking men. I, for one, deeply sympathise
with the distressed Lincashire operatives, and am
delighted to see all means are being used by all classes
of society to alleviate this distress. This assistance is
genuine and can be appreciated. But let not the
people of England be gulled by a newspaper pro-
prietor, who promise to do this, that, or the other, and
who does it merely to obtain back some of the
popularity he has so justly lost. The man who has
personally, through his editor, once insulted a large
body of working men who were always his patrons,
should hesitate before he once more makes himself con-
spicuous in a matter, the only interest he himself
having being that of personal aggrandisement.
Let the proprietor of this so-called liberal weekly
newspaper act on the square with the men who have
to vend his paper, before he appeals to the public,
promising to do mighty affairs for the distress in Lan-
cashire. This liberal man brings his paper down to
one penny, but he does not bring his cost price to the
retail seller in proportion.
The object of my writing this letter is, that the
public may know, and understand, what sort of stuff
these would-be philanthropists are made of. The news-
vendors are suffering, by allowing this greedy pro-
prietor the personal privilege of giving away what
should be in their pockets. JUSTICE.

NEWMARKET HOUGHTON MEETING.
THE CAMBRIDGESHIRE DAY.

There was a large influx of visitors on Tuesday, in
consequence of the attractions of the Cambridgeshire,
and the great event of the day proved to be well
worthy the interest it had awakened. The enormous
number of forty-three horses went to the post, this
being, with only two exceptions, the largest field on
record in English racing, and certainly the largest ever
seen on Newmarket Heath. It will be found that all
the favourites were decisively beaten by Bathilde, the
property of Lord Chesterfield. Though defeating the
favourites, Bathilde's victory was not altogether unan-
ticipated, as the mare ran very fast for a long way in
the Cesarewitch, and bad won her trial on Saturday,
last at Newmarket. There are no great winners re-
ported, and on the whole the result will be favourable
to the book-making fraternity.
