THE VOLUNTEER FORCE.—By the report of the Royal
Commissioners appointed to inquire into the condition
of the volunteer forces in Great Britain, we find that
the number of volunteers is steadily on the increase.
The enrolled number on the Ist April, 1862, was
162,681; in the corresponding period in 18E1 the
numbers were 161,400; and in 1860, when the move-
ment was in its infancy, 119,285.
DINNER TO THE EMPLOYES AT THE EXHIBITION.—On
Monday evening the British and foreign employes of
the International Exhibition, to the number of 1,000,
dined together in the refreshment department of Mr.
James Ellis, in the eastern. annexe of the building.
The expense of the dinner was defrayed partly by the
exhibitors and others who took an interest in the em-
ployes, and partly by the employes thamaelves. It
was expected that Earl Granville would have presided,
but he was unavoidably absent, and his place was
occupied by Mr. Sandford, the secretary of the Exhibi-
tion. After the cloth had been drawn, a letter was
read from Earl Granville, stating that it would have
given pleasure to have occupied the chair, but an en-
gagement with Lord Palmerston prevented his atten-
dance. This letter occasioned a great deal of dissatis-
faction. Mr. Sandford then gave the usual loyal
teats, after which he proposed The health of her
Majesty's Commissioners: The toast was received
with but moderated enthusiasm. The next toast was
The Foreign Commissioners, Exhibitors, and Em-
ployes,' and it met with a much more favourable re-
ception. The Chevalier Schwarz responded in an ex-
cellent speech. Captain Maynard next proposed The
British Exhibitors and Employes,' which was well re-
ceived. Major Moffat then gave the health of the I
chairman, which was drunk amid much applause.
Some other toasts were afterwards given.
FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE SOUTH-EASTERN RAILWAY.
—An inquest was held on Monday before J. Minter,
Esq., the coroner for Folkestone, on the body of James
Hammon Finnis, aged 24, the son of a farmer at Swin-
field, who had met his death the day before by being
knocked down and run over by a railway train. A
train arrived at the Folkestone Junction from Dover at
12.31 p.m., and detached a break van outside the
station. The harbour train then came up, and the
carriages of that train were attached to the main train,
which then backed to take up thebreak van. Deceased
appears to have been crossing at the time, at the proper
crossing from the down station, and he was struck by a
carriage buffer on the breast, and thrown down, one
wheel passing over his right leg. The station-master
instantly signalled, and the train was as instantly
stopped, so that the leg did not pass under the second
wheel of the carriage. The poor fellow was at once
taken up, and conveyed to the dispensary, where Mr. ,
Fitzgerald, surgeon, amputated the leg. Deceased
rallied for a short time, but, in an hour after the
operation , died. The coroner, in summin g up, exonerated
the station-master from blame; but he thought there
could be no doubt that the crossing was a very
dangerous one, and means ought to b. taken, by the
erection of a bridge, to prevent people using it. The
jury expressed a similar opinion, and returned a verdict
of Accidental Death.' _ _

MURDEROUS ATTACK ON ONE OP HER MAJESTY'S
KEEPERS.—On Friday afternoon last five privates of
the 2nd Battalion of Coldstream Guards, now on gar-
rison duty at Windsor Castle, committed a murderous
attack on one of the royal keepers in Windsor Great
Park, named Mortlake, whose life is despaired of. It
appears that the cause of this savage attack arose from
the keeper having the day previous cautioned several
soldiers against breaking down the trees in getting
chesnuts. These men, it would appear, returned on
the following day with other comrades, five altogether,
for the deliberate purpose of committing the assault or,
the unfortunate keeper, whom they found in the park
between the double-gates and Bi3hopsgate• They said,
Ytu are the fellow we want,' and immediately
knocked him down, and whilst on the around kicked
him in the most savage manner about the head and
body, his skull being fractured, and his front teeth
kicked out. He was removed to his home at Old
Windsor, where he received prompt surgical attention,
but now lies in a most dangerous state. Information
was immediately given to the commanding officer at
the barracks, who took the most active mea,ures in ,
endeavouring to trace out the offenders by confining
the whole of the battalion to barracks and sending out
pickets in every direction. Two of the five have
already been apprehended.

articles.title: DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.
articles.text:
DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.

GREAT FIRE AT WEST HA.—About two o'clock on
Saturday morning a very devastating fire involving
loss of property to the extent of nearly £20,000, broke
out at the works of the London Indiarubber Company,
at West Ham. The premises covered about an acre
and a half of ground, with a frontage of 350 feet, all
substantially built. It originated in the offices and
stores, and was not discovered until the flames had burst
through the room. The company's servants were soon
on the spot, and every means were taken to stop the
progress of the fire, but without avail, and it speedily
extended itself into the main portion of the works,
where, on account of the highly inflammable character
of the contents, the flames raged with fierce violence,
and the result was, as may be expected, it spread
throughout the entire range of mills, destroying the
plant, machinery, and buildings. How the fire origin-
ated is not at present known. The company appear to
be insured for £15,000.

FIRE AT BETHNAL GREEN.—On Tuesday morning Et
fire broke out on the premises of Mr. F. Garner, trim-
ming manufacturer, 28, Hart's-lane, Bethnal-green.
The discovery was made by a police-constable
noticing smoke issue from the hack of the shop on the
ground floor. He at once set about awakening the
inmates, in which he succeeded, and they all managed
to reach the street, but nearly stifled with the heated
smoke. Several engines speedily attended, and by
their aid the ;fire was confined to that portion of the
building in which it commenced. The cause of this fire
is also unknown.

FIRE IN CLERKENWELL, AND PROBABLE LOSS OF
LIFE.—On Monday evening, between seven and eight
o'clock, considerable alarm was caused in the neigh-
bourhood of Clerkenwell, owing to the sudden out-
break of a fire in the premises occupied by Mr. Bold-
ing, situate in Pear-court, near the House of Detention,
at Clerkenwell. It appears that the parents had gone
out, and left two of their children in a room where a
fire was burning. By some means the bed
furniture became ignited, and in an instant the
flames rushed round the room and seized hold of the
dress of a girl, named Elizabeth Bolding. The inmates
and neighbours ran into the room, and fortunately
succeeded in extinguishing the fire, but the poor girl
was so terribly burnt that she was obliged to be
removed to the hospital. The parish and brigade
engines, under the direction of Mr. Fogo and Engineer
Perryer, quickly attended, but their services were not
required, as the fire by that time was extinguished. •
FIRE AT BAYSWATER.—On Tuesday morning, about
three 'clock, the inmates of 43, Queen's-road, Bays-
water, occupied by Mr. Weeks, toy dealer, were
aroused from their slumbers by experiencing a
suffocating smell, evidently arising from wood under-
going the process of combustion. The residents having
jumped out of bed, found the flooring of their sleeping
apartments so hot as to nearly draw the skin from their
feet. It was then ascertained that the premises were
on fire, and that the flames were raging with great
impetuosity, and had already seized upon the staircases.
Scarcely had the inmates succeeded in escaping, when
the flames shot forth through the windows of the
building, and also through the roof. Information of
the disaster having been forwarded to the proper
quarters for assistance, with all promptitude several
engines arrived, and plenty of water being at hand, the
firemen went vigorously to work. In spite, however,
of the exertions of all present, the flames could not be '
extinguished until the premises of Mr. Weeks and the
stock in trade were destroyed. The adjoining pre-
mises of Mr. Eason, beer-shop-keeper, are also much '
injured by the action of the fire; and so are those '
belonging to Mr. Russell, a saddler and harness-maker.
The origin of the fire is at present unknown.
FIRE IN THE CITY.—On Wednesday night, a fire,
attended with a great loss of property, took place in
the extensive range of premises occupied by Mr. Burt,
a crinoline dealer, and Mr. Osborne, a merchant carry-
ing on business in Silver-street, Wood-street, Cheap.
side. The fire, when first discovered, was raging on
the first floor, and in a few minutes it extended to the
second floor. The Royal Society's escapes, the engines
of the parish and several of the London Brigade,
quickly attended, as also one of Shand and Mason's
land steam-engines. Plenty of water was procured, but
they were unable to get the mastery over the flames
until a serious amount of mischief was done; in fact,
the first and second floor warehouses may be described
as being burnt out. The loss will fall upon the Sun
and other fire offices. The origin of the fire is not
known.

FIRE IN THE CITY-ROAD.—On Wednesday morning
a fire of rather an alarming character happened in the
premises belonging to Mr. William Marks, a cabinet-
maker, carrying on business at No. 25, Cowper-street,
City-road. The fire commenced from some unknown
cause in the workshop on the first-floor, and was
making rapid progress, when a number of the neigh-
bours and the parish engineer, and Mr. Cooper, of
Whitecross-street brigade station, attended with their
engines, and by great exertions on the part of all
present the flames were prevented ftom extending
beyond the workshops in which they originated, but
a considerable amount of stock was destroyed, and the
building severely damaged by fire and water. For-
tunately the sufferer was insured in the Sun Fire
Office.

FIRE AT VICTORIA PAEK.—On Sunday forenoon
between the hours of 7 and 8 o'clock, a fire of a very
serious character, and attended with the loss of several
thousand pounds worth of property, took place on the
premises belonging to Messrs. Qharles and Thomas
Lloyd, steam saw - mill proprietors and timber
merchants, carrying on an extensive business in
Waterloo-road, Bishop's-road, Victoria-park. In spite
of the exertions of the firemen, of whom a largo body
soon arrived, the flames could not be wholly extin-
guished until the steam saw-mills, and the two floors
over, together with the vamable stock in trade and
machinery, were destroyed, the roof burned off and
stock in open yard considerably damaged by fire and
water. Fortunately the horses were all taken out.

articles.title: EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A YOUNG ITTNIAN Esr THE THAMES.
articles.text:
EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF
A YOUNG ITTNIAN Esr THE THAMES.

On Tuesday the investigation was resumed by Mr.
H. Raffles Walthew, the deputy-coroner, at the George
and Dragon Tavern, High-street, Shadwell, into the
circumstances of the death of Hannah Brooks, aged IS,
who lost her life at Paul's-wharf Pier on the night of
the 10th inst., in a manner that gave rise to a strong
suspicion of foul play. It will be recollected, from
the evidence taken on a former occasion, that the 'de-
ceased had lived with a young man named john
Archer, a lighterman's apprentice, as his wife, for
twelve months; but that, having aroused his jealousy,
she was most brutally illused by him.
Mr. Hann, the coroner's officer, handed in the fol-
lowing letter, found in deceased's bandbox, which was
read by the coroner:—
'John Archer,—l hope you will not drive another
poor girl to an early grave, as you have driven me.
It is through you that I have done this, for I could
not endure the shame you have brought me to, and
then your laughing at me for being a poor silly fool
to you. I hope God will forgive me for this act.
Mother, you have cursed me when I was a girl, and
your curse has clung to me, but I hope you will not
curse my sisters in case it might ding to them. I
hope God will forgive me this crime . . . but I
could not bear the disgrace. None of you will grieve
for me, I know, for you will all say I brought you into,
shame. . . While lam writing this lam shedding'
bitter tears, for I have no one even to speak a kind
word to me, I have been so wicked. J. Archer said
I may go on the streets for my living after my being
to him what I have been for two years and ah.alf, and
then to be cast off! * I would rather die like
this than do as you told me to do. Mother, pray for
your poor girl, and kiss my poor sisters for me, and
let them have my books between them. My brain is
all at work. J. Archer, when you see my poor body, I
hope you will say, "It is through me "—which you
know it is. To think I could have thought of loving
you] .* * * Oh, Godl look down in mercy on
me. My name is HANNAH BROOKS,
'l, Bromle7-buildings, City.'

Dr. J. Brown Ross said that the pest-mortern
examination showed deceased to have received con-
siderable bruises on the head. The body had apparently
been ten days in the water, and death had resulted
apparently from drowning. She was not pregnant.
She was ruptured, probably from a kick, but more
probably from lifting a 'weight.
The Coroner said that the letter which was discovered
showed clearly that the unfortunate deceased had
destroyed her life in consequence of the barbarous
cruelty of the man Archer.
The jury returned a verdict 'That deceased com-
mitted suicide while of unsound mind; and that the
said suicide was caused by the cruelty and ill-usage of
John Archer.'

articles.title: LAW INTELLIGENCE,
articles.text:
LAW INTELLIGENCE,

COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.

(Before Mr. Commissioner Fonblanque.)

IMPORTANT QUESTION UNDER THE OLD INSOLVENCY AND
NEW BANKRUPTCY ACTS.-IN RE O'ROIJRICE (EDWARD

FALCONER).
This was an action to rescind a final order obtained
by this gentleman, the lessee of the Lyceum Theatre,
and generally known by the name of Falconer, the
object of the proceedings being to ebtain an account of
and the control of a large sum of money, being
moneys acquired since the granting of the final order.
Mr. Keene appeared for the petitioner, and the
affidavit in support of the petition stated that since
August, 1861, Mr. O'Rourke, as manager of the
Lyceum Theatre, had made a profit of £20,000 by the
production of a piece called the 'Peep o' Day;' that
he had an interest in Drury-lane Theatre of the value
of £3,000; that he received large sums for several
pieces, and for the allowance of their performance at
different theatres; that he had valuable property at
his residence, and that Mrs. O'Rourke, under the
name of Weston, was an actress at the Princess's
Theatre.

Mr. Sargood and Mr. Reed contended at great length
that this court had no jurisdiction, as it was not alleged
that the property had not been acquired until after the
last Bankruptcy Act came into operation, at which
time the functions and jurisdiction of the Commission-
ers in Insolvency expired, but the court was not
abolished, and that the commissioners of this court
did not succeed the commissioners of the Court of
Insolvency to create any rights under the new Act.
His Honour ultimately said he had very little doubt,
he could not say be had none, that this court succeeded
to the functions of the Court of Insolvency, and should
decide that he had; and if wrong there was a power of
appeal which could not be made if he decided he had
not; but he would grant an adjournment, and it was
just possible that an amicable and just arrangement
might be come to for the benefit of the creditors gene-
rally.
Adjourned accordingly.
CENTRAL CRIMINAL COURT.

(Before the Recorder.)
BIGAIIYA HARD CASE.-James Charles Camplin
surrendered to take his trial for bigamy. He pleaded
guilty to the charge. The second wife, a very respect-
able modest-looking young woman, stated, in answer
to questions put by the court, that she was not aware
the prisoner had a wife living when she married him,
and he behaved most kindly to her, and she had no
complaint to make of him. She had no money when
he married her, and their union was one of pure affec-
tion.—Mr. Metcalfe, who appeared for the prisoner,
said that soon after he married his first wife he dis-
covered that she had had a child before marriage, and
that she was still keeping up a correspondence with
the father. He had intercepted the correspondence,
but she persisted in her course, and he gave her
the sum of £3OO, acid separated from her, and
heard nothing more of her for some time. He
subsequently married his second wife, and his
first wife finding this out, commenced a system
of persecution. He allowed her a small sum, but she
was not content; she followed him about to his place of
business, compelling him to leave first one situation and
then another; and all this while she was carrying on
an intimacy with some other men. She persecuted him
to such an extent that he voluntarily gave himself up
to the police.
His lordship sentenced the prisoner to six months'
imprisonment, adding that it was entirely for the sake
of the young woman that the sentence was so light.
(Before the Lord Chief Baron.)
ATTEMPTY.D MURDER OF A SWEETHEART.—EcIward
Cramphern, 30, gardener, was indicted for feloniously
and maliciously stabbing and wounding Bridget Mary
Hartnell with intent to murder her. In a second
count the prisoner's intent was :said to be to do the
prasecutor some grievous bodily harm. From the
evidence it appeared that the injuries inflicted were
done in consequence of the young woman being
desirous of breaking off an agreement of marriage
existing between the parties. The prisoner was found
guilty and sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude.
THE WIFE MURDER IN THE ClTY.—Samuel Gardiner,
38, sweep, and Elizabeth Humbler, were jointly in-
dicted for the wilful murder of Elizabeth Gardner,
the wife of the male prisoner. The parties lived in
Northumberland-alley, Fenchurch-street, and it was
said that Gardiner had been improperly familiar with
Humbler, who was a lodger in the house. The facts
are doubtless in the recollection of our readers. 4t
the conclusion of the opening statement of the counsel
for the prosecution the Chiet Baron said there appeared
no case against the woman Humbler, and a verdict of
not guilty was taken against her. The trial of the
male prisoner then proceeded and continued the whole
of the day. The trial concluded at a late hour
on Friday evening with a verdict of Guilty. Sentence
of death was passed in the usual form.

articles.title: MIDDLESEX SESSIONS.
articles.text:
MIDDLESEX SESSIONS.

CHARGE AGAINST THE GOVERNOR OF THE HOUSE OF
DETENTION.

Captain Codd, governor, and Foster, a gaoler, of the
House of Detention, were called up before the Assis-
tant-Judge to answer a complaint made in the case of
a female prisoner named Deacon, who had written to
Mr. Wontner' solicitor, to defend her. Mr. Wontner,
jun., attended at the prison, and requested to have an
interview with the prisoner to take her instructions;
but although he was well known, and produced the
prisoner's letter, he was refused admission by Captain
Codd and the gaoler, on the ground that he was not
the principal. The Assistant-Judge observed: Here
was a poor woman whose trial had been postponed
that she might employ professional assistance. She
writes a letter to a respectable solicitor, and his accre-
dited agent attends, and is refused admission. He con-
sidered their conduct was most improper, and a mon-
strous and careless neglect of duty.

articles.title: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

MARLEOROUGH STREET.

SHAM DISTRESSED LANCASHIRE WEAVERS.—CAUTION
TO THE BENEVOLENT.—TWO fellows, named Thomas
Opborne and Daniel Donovan, both of whom were got
up to represent distressed Lancashire weavers, were
charged before Mr. Tyrwhitt by Thomas Turner,
Mendicity Society officer, with standing in a public
place with a placard exciting charity. Turner said
that between six and seven the previous evening he
saw the two prisoners standing on the edge of the kerb
in the Tottenham-court-road, near a public-house.
Donovan had a placard round his neck, with the words
Cotton weavers, in very great distress,' and Osborne
had a small box in his hand with a few pieces of cotton
in it. He (Turner) heard a lady ask one of them where
they were from, and he replied, Ashton, in Lanca-
shire,' and he then watched them and saw them receive
money from nine different persons. He then went to
get a constable to assist in taking them into custody,
and as soon as they saw the constable making his
approach they ran off. They then went to the corner
of the Tottenham-court-road, where they said they
were from Preston, and received more money. We then
took them into custody. They were both residents in
Westminster and well known to the police. Mr.
Tyrwhitt would make some inquiry about them, and
would remand them. If they were Westminster men
and not what they had represented themselves to be,
he should punish them severely.

articles.title: 3tARYLEBONE.
articles.text:
3tARYLEBONE.

MR. BABBADE IN THE WRONG.—Dominico Molio,
aged 20, was charged by Mr. Babbage with continuing
to play on a barrel organ, after being requested to
desist by the complainant, of No. 1, Dorset- street.—
Complainant in his evidence deposed that about half-
past nine the previous night he was disturbei by the
sound of an organ, and he went out and saw the pri-
soner play at the end of Manchester-street, near a
baker's shop and a public house. He told him to desise
and go away. He (prisoner) took no notice of his
request and continued playing. He went and got a
constable and requested him to get the man's name
and address, and, as they could not understand him,
he was taken to the station-house. Where he was
playing was twenty houses away from his own.—Mr.
Gaselee said if he was playing twenty houses off it
could hardly be said he was playing in the neighbour-
hood, without a forced construction of the Police Act.
He should discharge the prisoner.

articles.title: CLERKENWELL.
articles.text:
CLERKENWELL.

EFFECTS OP A HASTY TEMPER.—Thomas Jenkins,
carpenter, was charged with assaulting William
Anderson, aged 11, and fracturing his thigh. On the
28th of August the boy was playing with other boys
before the defendant's house, when the latter rushed
out and struck the complainant with a heavy stick end
broke his thigh. The complainant was taken to the
hospital, where he remained till the 17th inst., and he
could now only move about with the aid of a crutch,
and would in all probability be injured for life. The
defence was that the boy was leaning on a pillar when
the landlady threw up the wi!idow, and the boy, in a
fright, fell and received the injury. The magistrate
asked whether compensation was the object to be
attained. Mr. Lewis, who appeared for the defendant,
said that if a remand were granted the subject
of compensation would
.be entertained. This would
be far better than to incur the heavy expense of a
defence to an action. The defendant was remanded
on bail.

articles.title: WORSHIP-STREET.
articles.text:
WORSHIP-STREET.

STRANGE CASE OF issAuvr.—Sarah Hawkins, a
pretty and respectably-attired young woman, stated
to reside in Wilton-square, New North-road, was
charged before Mr. Cook with striking John M'Naugh-
ten, about 12 years of age, the son of a gentleman.
The young complainant. stated that last evening im-
mediately after descending from an omnibus at the
Kingsland-gate, for the purpose of proceeding home,
at Woodman's Cottage, Shakspear's-road, Dalston, the
defendent, who was a stranger to him, suddenly and
without any provocation struck him on the head with
her hand, from the effects of which he fell. He was
advised by some by-standers to give her into custody,
and. did so. She said directly after striking me, "rake
that, you little devil.' Mr. Cook (to defendant) :
What answer can you make to this? Defendant:
I am very sorry, but really I don't remember the
assault. Mr. Cook: You have been exceedingly
culpable, that is very clear, however, your memory
may serve you. I order you to pay a fine of 55., or
be imprisoned for three days. The money was in-
stantly forthcoming from the defendant's friends, who
appeared to be a.ilso respectable.

articles.title: LAMBETH.
articles.text:
LAMBETH.

ROBBERY BY AN Ex-Crry-PoLicEmwx.—John Pallet,
late City police-constable, was finally examined on a
charge of stealing various articles of property belong-
ing to Fanny Walker. The prisoner became
acquainted with the prosecutrix last Easter, and sub-,
sequently went to live with her, and she supported him
by her prostitution. She wished, however, to get rid
of him, and an altercation ensued, in which he
threatened to cutler throat. Ultimately he left her,
and carried away the whole of her property. Since
the prisoner was first in charge he had made disclosures
by which most of the stolen property had been
recovered, and it was therefore not the wish of the
prosecutrix to press the case further.—Mr. Norton
senteneed him to prison for three months.

THE VALUABLE BROOCH ROBBERY. - Elizabeth
Wilson, alias Goodsell, the gay' young woman who
has been in custody for some days on a charge of
being concerned, with a Frenchman not in custody, in
stealing a diamond brooch of the value of £67, the pro-
perty of Mr. Richard Attenborough, the pawnbroker,
was placed at the bar for further examination. The
robbery, it will be recollected, was a most impudent
one. The Frenchman purchased the article, and re-
quested that it might be sent to the house where the
prisoner lodged, in Walnut Tree-walk, Lambeth,
when he said he would pay for it, but, vbile pretend-
ing to show it to a friend, he disappeared with the
property. The defence was that the Frenchman was a
stranger to the prisoner, having only been there one
night; but Mr. Norton deemed it necessary to remand
the accused again, and refused to accept bail.

articles.title: THAMES.
articles.text:
THAMES.

SINGULAR CHARGE AGAINST A CABMAN.—George
Tibbs, aged 43, a cabdriver, was charged with stealing
a carpet bag, containing sixteen silver sooons, a muff,
a bottle of brandy, some toys, and other property,
value £9, belonging to Mr. John Marshall, of Leeds.—
On the morning of Tuesday, the 21st inst., the prose-
cutor hired the prisoner at King's-cross to convey him
and his family to a ship bound to New Zealand, in the
Shadwell basin of the London Dock. There was a
good deal of luggage, and, among other things, a
carpet bag, to which the prosecutor called the prisoner's
attention, and said it contained valuable property. The
prisoner immediately deposited the bag in the dickey
under his feet. The party alighted in the London Dock,
when the prosecutor recollected that the carpet-bag
was missing, and that it had not been taken out of the
dickey. They went after the cab and could not over-
take it. Mr. Marshall communicated with the•police._
Police-constable, 198 S, went to the prisoner's lodg-
ings at No. 93, Snow's-fields, Bermondsey, and put
some questions to him. The prisoner admitted taking -
a fare, as described, from King's-cross to Shadwell
Basin, and said he gave up the carpet. bag along with
the rest of the luggage. Mr. Marshall and his sister-
in-law were quite certain the carpet-bag was not re-
moved from the cab, and that the prisoner drove away-
with it in the dickey.—Mr. Knox said there was a
case of suspicion only against the prisoner, and per -
mitted him to go at large upon entering into his own
recognisances to appear next Wednesday.

articles.title: _LINK NOTE RIPER ROBBERY__
articles.text:
THE _LINK NOTE RIPER ROBBERY__

LATEST PARTICULARS.

William Burnett, 32, described as a labourer, and
Ellen Burnett, 31, describing herself as a dressmaker,.
both residing at 34, Brook-street, Kennington.lane,
were brought before the Lord Mayor, at the Mansion
House, yesterday, to undergo a preliminary examina-
tion upon a charge of being concerned with George
Buncher and Robert Cummings, two men who were
before his lordship on Tuesday, and others, in forging
and uttering Bank of England notes, with intent to.
defraud the Governor and Company of the Bank of
England. Burnett was taken into custody at
Birmingham on Tuesday morning. He declared the
female prisoner, who was not his wife, knew nothing
of the matter, and hoped she would be liberated.
The Lord Mayor, however, declined to accede to this,
and they were remanded. It is said that the officers
will be able to prove that this man stole the bank-note
paper from the manufactory of Messrs. Portal and Co.,
at Laverstoke. He was formerly in the employment
of those gentlemen, but was not seen at the works•
after the robbery. It will be proved that he, previous •
to the robbery, contrived to get an impression in wax •
of the key of the room in which the paper was kept ;•
and, although none of the stolen paper was found in his
possession when he was apprehended, there are other
circumstances which tend to prove that he alone stole
the paper.

THE R,IOTS AT BIRKENHEAD.

COMMITTAL OF THE PRISONERS AT
CHESTER.

The prisoners remanded from Wednesday, in order
to have the depositions completed, were again brought
up at the Nisi Prius Court, Chester Castle, on Satur-
day at eleven o'clock.
Mr. Bell appeared on behalf of the Birkenhead com-
missioners (in the absence of Mr. Conway), Mr. Pem-•
berton for the County police, and. Mr. Moore for the
prisoners. _ _

- By consent of the solicitor for the prisoners, some
preliminary alterations were made in the depositions
of two witnesses—Police-Constable James Bacon and
Captain Jones Smith, the latter of whom supplied
details omitted by the clerk, after which the evidence
was read over to the prisoners, who reserved their.
defence.

Mr. Moore then applied to have his clients admitted
to bail, especially in the case of two of them—Michael
Fahey the elder and Elizabeth Curtis.
Mr. Pemberton opposed the application, and stated
that the complicity of the parties mentioned in the riot
could not be doubted from the evidence.

The Chairman (Sir Edward Oust) said: Before I
came into court I consulted with my brother magis-
trates on this question, and we unanimously deter—
mined that bail should be refused against all. They
have all been clearly impHcated in the disturbance.
Different degrees of guilt may be made to appear
before another tribunal, and may receive different de-
grees of punishment; but it is the determination of
the magistrates to send them all for trial, and without
bail.

Mr. Moore: Then I must apply to a higher court.
The prisoners were then committed to stand their
trial at the next Cheshire assizes, bail being refused.

Meetings for the expression of sympathy with Gari-
baldi and condemnation of the French occupation of
Rome were held on Monday night at Halifax and.
Bradford. There was no attempt to disturb the pro-
ceedings, and the resolutions were carried with accla-
mation.

REMOVAL OF WILLIAM ROUPELL FROM NEWGA.TE:
An order from the Home Office having been received
by Mr. Jonas, the governor of Newgate, for the re-
moval of this criminal, he has, accordingly, been sent
to Millbank Prison, preparatory to undergoing the
term of his sentence.

THE AMERICAN WAR AND SLAVERY.—LEIGH, OCT.
28.—At a crowded meeting held in Leigh Town-hall
on Tuesday, the following resolution, after an excellent
lecture on the crisis in America, by George Thompson,.
Esq., was adopted :—‘ That this meeting, while de-
ploring the distress at present prevailing in the manu-
facturing districts, owing to the suspension of the
supply of cotton, would express its condemnation of the
slaveholders' rebellion in America which has caused it,.
and its sympathy with the efforts that are being made.
by the friends of impartial freedom in the United..
States to effect the abolition of slavery and the esta,-
blishment of a system of free labour and just compen-
sation.

AMERICA:

Nww- YORK, OCt.: .13 (Evening). • The: Confederate
General Stuart,. with- 'his whole force, has recrossed the
Potomac at 'Edward's Ferry into Virginia, carrying
away 1,000 horses and "large 'quantities of bets and
clothing, taken in Pensylvania.• Driring this sitecesiful
raid in Pennsylvania, the Confederates passed entirely
around the array of the- Potomac. .The Confede-
rates have respected t rivate 'houses but have
torn up the' railway tracks, arid damaged a
considerable amount of Government property along their
route. Private- dispeches, received in Louisville, re .
portthat another-severe battle has been fought between
Harrodsburg 'and Danville, Kentucky. The sanie (Es,
patcheS assert that the Federals have captured 1,000.
prisoners, and that the'COnfederates were retreating to
Camp Dick Robinson. 'lt -is renioured that the. Con-
federate General Bragg was killed. The farther pur-
suit of the Confederates. from Corinth has been'relin •
quished. The latest dispatches say that the Con-
federates were demoralised, that they have abandoned
.eleven guns, which they had spiked, and lost 2,000

NEW YORK' Oct. 14 (Evening).--It is reported that
General M'Clellan's army will immediately cross into
Virginia, and commence offensive operations. The
Federals will establish their. head-quarters at Rienzi,
Mississippi,, instead. of Corinth. The ,Southern
journals acknowledge the defeat of the Confederates at
Corinth, and estimate their, loss at 5,000; Nashville is
reported to be entirely surrounded by the Confede-
rates. The news of. the 'abandonment of Win-
chester by the. Confederates is not confirmed.
The Federal General Dumont has captured two pieces
of artillery and 150. Confederates at Versailles, Ken-
tucky. The, Confederates have captured a large quantity
of Federal waggons and 500 Federals at Frankfort,
Kentucky— The Secretary of the Treasury, Mr. Chase,
is seriously ill. . At. a large Democratic ratification
aieetiirrheld at New York, resolutions were passed
requiring the Aelministration to fulfil its promise to carry
on the war 'constitutionally,- condemning President
Lincoln's emancipation •proclamation, and deuouncing
the suspension of the writ of habeas corpus. .The
Republicans were denounced as a party. advoCating.
revolution.. A letter from General Scott to Mr. Seward,
dated, March 1661, was read. In this letter General
Bcott said that the only plans open to President
Lincoln were the adoption of the compromise pro-
posed by Mr. Crittenden, or to attempt the conquest:
of the South, whhh was practicable.in three. years
with 8:00,000 men, under generals like DessaiX, Wolfe,
and Roche, but at an enormous cost of blood and trea-
sure. But the people would never afterwards be brought
into harmony.with their conquerors, and would have to.
be held in subjection for generations :b large. garrisons.
General Scott favoured the adoption of the Crittenden
compromise, or allowing the South to depart in peace.
The draft in New York has been postponed till after the,
elections. General Butler has officially announced that
no plea of neutrality will be received from native in-
habitants• of New Orleans; that all refusing. to take the
oath of allegiance are enemies of the United States, and
mustsend their names and a list of their property to the
provost-marshal.
Nisw. YORK, Oct. 17 (Evening).--A portion. of
General M'Clellan's army has advanced from Harper's
Ferry, .'and has occupied Charlestown, in Virginia,
afterwards . continuing its advance two miles, beyond
Charlestown. General M'Clellan's head-quarters are at
Charlestown. The Confederate pickets retreated before
the Federal advance, slight skirmishing occurring along
the route. The main body of the Confederates occupy
a position extending from Bunker's Hill to the Shenan-
doah River. Another division of General M'Clellan's
army advanced to .Shepherdstown ; but,, meeting the j
Confederates in force, retreated. Skirmishing continues j
between General Bud's army and the rear of the Con-
federate army in Kentucky. General Buell is pressing ,
forward. The Confederates were in large force near
Nashville on the 11th, and demanded the surrender of
the city. The demand was refused. It was stated that
the Federal force was amply sufficientto defend the city.
News received here from Mexico states that General
Forey arrived at Vera Cruz on the 22nd of Sept.

()tithe 251 h a young man, named Robert Thornton;
a painter, residing in Bradford, was apprehended in
that town, by Police-constable Gibson, of the Halifax
division of-the West Riding constabulary, on a charge
of stealing a silver watch in his division. The prisoner
at once admitted the robbery, and volunteered,. very
good.naturedly, to show the officer where the watch was
planted,' somewhere in the neighbourhood of Sowerby-
bridge. The officer was elated.; he thought all difficulty
was at an end and the case' quite complete for pre-
sentation before the Halifax bench of magistrates; and.
so, with Thornton in custody, he departed from Brad-
ford by the 3.25 train for Sowerby-bridge in the ex-
pectation of there soon discovering the 'plant.' But, to
the dismay of the unsuspecting officer, when the -train
emerged from the Beacon Hill Tunnel, in its appro.:ch
to the Halifax station, his bird had flown. The
prisoner, taking advantage, probably, of the slackening
of the speed of the-train as it neared Halifax, had left
the compartment in which he and the .officer were, the
latter being unconscious of his companion's 'absence',
till daylight made it apparent. All repinings were in
vain; the prisoner was not there, and could not be seen,
and the officer accordingly retraced his steps to Brad-
ford. He heard of the prisoner on the way; he had
been, seen by some platelayers leaving in hot haste from
the Hipperholme side of the tunnel, immediately after
the train entered, and other persons had also noticed his
rapid flight along the valley leading towatds Hipper-
holme ; but no one suspected what he was and why he
ran. The officer Gibson,- with,two other police officers,
spent a great portion of the following .night in a vain
search fot the -"pridoner in Bradford atid the district
Gibson also prosecuted the search again on Thursday,
up to a late hour on Friday morning, and at length,
finding the pursuit fruitless, he departed for Halifax.—
Manchester Examiner.

DISTRESS IN THE NOR.—On Tuesday the Lord
Mayor received the munificent contribution of £lO,OOO
the first instalment of a sum of about £25,600, sub-
scribed by the inhabitants of Bombay assembled in
public meeting, at which his Excellency Sir Bartle
Frere, the Governor, presided, and which was largely
attended by all classes of the community, both native'
and foreign.
On Saturday two additional lifeboats, on the plan of
the National Lifeboat Institution built for the Portuguese
Government, had their harbour trial in the Regent's
Canal Dock, Limehouse. They satisfactorily underwent
the usual testing of their qualities of self-righting, self-
ejecting of water, and of stability. They leave on board
a steamer in a day or two for the Peninsula.

PETITION FOR THE REMISSION OF A SENTENCE FOR
FORGERY.—An effort is being made at Nottingham to
obtain a remission of the remaining portion of the' sen-
tence of three years' penal servitude passed on Francis
Edward Shipley, who was convicted at the Nottingham
assizes of forging a bill df exchange in 1860. A petition
to the Queen has been drawn up by Councillor Page,
and signed by the Rev. Canon Brooks, vicar of St.
Mary's, and four magistrates?' From the -general
sympathy felt for the prisoner and his family in the
town, a very large number of signatures, it is stated,
Jaight be obteined, but it is intended to confine
the - number to these who, from their position,
are likely to give weight to the document. It
is stated in the petition that up to the moment
of his trial he had borne a most excellent and exemplary
character' had filled the office of sheriff; and was other-
wise held by his fellow-townsmen in the-highest estima-
tion. That the prisoner was a young man just entering
with bright prospects upon life, but he unfortunately
embarked upon the working of a colliery without suffi-
cient capital to meet the current expenses, and in an
evil lour, induced by the facility of discount, was led
into temptation. It is also alleged that the case was
one evidently in which no fraudulent loss was intended
to be inflicted upon an unknown or innocent holder, for
the bill alleged to be forged was an accommodation bill,
given to a discounter direct by the prisoner, and would,
there is no doubt, have been duly taken up at its ma-
turity. Two years of the sentence having been endured;
and the conduct of the prisoner having evinced his deep
repentance for his crime, a strong hope is expressed that
her Majesty, after due inquiry, may be graciously
pleased to remit the remainder of the sentence.
THE HOMBURG GAMING TABLES.—With regard to the
movement for the gradual suppression of the public
gaming-tables in Germany, a letter from Homburg men-
tions that a meeting of the shareholders of 'the Bursaal
Company on the 13th inst. certain propositions of the
Government of the Landgraff were accepted by the
eompany, under the operation of which the future
dividends will be limited to 10 florins a share for six
months' and cannot, therefore, exceed 20 florins for the
Year. Any amount of profit beyond 10 &ring a half.
year will be laid out in the purchuse of shares( at the
fixed price of 250 florins, sueh shares to be drawn by lot.
In this -way it is intended to gradually buy up 32,000 of
the 42,000 shares comprising the capital of the company,
when the remaining 10,000 shares will be entitled to all
the profits, but nothing is stated as to the steps that are
then to be taken.

CBINA.

The following is from the• China Mail of the 11th
ultimo :--

, The events of the past fortnight in China and Japan
are neither numerons nor remarkable. As regards the
rebeltyre have to record the reappearance in the imme-
diate 3ieighbourhood of Shanghai of those plundering
bands whichnsirally precede the main 'body when the
Tadpings meditate attacking a large city. The strategic
purpose fulfilled by the approach of the irregular compa-
nies thus sent on is- to spread alarm previous to the ar-
rival of the general force, and it has rarely been found
unsuccessful where a city has been held only by Imperial
troops. On the 22nd ultimo the smoke of burning ham-
lets showed to the residents of Shanghai the now well-
known signs of an advance into the district by rebels.
On the 29th iLirao the same indications' were'
most marked, and a reconnoitring force was dispatched
from the settlement to check the further appronch of the
marauders. Refugees, as before, continued to pour into
the city and settlement in large numbers,. and the desti-
tute among them had their immediate wants relieved by
a charitable committee, which has been doing-the work
of the Good Samaritan for some time back. Unfortu-
nately the means at this committee's disposal is not at
all coramensurate with the demand'already made upon
it, but the best is being done that can be done: Doubt-
less all the provisions taken in future excursions
against the Taepings will be placed in the hands of pro-
per persons for dae distribution among the sufferers,
instead of being appropriated as spoil by the troops who
;may happen to find them. On Anaday, the 25th,
a reconnoitring party prOceeded into the country,
to inspect the state 6f affairs. According to the North
China Herald; this party must have consisted of eleven
individuals, ten of whom were civilians.' The party was
composed of Captain Borlase, R.N., Mr. Alabaster of her
Britannic Majesty's Conulate, Captain Panmure Gordon
and eight troopers of the Shanghai Mounted Rangers.
After 4sassing some hundreds of affiighted villagers on the.
way, they reached the second. -hartilet' beyond the stone
bridge north of the Soochow Creek, where they. dis—
covered some Tapeings plundering the houses. These)
fled on their approach, but the gallant Rangers, it ap-
pears, not content with this proof of their usefulness,
pursued and sabred all they could come up with. It ia a pity
that our attitude towards the .rebels should be fated to
have a demoralising effect 'upon most of the agents
employed in maintaining it, for we cannot very cordially
applaud the prowess of a few.mounted, and mall-armed
mercantile gentlemen who merely pursted and cut down
flying wretches that were offering them no resistance.
It is reported that these straggling skirmishers, or plun-1
(Yrers, had been sent on :w.stAnce' from the army
Chung Wang, who i§,slTActed to be re-organising an
attack upon ShiingM against the time when the hot
weather shall Ithe abated.

THE FOA.CHING AFFRAY IN NOTTINGIIA3I.-011 the
20th Charles Maltby, William Smith, and Absolom
Bickley, three of the poachers; eonneeted With the affray
in Nottingham on Wednesday night, were brought up
en remand before the town bench of magistrates at the
police court. The case had been adjourned to allow of
the attendance of Brooks, Lord Chesterfield's game-
keeper, who had been seriously injured en the head with
a life-preserver, he not being able to attend that day.
He is still in a very precarious state, and was not able
to he.present at the examination. Superintendent Horne
and Police-constable Rudkin gave evidence to ,the
that when they entered the public house to apprehend
Walker and Worthington Bickley said to Walker, Do
you mean to go, Tom?' Walker replied No.' Bickley
then rejoined, Tip and at !ern,' and immediately struck
the officers ultimately escaping with, Walker. This
morning, however, he was apprehended by the town
poltce. The bench said they would summarily convict
Bickley and Smith, who were each sentenced to one
month's imprisonment with. hard 'labour, in default of
paying a penalty of p. Upon. being removed both the
prisoners looked at the police-officers and said, They
shall pay for it when we have .done.' Maltby was re-
manded for 'a period not exceeding eight days.
Mr. Lees agaiu applied for bail. Mattery appeared
on behalf of the Earl of ChtSterfierd, stating that
his lordship's own 'surgeon was attending the keeper, and
it was uncertain whether the wounds would not prove

should therefore oppose bail. The prisoner was then-re-.

HYDE PARE.—The measures taken by the police
commissioners to prevent the diigraceful viOlations of
the public peace which occurred three weeks and a month
since in Hyde-park, appear to have fully, attained their
object. Though the lapse of each week renders the pro-
bability of a fresh outbreak less likely, the precautions
adopted have been but little relaxed. Detachments of
troops and a large body of police were posted in the Ma-
gazine barracks on the 26th, ready for immediate use if
their services should unhappily have been required. The
day, however, passed off without the slightest distub -
ance. Large numbers of persons tempted by the fine
afternoon, visitedthe park to gratifYan idle curiosity ;but
they were not of a class i cause disturbance, or to take
part in a riot if it had occurred. .There was a noticeable
absenceof the roughs,' and even of the respectable ar-
tisan element that preponderated so largely in the tumul-
tuous assemblies of the previous Sundays. The few
blackguards who ventured to show themselves skulked
about with a hang-dog air that evinced a wholesome
dread of attracting the attention of the few police that
patrolled the park. Judging from, the behaviour of the
visitors there is every reason to hope that the noble area
of Hyde-park will now resume its normal condition of
a place of public promenade and recreation.

f EXTRAOADINARY StAINfENT BY
CATHERINE WILSON.

The following is a copy of the statement of her czzse,
, drawn up by the prisoner herself a few days before her
; execution, and transmitted, to the Home Secretary to be
laid before her Majesty, imploring the clementy.of the
Crown. The expressions made use of,are the prisoner's
' own, and the document was written in a firm legible
, hand, and there were merely a few errors in the spelling.
`. To her,Most Gracious Majesty—l most humbly beg
['your Majesty's pardon for the liberty I.have takers in
sending this', paper, and crave your Majesty's most
merciful consideration of my ease. lam now being under
i; sentence of death for the dreadful grime of murder by
poisoning, which I solemnly declare.l am innocent of. I
am very deaf,: and was unable to hear any of the
evidence upon my trial, therefore could . not con-
tradict anything that was said. I have been in
prison six months, and, unable to get the evidence to
come forward on my behalf for want of means, my means
being all exhausted; and yet without one witness,
there has
_never been proved one person or place I had
ever had poison ofy nor that I had. ever had poison in
my possession. One witness says I told- her the day, of
the death of Mrs. Soames the death. was. not a natural
one, for Mrs. Soames had taken poison in my room
on the
_Wednesday night before, yet this witness,
though a friend of the family's for six years before,
living: with the daughters two years afterwards, never
named. it to anybody till now, six years afterwards,
, when I am tried Ihr my life, then comes forward to say
11. told her this, which I never did. Then 'comes another
['witness and friend of the family for twenty years,. who
h declares I told her there would; be a letter come to: the
house on the Monday. ,She says I told her this on the
Sanday before the lettei- came, yet before this letter did
come it was never told to Mr. Barnes, Mrs. Soames,
, brother, nor her two daughters, nor any one else
_until
my trial. I never did tell either of those witnesses any:-
thing of the kind. How strange those two Women
'should be friends of the family both before and after
death. When the inquest was held not a word .was ever
.'said by either of the parties of what I had, said.
'because I had never said anything of the ' kind
to . them: . Mrs: Hawkshaw, a niece of Mrs.
Soames, was in attendance upon her most all the
time -on the Thursday, and ' Thursday night.
she: attended her alone; not until Thursday and Friday
'night did I attend and it up Witlithe daughter until she
died. Mrs. Hawkshaw was sent for by her aunt to buy
the penny strrap Paper to give me. for tp show that I
had lent Mrs. Soames £lO ;. it was: wrote every
word by Mrs. Seethes 'herself. It was never disputed
by the family or said one' word against -until now, 6.x
. years afterwards, yet this witueas was not called. Mrs.
Soames's,circurapstancea were not good, and she could not
meet her tradesmen's bills. She belonged to a building
society ; she had a certain sum of money to pay evera
week, and to pay that with she always had to pledge her
property. The two daughters say they never knew
'their mother-to lend me any, money, and I always paict
rent every week, Bs. ,6d. I could have no"motive
'for taking this poor woman's life. It was shown by the
witnesses, that Mrs. Soames thought of marrying
,again, to better her circumstances, to. a man I
had frequently heard her talk of, but I never-
! saw. The letters produced in court a day 'or two after
the death of Mrs. Soames,, came to the house. Two
people is called to say they believe it to be wrote by me,
although in a disguised hand. When asked if ever they
saw me write, one says he never saw me write, the
other says he saw me write seven years ago. Neither,
of these two men never saw me write in their lives. I
am sure I did not write that letter. A part of it was
torn away. A false report has been circulated in the
papers that' I imderstood the 'nature of medicine for I '
,had lived with a Dr. Mower. of Boston, which I never
did, nor was there a Dr. Mower living there at any time.
All this Proved very injurious to. me. Every person
that 'I 'have 'attended upen,. and done my best for,*those
that have 'died, has* been exhumed, and nothing. found.
in them like poison, or any poison traced to My posses-
sion, or any doctor says anythingagainst me except one,
whose evidence, is false, and yet I am condemned to die..
.1 therefore through (throw) myself on your Majesty's
most merciful consideration, and.pray to God to be more;
merciful than' man:

'I remain your Majesty's most humble servant,
CAIIIERINE WI LS Olt'

articles.title: .EXTRAO.RDINARY CASE O.F
articles.text:
.EXTRAO.RDINARY CASE O.F

POISONING.

A melancholy case of accidental poisoning, which
has already resulted in the death of one person and,
dangerous injuries to many others, has occurred in
Liverpool. A wooden vessel, the bark Robert, has for
'l7 or 18 months been lying up.in the Great Float at.
Birkenhead; and on Monday last she was brought
across the river to Liverpool, and placed in the
Clarence graving-dock for the purpose of undergoing
-repairs. When she was brought into dry dock, it was
found that the bottom of the vessel had become covered
with. thousands of muscles and large quantities of weeds.
In the process of repairs the muscles were on Friday
scraped Off, the ship's sides, and as a delicacy these
shellfish were distributed among the men employed on
her. Ameng the amber a ship carpenter, named.
Cunningham, who lives ia,'No. 5 Ceurt, Prussia-street,
Oldhall-street„ carried home about a quart;. and about
,halflpa.st 6 o'clvck in the evening, upon his. arrival at
'home, he requested his sister, Bridget Cunningham,
years of age, who keeps house for him, to cook the
muscles. Afterwards both brother and sister partoOli
of the muscles, and ka.ve some to three children—Mary
Ann Hagan, Sarah Hagan, and Ellen Toner—who live
in the Same court. About 8 o'clock, soon after they
had partaken, all the persons who had eaten the fish
became very ill; Bridget Cunningham became rapidly
worse, and at a quarter to 11 o'clock the same night
she died, after suffering extreme pain.. Shortly before
the death of the young woman the symptoms of the
others beeaine so alarming that Mr. Williams, surgeon,.
Vauxhall-road, was sent for; his efthrts, though
' unable to save the life of the young woman, were
happily successful in the other cases, and soon the
patients, though not out of danger, showed symptoms
-of recovery. Mr. Williams was also called to attend
another- Ship carpenter, William Kilread, living in
No. Court, Johnson-street,, who. under similar.cir-
cumstances had partaken of muscles, in an uncooked
state, obtained from the bottom of the Robert. In the
course of Friday night this man's life was despaired of,
but under medical treatment he was ultimately placed
out of danger, though on Saturday he was still unable
'to move his limbs. Several other persons who had
"eaten ,some of the muscles were likewise rendered
exceeding ill, but we have not heard of any fatal ease,
except that of Bridget Cunningham. The patients are
reported to have displayed all the symptoms of.
arsenical poisoning, and it is supposed that the shell.'
fish had become tainted with that poison from the
ship's bottom. The vessel was not sheathed with'
copper or yellow metal, but was coated with some
green-coloured composition generally used for the
'preServation ofiron hulls, and it is betieved that arsenic
is a principal,ingredient in the manufacture of the com-
pound. The extent to which • the poisonous muscles
have been circulated cannot easily be ascertained, as
almost all the workmen carried off basketfulls from
the dock, and some are even known to have sold them.,
The officers of the' Health Committee were as speedily
as possible apprised of the mischief, and they took ail
available steps to collect and destroy the e's-ted shell-
fish.

THE' ROYAL SOVEREIGN.—Great interest is felt in
the progress towards completion of the new man7er-
war now°buildin gat Portsmouth. It is expected or hoped
that she will even supersede the Model of the Warrior.
She is a shreld Ship, and is constructed with the view of
her being able to carry guns whose weight would sink the
Warrior or any ether ship?aow afloat. She is to be fitted'
to carry Sir WILLiANI AIIIATRONG'S guns of 12 tons each,
and so iron-cased as to- defy even Shore batteries;
in fact, if the plan succeeds, she ought to'be able to
carry h gun of 30 tons mounted on one of her turrets. The
difficulty is to reconcile such powers of burden with
tho qualities that constitute a. handy and safe seaboat.
When will these experiments and their frightful expenses
come to a stop? If other nations would not inaitaterand
equal everything we can produce in this way, almost
instantaneously we could understand the profit to our'-
'selves; but at present we can see nothing but vast
expenditure, and the probability that all skill and
courage and glory in war will be utterly swamped in the

THE HIOHWAY ACT.--The measure of last seasiOn
'
for the better regulaiam of highways seems to be gra-
dually coming under discussion. At the Suffolk Quarter
Sessions Lord Henniker, M.P., moved that a provisional
order should be able to constitute a number Of parishes
in the hundred of Hartismere into a highway district.
The noble lord stated that, according to the present
system, so greatly did the highway expenses vary in
different parishes, that in one place he had known them
to be 13s. 6d. and in another £52. As the order 'pro-
posed was merely of a provisional nature, the motion
was carried, and it was agreed that the question should
be taken into consideration at the next sessions with a
view to final and definitive action hi the matter. At
the Norfolk Sessions Lord Sondes proposed that the
parishes comprised in the Mitford and Launditch Poor-
law Union (with the exception ef Milcham, respecting
which there was some legal diffiulty), should be consti- •
tuted a district. The Rev. P. Gurdon, in seconding the '
motion, said the cost of the maintenance of the high-:•
ways in the several parishes alluded to varied' consider-
ably in cost per mile, ranging from 14s. to £l4 88. The
high figures were no doubt due to the pressure of great
and heavy traffic, but still he thought that under dif-
ferent management the expenditure might be reduced.
Gentlemen who were surveyors before 'would now be
sent by the parishes to represent them as waywardens;
and in future the roads would be managed by the jus-
,tices and waywardens, instead of by the justices and
surveyors. He thought the Act was an excellAnt mea-
sure, and likely to carry out the objects intended as well
as could be desired. The motion was agreed to. Mr.
Blyth made a similar proposition with regard to parishes
comprised in the Docking Union, expressing his entire
concurrence in what had fallen from Mr. Gurdon. This
raotion was also assented to.

• At Norton,. near Melton, there- seems to, be ge ,
'organized gang of burglars, whose haunt is unknown to
the police. On the Wolds and other parts various bur-
glories have fromtime to time been committed, and only
a week .or two ago a daring attempt was made at a villa
belonging to Miss Marshall, in Norton, the perpetrators
of which-are yet 'undetected. On Friday afternoon it
was discovered that a still more extensive burglary had
been committed at Hungerford-house, the late residence
of Chariton, the* jockey, deceased. Hungerford,house,
Norton, consists-of Charlton's residence and a smaller
semi-detached villa, occupied by Mrs. Spence, en elderly
lady, who left home te avoid the. bustle of the sale of
Charlton' i effeets- last week, leaving the key of hen house
With Mr. T. Pearson, merchant, the purchaser of the
property. Mr. Pearson was about to occupy Charlton's
villa, and for convenience obtained permission from Mrs.
Spence to deposit certain valuables in her louse during'
removal. The last lot of these was being sent for on
Friday, which led to the' discovery of the burglary.
-Upon entering a scene of confusion beyond' description •
was displayed, revealing a burglary of a vast nature
to have been recently and successfully committed.'
An examination shows that the 'thieves had gained
an entrance by an upper window, by cutting out
a portion of a pane of glass and undoing- the
catch, entering and carefully fastening the window and'
puffin& down the 'blind after them. In the house was
a chisel, with which they had forced some twenty locks
or more; every thing and place in' the house having
been subjected to an examination,- and, after selecting'
valuables, the contents had been thrown about the
rooms in- confusion. The whole of the plated articles
had be'en carefully weeded out and left behind as value-"
less. The will of Mrs. Spence and several other docu-
ments had been read and thrown aside, and,, after ob-
taining all the booty peisible, a campaign of seine
hours' duration Seems to have been Concluded by a
carouse, the spirit bottles havingbeen emptied to the
last drop. The burglars had then departed by the back
door, the key of which, after locking the 'door, they
threw away into the adjoining grounds. ttis believed,,
the burglary was committed on Thursday night, and no
estimate of the amount of booty can be made until the
arrival of Mrs. Spence, to whom a telegram has been
forwarded at Market Weighton. Had the thieves hit
upon a night or two previously, they would have met
with the whole of Mr. Pearson's silver plate and Mrs.
Pearson's jewellery, which -was. only removed the pre-
vious day. So cool and deliberate a burglary has not
been known here for many years, and up to Saturday
night no clue to the thieves had been obtained, although
the police are on. the alert. • -

THE KINGDOM-OP BEinN.—The Kingdom of Benin, 9n
the coast of Guinea, borders on Dahomey. In their fiend—
ish charapteristics, its inhabitants equal those of that
barbarous land of blood and terror. The ramparts of the
chief town of Benin are twelve feet high, and composed
of the trunks of trees; pegged together and Plastered over
with rd clay, but loopholed for arrows or musquetry.
Those parts of the town which are Without a rampart
are protected by a ditch of great depth, full of slime and
poisonous serpents, and:bordered by an impassable hedge
of brambles, through which fire alone 'could make its
way. There axe wooden gates in the ramparts, and the
guards, composed entirely of women, are well armed, and
some richly clad in braided vests, and scarlet petticoats
reaching below the knee, heavily hung with beads and
lions' teeth. Amongst them are some veteran warriors,
whose skins, long subjected to the influence of a tropical
sue' have become blotched and spotted till they resemble
thehides of the leopard aud panther. Their looks are
dyed alternately red and white, and they wear great
metal rings on their otherwise hare arms. Like his
,royal cousin of Dahomey, the sovereign of Benin has
somewhere about four thousand wives, most of them
stout, handsome nikesses. - These, formed into troops,
constitute his body guard; but when off duty, make pots
and pipkins of clay, gourd bottles, calibash basins, wood-
en spoons, and ladles of all sorts and sizes,, which they
expose for sale in the market-place at their own prices'
for these industrious Amazons enjoy the entire monopoly
of this branch of trade, and as a hint to those who would
encroach upon their rights, there hatig by iron hooks
upon a gibbet the headless trunks of seven men, in a
frightful state of decay, with buzzurds feeding on the
fragments that drop from them as they welter in the
burning sunshine. In the centre of the market-place
there is a pyramid, SOM6 twenty feet high, formed entirely
Of human skulls, bleached white as snow by the wind,
rain, and sun,—a ghastly and terrible trophy of barbarism
and cruelty, which reminds the beholder of the tower
formed of the skulls of vanquished Spaniards in the
Mahcmedan isle of Jerby, and similar monuments whiah
adorned the cities of the Incas.—Livingstone' s Negro
.Prince.

THE CHANNEL SaTJADRON.—The Channel squadron,
which will procPed to sea under the orders of Rear-
Admiral Smart, K.l-1., will consist of the Revenge, 73
guns; Defence, 18 gulls ; Resistance 16 guns; and one
other ship. The Admiral will proceed first to Gibraltar,
where he will be joined by the Warrior and Black
Prince iron-cased ships, each of 40 guns. He will then
cruise in the vicinity of the ROck of Lisbon, so as always
to be convenient/y at hand in the event of any
emergency arising calling for his presence in any other
quarter.—Army and Navy Gazette.

the fine barque Usk, built in l3ristol three years

of April last. After being a short time out, Captain
Mathias, the master, put back to Newport, and the
owner had the vessel thoroughly re-caulked and re-
metelled..; She proceeded to sea from Newport in May,
and; after a fine passage,' reached Falkland Islands,
having been 59 days out, and Cape Horn in 62 days.
Here a gale came on, Which rapidly increased' to a

, such being the will of the Almighty, ,he should not
place himself in opposition to it for the Sake of the
,ownere•the -ship; or maything else.' This intelligence
must-have startled the mate, hirt'he rentonstrated with
the :captain With sonic firmness. He said, Con'.
sidar the serious loss yea, will caera. the owner
by ,pursuing this -course. And "willing at any rate

that Captain Mathias should go ashore, leaving
him, or putting some one else on board to take
,conainand 'toad prosecute the voyage. This course, he

tif ctiaobeying the COMmands of theaMost High. Captain
'Mathias immediately said, When my conutfand of
this :ship is taken...from me, take a knife and stab me
with it till I die. ,It cuts me to the heart to take the
ship liame' and,perhaps ruin
,the eviners, but such being
the 'will ofGod,,l cannot disobey it for the Sake Of man.'
The mate appealed to the. crew, ;but they said they saw
nothing the matter with the captain, and they therefore
thought it was their duty to continue to obey him. Con-
sequently he ceased all opposition to the captain's will,

-' conversion' ,ef•hii crew. Prayers were held every

manded./ ',report of how he had acquitted himself of the

articles.text:
HANCITESTER.

A good deal of excitement was created at Manchester
on Saturday, by the arrest .of Mr. Jonah Andrews,
manager' ofithe City Bank of Manchester, onn charge
of abstracting and applying to his own use property of
the bank to a very large amount. The bank stopped
payment last Tuesday, and on Saturday evenings, meet-.
ing of from 309 to 490 shareholders and creditors of
the concern was held in the Amembly-room, Free Trade-
hall, to hear from the manager an exposition of its affairs.
The meeting had just commenced, and the nisuseer ,was
,about to. speak, when it *its observed that there was a
stranger in the room: The intruder was no otherathan_
Sergeant Shanley, or the city
_police, who on being
ordered to withdraw, produced a warrant for the appre-
hension of Andaews, and at onoe proceeded to execute
it. The prisoner was conveyed in a hackney °oath to
the lock-ups at the Town-hall. The warrant had been
granted by the city magistrates en Friday, at the in-
.staame of Mr. Samuel Lyon, merchant and broker, and
,charges the prisoner with having taken and applied to
his own use the sum of £37 17s. Ed„ entrusted to him
for the purpose of aneeting a bill of _exchange at the
I Unien Bank, Moorgate-street, London. There are otber
,charges against hina.one of which is that he has ab-
stracted and pledged seourities held by the bank, and
the semalpractices will involve, it is said, a loss to. the
oproprietors -of something. like- £120,000. The City •
Bank Of Manchester, we are informed, was originally
_started by Mr. Andrews-on his own account, but with
&Avery insignificant capital, as a savings' bank, but
by degrees it changed. its character and become a loan
and insurance as well as a savings' bank, the per-
sons wholodged their -savings in tha bank becoming,
under the scheme of Mr. Andrews, proprietors, and
loaning -their money at high rates of interest. . The
stares were fixed at £5O. each, which a depositor might
pay eitherin one sum, or by monthly instalments of £1
extending o.ver fifty months. The proprietors were. di-
vided-into and worked in classes, each class 'appointing
a cotarnittee to act on its behalf and receive and deal
with applications for loans under the advice and with
the assistance ,of Mr. Andrews, who for these services
was paid a salary of £5,000 per Annum, and was in fact
the manager. We do not know how many shareholders
there are in the bank, nor how many constitute a class;
but we learn that there are 120 classes, and that the
holder of two shares (£100) is eligible for election upon
the committee of his class. Some of the proprietors are
men of property, many of them shopkeepers and small)
tradesmen, and some of them warehousemen and clerks,
who have come in under the monthly deposit scheme.
The shareholders appear to have 'had. almost un- .
_Bounded confidence-in their manageaa- aad, he had conse-
quently access to, all the deeds and other securities
*held for loans, and some of these securities are said to be
for as much as £7,00,0. The charges for loans varied
from On to fifteen per cent.; according to the 'sup-
posed value of the security offered, and where advances
were large the borrower was required to give a life
policy of insurance as an additional security. Of the
antecedents of Mr. Andrews we have not heard much,
except that he has been a methodist local preacher, and
professed to be a teetotaller and a vegetarian. He is not
known to have lived extravagantly, or to havispecuiated
largely, and therefore people are at a loss as to what he

THE SUPPOSED IMRDER OF PETER MAWE,B.,

AT BOSTON.

A letter from Catherine Wilson, who was executed at
the Old Bailey on October 20, for the murder of Mrs.
Soames, was lately received by John Mawer, a brick-
layer, residing on the Burton-road, Lincoln, and was
written in answer to a letter from him. John Rlawer,
who has been twenty-five years in the employ of Mr.
C. Ward, of Lincoln, was• brother of the late Peter
Mawer, of Boston, and it ;will be remembered that
Catherine Wilson was ho-usekeeper to the deceased, and
that she was suspected of having poisoned him in 1854.
,On his' body, however, 'being exhumed some months
ago, no trace pf poison was discovered. Peter
Mawer, it appears, had made a will in favour
of his brother John, who was not only heir-at-law,
but was held in affectionate ree.acl, by him. Peter
Maiver, frequently. told- -his brother that what little
he had would go to him on his death, and about
twelve months before that happened, 'John went
over lo Boston, and in the course .of the after-
noon Peter said 'to him, in the presence of the
prisoner, All will be right .for you, Jacky ;
get what little I have when I die, for thete's no one
else for it.' The same afternoon Catherine Wilson, as
housekeeper, made tea, and after John had partaken of
it he became exceedingly ill, and was taken with sudden
vomiting, and was 'violently purged--the symptoms ex-
hibited by the several victims of Wilson. Peter sent for
a :medical man, who at once came.; he said he could do
-John good, and that he was only'suffering from bowel
,complaint, brought on by change of air. He forwarded
,some medicine, but after takinga dose, whichWaS admi-
nistered ,by Catherine, he became worse. Late in the
evening, Peter Mawer -was so vexed at the medicine
having a contrary effect to what. was ,expected, that he
threw the bottle containing it at the wall, and smashed
it to pieces. The next morning the medical man sent him
some Moiieenedicine, but: as the violent symptoms still
continued,,John, ill as he was, went home to Lincoln,. and
consulted his own medical attendant, who, after hear-
ing a statement of the .case, remarked that it was very
odd a medical man should thave prescribed a medicine
.which had such an effect. A bottle of medicine was
. given to him; and he soon recovered. 1854 Peter
dllawerenade a fresh will, 'leaving his&roperty, which
was worth about £5O &year, to Catherine Wilson, thus
setting aside the will he had previously mede in favcur
of his brother; a month afterwards he died, under eir-
curastances of a suspicious nature, and although it
could:riot be proved he VAS poisoned, there can be no
moral doubt that he was, and that -Catherine Wilson
was the murderess. -Immediately after the death of his
brother, John Mawer•tonsulted Mr. -Tweed, solicitor, of
Lincoln, with referenee to takingstens to • set aside the
ill; but as it was ,preperly draWnitlp and attested there
appeared no chance .of '...success, and the matter was
allowed to dreg): After the cOnviction Of Catherine
Wilson, however, John MaWef stated these facts to his
employer (Mr. Ward)' .and the latter, at the requested
John, wrote to a -soliciter at Boston, for infornaatien
,about the will, but. reeeivgd no .answer. Mr. Ward,
then, thinking it , possitde to :obtain an admission
from the condemned murderess that coercion and
amine influence was nised ,to induce Peter Mawer -to
sign the last will—especially as it ,could do no ',arm to
her to now acknowledge it if such was the cue—en-
•deavoured to obtainan interview with her. He accord-
ingly wrote to the Sheriff for permission to visit the.
condemned, at the same time statinghis object. In reply
he received a letter Jstating that Catherine Wilson
refused to see him, and therefore he could not gnat the.
,permission required. At this time .Mr. Ward happened
-to be in London, and he saw Ur. Under-Sheriff Maekrell,
and stated the above :facts to
,hiel The .IJ/Kies,sheriff
said there' Was not the slightest reason to believe
...that
the condemned woman would :give the information
sought for, but at the taraa time he offered to give Mr.
Ward an order to see her. This .was declined, but on
.reaching home /gr. Ward advised John Mawer,to write
to' Wilson himself with reference to the wid. • A ,letter
was accordingly written by Maser's wife, and the
following reply (in the handwriting (A: the prisaner)mras
,raceived

Gaol of Newate; 13th Zaylof Oct., .186,1
Sir,:--I received yor.r.' 'letter this morning. .must
,decline your visit with thinks. YOU Say YOU eineenly
forgive the past. You .never had .anything to forgive

I have been in 'prison

r 1 will not see any of

A CuitoYMAN CONVLCTED or POACHING.—At
the weekly petty , sessions of ,Chorley, the Rev.
.Tohn Williams, incumbent of Enxton, was charged with
'respassing in pursuit of game on land belonging to Mr.
t. B. Crosse, in the township of_ Whittle-le-Woods.
Mr. Wilson, who appeared for the complainant, stated
that his client felt it incumbent upon him to notice this
offence on the part of the rev, defendant, inasmuch as it
was not the first offence of which he had had to complain.
The defendant had often had the privilege of going upon
Mr. Crosse's land with others, and he had frequently
taken the opportunity of poaching thereon. On one
occasion he was seen in a tree with a gun in his hand, on
another he has secreted in a pit, and on a third he was
feu.nd hidden in a hut which he had erected to carry on
these practices. Edward Seger, gamekeeper to Mr. Crosse,
deposed that on the 18th of Oct. he saw the defendant on
a cop of land belonging to Mr. Crosse, but close to land
in the occupation of one Peter Smith. There was' also a
ditch anda hedge near, but ditch, cop, and hedge were
all an Mn Crosse's land. The defendant was looking
in the direction of the wood, and he had a gun in his
hand. Game occasionally came through the hedge near
which he was standing. Corroborative evidence having
been given by Mr. Crosse, Mr. Williams admitted the
facts as stated by the gamekeeper, but contended that
the, hedge was the boundary of the land. Mr. Crosse
evidently entertained an erroneous idea as to the boun-
dary. The defendant said he did not profess to be a
sportsman, but sedentary habits did not agree with him,
and he went out occasionally. Thehench informed de-
fendant that the law- provided him with a remedy, if the
boundary, as stated, was not correct, but the ditch
would have to be considered the line. After a short
consultation, their worships inflicted a fine of 20s. and
costs. Another case of a similar character was then
preferred, the offence
'having been committed on the
15th instant. The rev, gentleman admitted' that
he was guilty of the second offence if guilty of the
first, and he was again fined 20s.

MR. LAING AND THE PUBLIC MEETING AT CALCUTTA.
—At this meeting, on the 6th of Septemberlast, Mr. Lame
was highly complimented On the manner ill which he
had fulfilled his duty as the Indian Chancellor of the
Exchequer, and Sir CHARLES WOOD, tkie Secretary
of State for India, was severely bland for his want of
courtesy and consideration to both Mr. LALNG and the
late Lord CANNING. An address was voted to .Mr.
LAING recording the sense of the meeting that he had in
the fullest manner realised the expectations the British
inhabitants of India had formed of the value of his
services. There are now upwards of 14,00,000 in
the Calcutta treasury.
INTELLIGENCE FROM NEVADA TEaßrronY.—Ths
Secretary Of Nevada Territory writes to the Commis-
sioner of the General Land Office, under date of July
28, that 83 quartz mills are now in operation there; and
20 are in process of construction. There are many
springs in the territory, and some haling ones, whose
waters rise two and three feet from the surface. There
is little timber in the territory, except a belt of pine in
close proximity to the Sierra Nevada. The surface is
generally composed of sandy or alkali plains, covered
with sage bushes. Communication is had daily with
California, and the eapital invested in transportation
across the zuountaia araounts to 'five inillions of dollars.
