MORE CAPTURES DY THE CONFEDERATE ALABAMA--
LIVERPOOL, Oct. 27.—The ship Tonowanda, from
Philadelphia, which arrived to-day, reports that on the
9th of October, at 4 p.m., in lat. 41, long. 55, she was
captured by the steamer Alabama (290.) Captain Julius
was taken on, board, and found there Captain Harmon
and crew of the late bark Wave Crest, from New York
for • Cardiff, end Captain Johnson and crew of the
late brig Dunkirk, from New York for Lisbon, all
all prisoners and in irons on deck-their vessels having
been burnt two days previous. The next day the pri-
soners were transferred to the Tonowanda, and Captain
Julius alone remained on board the Alabama as hostage.
On the 11th of October they captured and burnt the ship
Manchester, from New York for Liverpool. Her captain
and crew were also put on board the Tonowanda, which
Captain Julius was now informed was a cartel. No more
prizes were Olen till the evening of the 13th, and, there
being every appearance of thick weather, Captain
Julius was put on board the Tonowanda and allowed to
proceed, after having given a ransom bond. All the
-captains, officers, and crews are paroled prisoners of war.
. Loss OF A SCHOONER WITH ALL HANDS.—On the
25th the fishing smack Alarm, belonging to Mr. Mark-
row, of this port arrived in Humber. The captain
reports that he sighted a schooner in distress in the
North Sea on Tuesday last. The course was at once
altered, and the smack rapidly bore down upon the dis-
abled vessel, which was rolling in the trough of the sea
in a most fearful manner. On nearing the vessel it was
' seen that her decks were swept, and the men. appeared'
in a very exhausted condition. A boat was at once low-
ered from the smack and manned by two of her crew,
who proceeded to the rescue. After much buffetting the
brave fellows succeeded in reaching the sinking ship.
The master and the crew, six in number, were taken into
the boat, and the return voyage was commenced. Before
very long, however, a heavy sea struck the boat and
swamped her, when the whole Of the men were thrown
out and drowned. The men on board the smack used
every endeavour to save them, but without avail. The
crew of the Smack were unable to ascertain the name of
the lost vessel. The fishing smack Intrepid, Captain
Scott, belonging to this port, also arrived at Hull on
Saturday evening. She reports that on Tuesday last she
fell in with the brig Sovereign, of South Shields, in
distress in the North Sea. The crew, consisting of eight
men, were taken on board the Intrepid, and brought safe
to Hull. The wreck was also taken in tow by the smack,
which had herself sustained damage. When about 50
miles from the Humber the Sovereign sank.
We hear it rumoured that Major-General Sir Robert
Garrett is about to proceed to Code as Commander of
the Forces, in succession to the late Sir John Inglis.
THE LORD ADVOCATE.—A tale has been put forward
that the Lord Advocate has been persuaded by his
friend to accept the vacant judgeship in the Court of
Session, and that Mr. Maitland, the present Solicitor-
General, will certainly take his place as Advocate, and
will try to succeed him as member for Edinburgh.
The story is exceedingly improbable on the face of it;
and we have reason to:We- %at it is erroneous.

-there had been such a throng of worldly cares hurrying

It is not long since I felt myself quite sure of fortune's

ment At present I feel so tempest-tessed and weather-

My own individual interests are nothing: The merest
1 pittance would content me if I could crawl out from

'WALKING E=ILCISE.—The degree of walking facility
pessessed,by each person depends in a great measure
upon the constretiou of the foot. :The bones of a pro-
perly-shaped foot . form a double arch, being arcked
lengthways and sideways—although, when covered with
the Muscle and skin, theoutside of the foot, from the
heel to the little tee, touches the ground in consequence
of the archheing very low—and the weight of the body
oonsequentlY paesses solely on those parts ef the body
,which form, ac it were, the piers of this arch. This
arrangement renders the foot more capable of bearing a
,heavy weight, ankl,at the same time, gives it elasticity,;
.and for this reason we find that persons whose feet are
flat, either naturally or from wearing misshapen boots,
are unable to :walk any considerable distance without.

, LORD BYROIC—Iirs- POEMS, THE GIAOUR,' AND
LARA:—OcroiiER, 1_813.---' The Giaour ' is a trial of
skill how far the picturesque, animated, and eloquent
description will please without dignity or delicacy of
character, novelty of scene or manners, interesting
-narrative, or elevated sentiments. Evans similar to
those recorded in this tale have notonly been thrice told
:abut:three hundred times; and in point of manners,
everyone who has read a book of Travels in Turkey
knows too well all of which he is here reminded not to
:feel a certain disappointment at being carried so far, and
shown nothing new. Fragments of this uninteresting
story are tricked out in gaudy colouring, and, amidst a
greater portion of indifferent lines than are fairly admis-
sible in so short a production, we meet occasional proofs
of originality and genius. The Giaour' ranks far be-
low any former production of the same author. It con-
tributes, as far as its writer goes, to injure the taste of
the age, by reducing poetry merely to an amusement for
.a vacant hour, instead of employing it to elevate our
minds, soften alma hearts, and refine our pleasures.
Whether these effects are produced by sentiments, by
characters, by imagery is immaterial; when they -are
not produced, when poetry addresses itself chiefly,
through the ear to the eye, she must be on the decline;
and this decline works like The Giaour ' at once ac-
celerate and proclaim.—' Lam.' Hero are all Lord
Byron's accustomed powers of language and description,
his energetic edam.° of our attention, his forceful
manner of stamping images, so that we cannot erase
them if we would, of identifying them with our
11 thoughts, so that they pursue when we attempt to fly
them; his verses have fangs. Here is also his accustomed
celebration of the unnatural and unfrequent union be-
tween genius and crime. That it is a union not unfre-
quent, knaves endeavour to teach, and fools willingly
believe. But experience denies the fact, and it suits not
the higher walk of poetry, which, without giving direct
lessons, should always soothe, elevate, or mend the
heart.—Mrs. Trench.
THE ARAB AND THE BABYLE.—The normal state of
the Arab is that of a wanderer and a dweller in tents: he
has no instinctive attachment to the soil, and when he
does take to a settled life, it is, at it were, under protest;
contenting himself with an unsubstantial and flimsy
dwelling, and bestowing no more labour on the ground
than is required to raise a scanty crop of barley. The
Kabyle, on the other hand, clings as tightly to his rocks
as a limpet: he builds himself a comfortable, substantial
house, with stoned walls and a tiled roof, and changes
the rough mountain-side into a rich garden. The Arab
hates labour, and has few manufactures; the Kabyle is
industrious, and a clever handicraftsman, especially in
the working of metals. The Arab lies freely and ob-
jectlessly, and pilfers for the love of pilfering :-his state-
ment is valueless, except as the means of arriving at the
truth by a kind of inductive process. The Kabyle, as a
general rule' tells the truth, and, unless you are at
enmity with him, respects your property. He will make
a hard bargain with you, but, once made, he will keep to
it; unlike the Arab, who, if you leave him a loop-hole,
will wriggle out through it. With strangers there is a
mixture of shyness and obsequiousness in the Arab's be-
haviour, while about the Kabyle there is an unmistak-
able air of independence and self-reliance, as if he did
not much care what you thought about him. In short,
there is little or nothing of the Asiatic about the Kabyle.
Even his Mahometanism is of an un-Oriental east.—
Fraser's Magazine.

THE MONEY COST OP THE AMERICAN WAR. - The
expenses of the North in carrying on its vain attempt to
put down all efforts on the part of the South to obtain
the blessings of self-government are said to nave
amounted, during the second quarter of the present year,
to £38,800,000, being at the rate of nearly £160,000,000
per annum. The Confederate Government seems, it is
said, to have more carefully husbanded its resources.
From the beginning of the war to August last its whole
outlay fell short of £77,000.000.

OUR FUTCRE QUERN.—Mr. LINDSAY in his speech at tha
Chertsey Agricultural dinner, gratified his hearers with
an account of the good things said at Copenhagen of
the betrothed of the PRINCE of WALns. He had
lately spent an evening with a family there who were
intimately acquainted with her, and had known het
from her infancy. It was scarcely possible, he said, to
conceive the high terms in which the whole family
spoke of that young PRINCESS. 'By those who know her
best, she is considered well worthy to follow our good,
our virtuous, our truly noble QUEEN; and he believed
the PRINCE of WALES had made a happy choice for
himself. and a still happier choice for the future generi.-
lions of England.'

of innocence, or to advance the just and rightful claims
of those who are without the means of otherwise prose-

pARIS Permanent Universal Exhi-
TO BE OPENED IN 1863.
For many years National Exhibitions have beeen held
In various cities, with universal success iu stimulating
industry and developing trade between the countries
represented by the Exhibitions.
The central position of Paris, and the vast nninber of
visitors passing through the city every year, have sug-
gested there the establishment there of a Permanent
Exhibition: where specimens of the manufactures and
products of every country will be collected together in
one spacious building, in order that dealers and con-
sumers from all parts of the world may see them, and
base their orders upon the quality and cost of the arti-
cles exhi,ited.
The project has met with the entire approval of the
Emperor Napoleon 111. and a special license has been
granted by the Ministers of Finance and Commerce for
admission to the Permanent Universal Exhibition,
during the entire period that it is open, of all Foreign
Products, Free of Duty, Ai WI liberty to re-export them
without payment of duties, or to sell them on the spot,
on paying the duties imposed by the new International
Tariff.
'lle whole of the capital, amounting to £600,000, has
been subscribed in France, and the Palace (now in
course of construction) will be opened early in the sum-
mer of 1863.
The amount of space allotted to France and several
other continental countries has al:eady been taken up.
Admission will be gratuitous on at least five days of
the week.
The British Exhibitors will be reyresented by a Com-
mittee of twenty members, who, with those appointed by
other countries will form a General Committee, to
organise the distribution of space, and frame a code of
rules for general observance; and agencies will be este-
blished in Paris to receive Orders.
All products and manufactures will be classified, so
that those of the same nature from different countries,
being placed in ju-xta-position, may be easily compared.
Two rates of rental (payable annually In advance)
will be charged, the space being taken for six years.
The first rate (.£2 per square metre per annum) will
apply to all products and manufactures.
Tne second rate (£1 per square metre per annum)
will apply to wall surface for advertisements.
N.B.—Five square metres are equal to six square
yards.

Railway Stations and Exchanges in London and the
country; in the Refreshment-rooms of the present
London Exhibition; and at the Offices of Messrs. J.
